As a result, it has been combined with mechanical, chemical, and thermal techniques in an attempt to enhance percutaneous delivery 19–21 . Despite early promising reports of the treatment of lateral canthal rhytides ( Fig. 159.2 ) and primary axil- lary hyperhidrosis 22–25 with topical formulations of BoNT-A, to date, no such formulations have been approved by the FDA. For example, in contrast to the effectiveness of injectable daxibotulinumtoxinA 26 , topical daxibotulinumtoxinA gel did not meet primary endpoints for efficacy in a phase III trial. Nonetheless, topical BoNT-A remains a potential approach for the treatment of anatomic areas that are difficult to manage or particularly painful to inject. A Note About Dosing Most of the published information regarding the cosmetic uses of BoNT pertains to the use of onaA, followed in recent years by aboA and incoA. Data are scarce regarding other formulations of BoNT-A. Since most of our experience pertains to the use of onaA, the following discussion (including units and description of techniques) focuses on this formulation specifi- cally. However, a conversion rate of 1 : 1 U may be considered for all 100-U product vials (incoA, Prosigne ® , and Neuronox ® ) and 1 : 2.5 U for aboA. Question: According to this excerpt, what has limited the development of topical BoNT-A formulations for cosmetic use, and what was the outcome of the phase III trial of topical daxibotulinumtoxinA gel?

Percutaneous delivery of topical BoNT-A has been limited by its inability to cross the stratum corneum, requiring combination with mechanical, chemical, or thermal techniques to enhance delivery. Despite early promising reports for lateral canthal rhytides and axillary hyperhidrosis, no topical BoNT-A formulation has been FDA approved; notably, topical daxibotulinumtoxinA gel did not meet primary efficacy endpoints in a phase III trial, in contrast to the effectiveness of the injectable form. [Chapter: 159 Botulinum Toxin, p.3217-3218]

[Excerpt 2 | 113 Melanoma › RISK FACTORS FOR CUTANEOUS MELANOMA › Environmental Risk Factors | p.2431]
and neck. The genomic changes seen in high-CSD melanomas are distinct from those seen in low-CSD melanomas and more clearly illustrate the role of cumulative UV damage in their pathogenesis, as evidenced by their higher mutational burden and more frequent UV signature mutations 2,54 . In comparison, the development of low-CSD melanomas appears largely related to inter- mittent UVR exposure during childhood. Epidemiologic studies in young children have demonstrated a relationship between the frequency and duration of sun exposure and high numbers of melanocytic nevi early in life 55,56 . They also pointed to even moderate sun exposure as sufficient for the induction of nevi in children. The sites of subsequent melanomas often reflect the distribution pattern of melanocytic nevi 57 , with both low-CSD melanomas and acquired nevi commonly harboring BRAF activating mutations 6 . Within acquired nevi, the high frequency of the specific BRAF V600E driver mutation, itself a low-probability event, suggests a high mutational burden is present in melanocytes at a young age 2 . Accumulation of additional UV-induced mutations affecting TERT , CDKN2A , and other key regulatory genes may contribute to eventual melanoma development during middle age 2,4 . It is interesting to note that the BRAF V600E mutation is not itself a UV signature mutation, suggesting a role for indirect UV-related mechanisms or other complex factors in the development of low-CSD melanoma. The unique melanocyte response to UV damage, although not fully characterized, may provide additional explanations for melanoma development at both low- and high-CSD sites. In contrast to keratino- cytes, which undergo apoptosis following severe UV damage, melano- cytes do not undergo apoptosis as readily. Their function is to provide protective melanin to the surviving cells and so they are retained within the epidermis, even with damage that may have been sustained through either frequent, low-intensity UV exposures or infrequent, high- intensity exposures. Subsequently, melanoma can arise in anatomic sites with intermittent sun exposure. Both UVB and UVA radiation are associated with the development of cutaneous melanoma, with UVB believed to be the stronger contributor. Data supporting UVB as a causative factor come from: (1) animal studies in which UVB was shown to induce melanoma in susceptible mice and in xenografted human skin engineered to express melanocytic growth factors 58,59 ; and (2) the fact that there is a higher incidence of cutaneous melanoma in equatorial regions where UVB is most intense. All prescription and over-the-counter medications should be reviewed to identify any that have xerostomia as a side effect. Additional precipitating factors include iron, zinc, folate, and vitamin B 12 deficiencies as well as type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and menopause 114 . Lastly, depression and anxiety are more common in patients with burning mouth syndrome than in pain-free controls 113 . Any underlying disorders should be treated, which may require referral for dental or psychiatric evaluation. In primary burning mouth syndrome, reportedly efficacious treatments include oral tricyclic antidepressants (e.g. amitriptyline, doxepin), topical or low-dose oral clonazepam (start at 0.25 mg and slowly titrate to 1–1.5 mg per day, in 3 divided doses), and gabapentinoids 115 . Antidepressant doses should be low initially and then increased slowly to minimize problematic side effects such as xerostomia and sedation. In case reports and series, successful treatments have included topical antifungal agents (even when cultures were negative), capsaicin, and anesthetics such as lidocaine or dyclonine; in addition, mouthwashes containing various combinations of anesthetics, nystatin, tetracycline, hydrocortisone, and diphenhydramine have been utilized. Cognitive behavioral therapy and α -lipoic acid (600 mg daily) may also improve symptoms 116,117 . Burning scalp syndrome Burning scalp syndrome (scalp dysesthesia) 118,119 presents with diffuse burning pain, pruritus, numbness, or tingling of the scalp without objective findings. Secondary causes such as seborrheic dermatitis, folliculitis, lichen planopilaris, allergic or irritant contact dermatitis, and dermatomyositis should be excluded and treated if present. Burning scalp syndrome is often associated with underlying depression and anxiety. Like other dysesthesias, it can be treated with gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants, and topical capsaicin 118 . Red ear syndrome Patients have intermittent episodes of erythema involving one external ear and less often both ears. The redness can persist for minutes to hours and is associated with burning and/or pain. Triggers include heat, cold, and touch. Clinically, this disorder has been likened to erythromel­ algia and associated with migraine headaches, but the precise etiology remains unclear. One hypothesis is dysregulation of sympathetic outflow, while some patients have evidence of cervical spine disease. Reported treatments include indomethacin and β -blockers as well as therapies used for other regional dysesthesias. The aims are to maintain facial symmetry, preserve muscular functions, and restore the dynamics of the smile. Limb VMs may also benefit from sclerotherapy and resection; however, many are too extensive and invasive for such interventions to be advisable. Use of elastic compression garments helps to reduce swelling and pain in the affected extremity. Treatment with low-molecular-weight heparin can control chronic coagulopathy associated with VMs, especially before surgery and during painful thrombotic events 68,69 . This creates an inflammatory reaction with subsequent fibrosis and shrinkage of the treated cyst; repeated procedures are usually necessary. Question: In primary burning mouth syndrome, what are the reportedly efficacious pharmacologic treatments, and how should low-dose oral clonazepam be titrated?

Reportedly efficacious treatments for primary burning mouth syndrome include oral tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline, doxepin), topical or low-dose oral clonazepam, and gabapentinoids. Oral clonazepam should be started at 0.25 mg and slowly titrated up to 1–1.5 mg per day given in 3 divided doses, and antidepressant doses should be started low and increased slowly to minimize side effects like xerostomia and sedation. Question: How does eosinophilic pustular folliculitis of infancy differ clinically from infantile acropustulosis, and what is the typical age of onset and male-to-female ratio for this condition?

Eosinophilic pustular folliculitis of infancy primarily involves the scalp, frequently develops secondary crusting, and lacks an annular configuration, whereas infantile acropustulosis mainly affects the hands and feet. Disease onset is nearly always before 15 months of age, with a male-to-female ratio of 4:1, and the course is cyclical with recurrences every 1 to 12 weeks. [Chapter: 38 Folliculitis, Follicular Occlusion Tetrad, and Other Follicular Disorders, p.785-786]

Application of 10%–20% TCA with either a saturated gauze pad or sable brush produces erythema and a very light frost within 15 to 45 seconds. The depth of penetration of the peeling solution is related to the number of coats applied. Epidermal protein denaturation results in exfoliation without vesiculation. Jessner’s solution is a combination of keratolytic ingredients that has been used for over 100 years in the treatment of inflammatory and comedonal acne as well as hyperkeratotic skin disorders (see Table 154.4 ). Jessner’s solution has intense keratolytic activity, initially causing loss of corneocyte cohesion within the stratum corneum and subsequently creating intercellular and intracellular edema within the upper epidermis if application is continued 28 . The mode of application for the Jessner’s peel is similar to that of the 10%–20% TCA peel. The clinical endpoint of treatment is erythema with blotchy frosting (when used prior to application of TCA in medium-depth peels) or a more uniform frosting (when used alone for superficial peels). While Jessner’s peel can be used in extrafacial sites, care must be taken to restrict the total amount of peel solution, as salicylic acid is absorbed systemically. Salicylic acid , also referred to as a β -hydroxy acid, is one of the ingredients in Jessner’s solution. It can be used alone for superficial chemical peeling and is a preferred therapy for comedonal acne and inflammatory rosacea as it is lipophilic and concentrates within the pilosebaceous apparatus ( Fig. 154.4 ) 25 . Salicylic acid is quite effective as an adjunctive therapy for both open and closed comedones and for resolving post-acne erythema. Cosmetic Surgery Prior to the initial treatment, the patient must understand that the net effect of repetitive superficial chemical peels never approaches the beneficial effect obtained with a single medium-depth or deep peel. The improvements in cutaneous photoaging following superficial peels are usually subtle because there is little to no effect on the dermis. These peels thus cannot produce an appreciable effect on textural changes such as deep wrinkles and furrows, which originate within the dermis. Nonetheless, their ease of use and minimal downtime makes these “lunchtime” peels rewarding for patients with realistic expectations and are a favorite of busy patients. Superficial peels are best employed in combination with cosmeceutical agents and other minimal- to no-downtime procedures such as botulinum toxin A injec- tions, microneedling, and intense pulsed light treatments. Desired and expected results include a “brightened” skin appearance with a more uniform color and texture. Medium-Depth Chemical Peeling Medium-depth chemical peels consist of controlled damage through the epidermis and into the papillary dermis, with variable extension to the upper reticular dermis. Both medium-depth and deep chemical peels produce epidermal necrosis plus papillary dermal edema and homog- enization with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate within the first several days 15 . Postoperatively, over a period of 3 months, there is increased collagen production with expansion of the papillary dermis and the development of a mid-dermal band of thicker collagen fibers. These changes correlate with the clinical improvement in texture, fine lines, and color observed over time ( Fig. 154.5 ). For many years, 40%–50% TCA was the prototypical medium-depth peeling agent because of its ability to ameliorate fine wrinkles, actinic changes, and “pre-neoplasias”. Question: Why is trichloroacetic acid (TCA) considered unique among chemical peeling agents in terms of how its action is terminated, and why is salicylic acid preferred for treating melasma and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation?

TCA is the only peeling agent that is time-dependent, meaning its action must be stopped by washing it off with water or neutralizing it with 5% sodium bicarbonate after 2 to 4 minutes, rather than self-neutralizing. Salicylic acid is preferred for melasma and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation because it is safer and more effective at reducing epidermal pigment, particularly when combined with a bleaching agent such as hydroquinone and sunscreens. Suat Hoon Tan, Hong Liang Tey and Joel Hua Liang Lim Lipodystrophies 101 SECTION 16 DISORDERS OF SUBCUTANEOUS FAT Clinically, lipodystrophy can be broadly classified into inherited or acquired forms and then further subclassified based on the extent of fat loss, in conjunction with genetic mutations, age of onset, and systemic manifestations ( Fig. 101.1 & Table 101.1 ). Based upon the distribution pattern, lipodystrophy may be subdivided into three major groups: (1) generalized; (2) partial (extensive, but not generalized); and (3) localized (involving an isolated area). Localized lipodystrophy, which may be due to injections of medica- tions or vaccines, pressure, previous surgery, trauma or panniculitis, is the most commonly encountered form. It typically presents as lipoat- rophy but occasionally lipohypertrophy develops, e.g. at sites of insulin injection (see Table 21.22 ). Less often, lipodystrophy associated with antiretroviral therapy (ART) for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection 3 and with administration of immune checkpoint inhibitors are seen. Dermatologists may also play a key role in diagnosing acquired generalized lipodystrophy and its preceding panniculitis. Finally, there are several rare genetic syndromes that will be discussed (see Table 101.1 ). PATHOGENESIS Adipose tissue functions as an endocrine organ via its secretion of hormones and adipocytokines, such as leptin, TNF, interleukin (IL)-6, and adiponectin. Altered expression and activity of these factors play a role in the development of insulin resistance and other metabolic sequelae seen in lipodystrophic syndromes, which are similar to those observed in the metabolic syndrome and obese individuals 4,5 . There appears to be a final common pathway of defective adipocyte triglyceride storage in conditions characterized by fat loss as well as fat excess. This defect can result from impaired triglyceride synthesis due to an enzyme deficiency (e.g. 1-acylglycerol-3-phosphate O -acyltransferase 2), defective adipocyte development caused by mutations in genes critical to adipocyte differentiation (e.g. BSCL2/seipin, PPARG, LMNA ), adipocyte apoptosis, or autoimmune- or drug-mediated adipocyte destruction. These various processes impair normal adipocyte differen- tiation, development, lifespan, and/or function 6 . The destruction or impaired differentiation of adipocytes leads to a cascade of hormonal and metabolic consequences. Adiponectin, the protein product of ADIPOQ , is expressed in and secreted exclu- sively by differentiated adipocytes. It plays a positive role in regulating insulin sensitivity and glucose and lipid homeostasis. Individual ECM macromolecules are usually oligomers composed of one or several polypeptides. Intimate contacts between the subunits are formed by coiled-coil structures, such as the collagen triple helix or supercoiled α -helices comprised of three or more polypeptides. In addition, large matrix macromolecules can be regarded as linear sequences of structural modules that are similar in a large variety of proteins 1 . The modules can be recognized by several cellular receptors, but receptor clustering is determined in a tissue-specific manner, and the response may be different in different tissues. Our knowledge of matrix macromolecules has increased dramati- cally due to advances in molecular genetics and proteomics. Numerous molecules have been characterized and their expression, regulation, tissue specificity, and functions discerned 2 . The assembled ECM struc- tures are generally adhesive, enabling the attachment of tissue-specific cells, leukocytes, tumor cells, and even microorganisms ( Fig. 95.1 ). Through integrin-mediated interactions with cells, matrix molecules control cell proliferation, differentiation, and migration, especially during development and regenerative processes. Without contact with the ECM, many cells undergo a form of apoptosis known as anoikis . Furthermore, the ECM can function as a reservoir of information; certain proteoglycans and proteins bind growth factors (e.g. trans- forming growth factor [TGF]- β ), releasing and activating them as needed to control cellular functions 2 . To date, mutations in > 50 different genes encoding ECM molecules have been found to cause heritable disorders in humans and mice. Question: In evaluating a biopsy suspicious for cutaneous sarcoidosis, does finding polarizable foreign material within the granulomas rule out the diagnosis of sarcoidosis? Explain.

No. Although specimens should be polarized to exclude birefringent foreign material as a causative agent, up to 25% of known sarcoidal granulomas contain foreign material, particularly in lesions on the elbows and knees. Question: In a patient who develops disseminated eczema in the setting of allergic contact dermatitis, what conditions must be included in the differential diagnosis, and what is the mainstay of treatment along with the key measure needed to prevent recurrence or rebound flare?

The differential diagnosis includes other eczemas that can present in a widespread/disseminated fashion—atopic dermatitis, airborne contact dermatitis, textile-related contact dermatitis, photoallergic dermatitis, and eczematous drug eruptions (e.g., calcium channel blockers)—as well as mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome. The mainstay of treatment is topical corticosteroids and systemic antihistamines, with short courses of systemic corticosteroids sometimes required; however, identifying and aggressively treating the inciting dermatosis is necessary to prevent recurrence or a rebound flare. However, since most of these mediators exhibit multiple and sometimes overlapping activities, a strict separation into inflammatory and immunomodulatory cytokines is not possible. Due to structural similarities, some cytokines are grouped into families, e.g. the IL-6 family (IL-6, IL-11, oncostatin M, leukemia inhibitory factor [LIF]), the IL-10 family (IL-10, IL-19, IL-20, IL-22, IL-24, IL-26), or the IL-12 family (IL-12, IL-23, IL-27). Monocytes and Macrophages Monocytes are short-lived mononuclear cells with proinflammatory and regulatory activities. Two main subtypes of monocytes and one interme- diate stage with distinct functions have been described in human blood: classical CD14 ++ CD16 − ; intermediate/transitional CD14 + CD16 + ; and non-classical CD14 dim CD16 ++ 20 . Monocytes are derived from a common myeloid progenitor in the bone marrow, circulate in the bloodstream, and migrate into tissues to respond to inflammation and infection. Within tissue, they can give rise to inflammatory DCs and macrophages whose functions are defined by the tissue environment and tissue type 21 . Although residing in different niches, these cell types have similar functions: phagocytosis, antigen presentation to T cells, and production of cytokines. Monocyte-derived macrophages express receptors for carbohydrates that are usually not expressed on vertebrate cells (e.g. mannose). Through this mechanism, macrophages can discriminate between “foreign” and “self” molecules. Furthermore, macrophages possess receptors for antibodies and complement. Hence, microorganisms that are coated with antibodies and/or complement are more readily phagocy- tosed 22 . After phagocytosis, the microorganisms are exposed to a variety of toxic intracellular molecules, including superoxide anions, hydroxyl radicals, hypochlorous acid, nitric oxide, lysozyme, and antimicrobial cationic proteins. Macrophages can also present processed antigens to T and B cells. However, their T cell stimulatory capacity is less effective than that of DCs. Question: Describe how alkalis cause skin damage and explain how the resulting appearance and mechanism differ from typical acid burns.

Alkalis disrupt barrier lipids and denature proteins, causing fatty acid saponification that leads to cellular edema and cytotoxicity; the soaps formed also emulsify tissue, facilitating deeper penetration of the alkali. Unlike typical acid burns, alkali/base injuries are often more painful and severe (except for hydrofluoric acid), and they generally produce no vesicles—instead the skin becomes necrotic, first dark brown, then black, and ultimately hard, dry, and cracked. Question: According to the excerpt, what is the stratum corneum 'reservoir,' and how does its volume change between baseline conditions and states of hydration or topical agent application?

Question: According to Winter's studies, why do uncovered, air-dried wounds re-epithelialize more slowly than wounds kept in a moist environment?

In air-dried wounds, a crust and other dry fibrous tissue form over the wound, and the regenerating epidermis must migrate beneath this crust to reach a region of moisture where live cells can survive. Epidermal cells can only move to bridge the wound defect within such a moist environment, so the thicker the crust, the slower the re-epithelialization. [Chapter: 145 Dressings, p.2988]

The condition was characterized by severe purulent conjunctivitis, severe stomatitis with extensive mucosal necrosis, and “EM-like” cutaneous lesions. It became known as Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS) and was recognized as a severe mucocutaneous disease with a prolonged course and occa- sional fatalities 2,3 . SJS was later designated as EM major by Bernard Thomas in 1950. 6 However, recent clinical investigations have made it clear that the term “EM major” should not be used to describe SJS as they are distinct disorders (see Table 20.1 ) 2,3 . In 1956, Alan Lyell described four patients with an eruption “resem- bling scalding of the skin objectively and subjectively”, which he called “toxic epidermal necrolysis”. “Toxic” referred to toxemia – circulation of a toxin – which was thought to be responsible for the constitutional symptoms and epidermal necrosis. Lyell coined the term “necrolysis” by combining the key clinical feature “epidermolysis” with the charac- teristic histopathologic feature “necrosis”. He also described an attack on the mucous membranes as part of the syndrome, and noted that there was very little inflammation in the dermis, a feature that was later referred to as “dermal silence” 34 . This feature contrasted with the obvious inflammatory infiltrate of other blistering disorders such as EM, dermatitis herpetiformis, and bullous pemphigoid. TEN was considered at the time to be a cutaneous reaction pattern to multi- ple stimuli, including drugs (e.g. sulfonamides) and microbes (e.g. Staphylococcus ) 35 . The description of a subgranular epidermal split in neonatal mice fol- lowing exposure to phage group II S. aureus , the subsequent discovery of a new staphylococcal exotoxin called epidermolytic toxin, and the absence of overt keratinocyte necrosis led to the distinction between TEN and what would come to be known as “staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome” (SSSS; see Ch. 74 ) 36 . It should be noted here that one of Lyell’s original patients actually represented SSSS, and although by that time he had already noted the histologic differences between TEN and SSSS, they were attributed to different degrees of injury. As more patients with TEN were reported in the years following Lyell’s treatise, it became clear that certain drugs such as sulfon- amides, pyrazolones (e.g. phenylbutazone), barbiturates, and aromatic anticonvulsants were principally associated with TEN. Question: According to the historical background in this excerpt, what did Alan Lyell mean by the terms 'toxic' and 'necrolysis' when he coined 'toxic epidermal necrolysis' in 1956, and what distinctive dermal feature did he note that contrasted with disorders like EM, dermatitis herpetiformis, and bullous pemphigoid?

Lyell used 'toxic' to refer to toxemia—the circulation of a toxin thought to cause the constitutional symptoms and epidermal necrosis—and coined 'necrolysis' by combining the clinical feature 'epidermolysis' with the histopathologic feature 'necrosis.' He also observed that there was very little dermal inflammation, a feature later termed 'dermal silence,' which contrasted with the obvious inflammatory infiltrate seen in EM, dermatitis herpetiformis, and bullous pemphigoid. SKIN STEM CELLS Stem cells are present in each self-renewing tissue and are responsible for maintaining and repairing the tissue in which they reside. Stem cells often reside in a protective niche microenvironment that provides necessary signaling factors. During periods of homeostasis, stem cells generally divide very infrequently, a feature believed to protect them from acquiring mutations during cell cycle progression. After an injury, however, stem cells can divide more rapidly as part of wound healing. One distinguishing characteristic of stem cells is that they can be maintained in culture virtually indefinitely. For example, a subset of epidermal basal cells forms highly proliferative colonies that can be passaged long-term in vitro ; referred to as holoclones, they presumably represent stem cells 25 . Holoclones can reconstitute epidermis in vitro , and they have been utilized as skin grafts for the treatment of burns and inherited skin disorders (see below). Question: What is basal cell nevus (Gorlin) syndrome caused by, and how does this explain the range of clinical findings seen in affected patients?

Basal cell nevus (Gorlin) syndrome is caused by mutations in the PTCH tumor suppressor gene, which lead to overactivation of the sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling pathway. Because SHH signaling has important roles in neurologic and anterior–posterior axis development as well as hair follicle formation, its dysregulation explains the broad range of developmental anomalies seen in this syndrome, including craniofacial and skeletal defects, along with a propensity for medulloblastomas, odontogenic keratocysts, and multiple basal cell carcinomas. Question: In blisters that develop within healed burn wounds or skin graft sites weeks after healing, what do DIF studies and immunofluorescence mapping show, and how is this consistent with the hypothesized pathogenesis?

DIF studies are negative, ruling out an autoimmune bullous process, while immunofluorescence mapping shows diminished or variable expression of dermal–epidermal junction antigens such as type IV and type VII collagens, laminin, and bullous pemphigoid antigen. This supports the hypothesis that the blistering results from the enhanced fragility of a newly synthesized, "immature" dermal–epidermal junction that forms during wound healing, rather than an immune-mediated mechanism. Local Recurrences It is critical to understand the biologic differences between local recur- rence from inadequate excision of the primary tumor (termed persistent disease-type or “true” local recurrence) from that due to lymphatic metas- tasis in or around the scar (termed satellitosis ). Persistent disease-type local recurrence abuts the surgical excision scar, is histologically defined by in situ and/or radial growth phase, and should be surgically managed according to Breslow thickness of the recurrence ( Fig. 113.28A ). Local satellite recurrence is an intralymphatic recurrence within or adjacent ( ≤ 2 cm) to the excision scar, although AJCC-8 recognizes this distance as arbitrary, since satellite and in-transit (lymphatic) metastases have similar survival outcomes ( Fig. 113.29 ) 169 . Importantly, local satellite recurrence reclassifies the melanoma as stage III, prompting staging via imaging, referral for WLE and possible SLNB, and discussion of adjuvant therapy. Melanomas with a higher frequency of subclinical extension, e.g. acral lentiginous, LM, are at higher risk of persistent disease-type local recurrence ( Figs. 113.28A-C & 113.30 ), whereas melanomas that are thicker, ulcerated, have a higher mitotic rate, and/or lymphovascular invasion are at increased risk of metastatic local recurrence (satellites) despite prior adequate surgical margins. Thick desmoplastic melanomas with “pure” desmoplastic histology, extensive perineural invasion/­ neurotropism, and/or head and neck location may exhibit either type of local recurrence ( Fig. 113.28D ) and thus are sometimes considered for adjuvant radiation therapy following initial resection. Satellitosis presents as one or more indurated papulonodules within or immediately surrounding the melanoma scar (generally within 2 cm) and is strongly associated with the development of in-transit, regional, and distant metastases. As noted previously, satellite recurrence reclas- sifies the melanoma as stage III, with consideration of subsequent systemic therapy. There is no evidence that patient survival is adversely affected if local recurrence results from incomplete excision of the primary melanoma (i.e. persistent disease), provided that the recurrent in situ and/or radial growth phase tumor is promptly re-excised and there is no evidence of nodal or distant disease. Local recurrences of melanoma, particularly the persistent disease- type, can occur several years (rarely decades) after excision of the primary lesion. When a lesion previously diagnosed histologically as a melanocytic nevus recurs locally more than two years after removal, re-evaluation for possible melanoma should be considered. Question: How do 'persistent disease-type' local recurrence and 'satellite' local recurrence of melanoma differ in terms of biologic mechanism, histology, and clinical/staging implications?

Persistent disease-type ("true") local recurrence arises from inadequate excision of the primary tumor, abuts the surgical scar, and is histologically defined by in situ and/or radial growth phase disease; it is managed by re-excision according to the Breslow thickness of the recurrence and does not worsen survival if promptly excised with no nodal/distant disease. Satellitosis, in contrast, results from intralymphatic (lymphatic) metastasis within or near (~≤2 cm of) the scar, presenting as indurated papulonodules, and reclassifies the melanoma as stage III—prompting imaging, wide local excision with possible sentinel lymph node biopsy, and discussion of adjuvant/systemic therapy due to its strong association with in-transit, regional, and distant metastases. Question: In HIV-infected patients, what immunologic parameters have been associated with pruritus, and what treatment options are available for their pruritic symptoms?

Pruritus in HIV infection has been associated with markedly elevated IgE levels, peripheral hypereosinophilia, and a Th2-type cytokine profile, and has also been correlated with increased HIV viral load. Question: Why is ring block anesthesia practical for the scalp but not for the eyelid, and what additional step is recommended to achieve hemostasis at the incision site when using a ring block?

Ring block anesthesia works by injecting a ring of anesthetic around the surgical site, which is effective in areas where innervation arrives horizontally through the skin, as on the scalp, but not in areas like the eyelid where innervation arrives vertically from deeper tissues. Because a ring block achieves anesthesia but not hemostasis at the incision site, it is recommended to add intradermal anesthetic with epinephrine at the proposed incision site. Several case reports and small series have described atypical fractures of the subtrochanteric or diaphyseal femur in patients receiving long-term bisphosphonate therapy, but larger studies have demonstrated a very low absolute risk 23,24 . All bisphospho- nates, especially those with long half-lives (e.g. ibandronate), should be avoided in premenopausal women who might become pregnant, as these agents cross the placenta and produce teratogenicity, including fetal skeletal abnormalities. Furthermore, bisphosphonates should not be administered to patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of < 35 ml/minute. Several other agents that can reduce bone resorption or increase bone formation represent options to prevent and treat glucocorticoid- induced osteoporosis in high-risk patients or those who do not tolerate bisphosphonates. Teriparatide (a fragment of human parathyroid hormone [PTH]) and abaloparatide (a PTH-related protein analogue) are additional options that increase bone formation. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody directed against RANKL (receptor activator of NF- κ B ligand) that blocks osteoclast maturation and thereby leads to decreased bone resorption. Question: For a patient with an eGFR of 30 ml/minute who requires treatment for glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis and cannot tolerate bisphosphonates, why might denosumab be a suitable option, and what are its potential side effects?

Denosumab, a monoclonal antibody against RANKL that decreases bone resorption by blocking osteoclast maturation, is not cleared by the kidney, so it can be used safely in patients with an eGFR < 35 ml/minute, unlike bisphosphonates which should not be given at this eGFR level. Potential side effects include hypocalcemia, dermatitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw, increased risk of infections, and fetal harm. Because stopping denosumab can lead to rapid bone loss and increased fracture risk, sequential therapy with a bisphosphonate for at least one year is recommended afterward. Poroma can be a proliferation of either apocrine or eccrine lineage 83–85 . Eccrine and apocrine poromas probably occur in nearly equal numbers. The term acrospiroma is used by some authorities as a synonym for poroma and is used by other authorities as a broad designation that encompasses both poroma and hidradenoma. Clinical features Poromas usually present as solitary papules, plaques, or nodules ( Fig. 111.26 ) 4 . When sessile vascular plaques surrounded by thin indented moats appear on the palms and soles, an astute dermatologist can strongly suspect the diagnosis. They can appear on any cutaneous surface, where they are less readily identified with specificity. The scalp is another common site, with or without an associated nevus sebaceus 18 . Presumably, poromas arising secondarily within nevus sebaceus represent apocrine poromas. Occasionally, a poroma will be pigmented. Poromas commonly display highly vascularized stroma, and a clinical pattern suggestive of pyogenic granuloma is common, especially in poromas that involve acral skin. Rarely, multiple poromas will develop, either in an acral or in a widespread distribution, a clinical pattern referred to as poromatosis. Poromatosis can occur following chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy. Up to 90% of sporadic poromas contain YAP1 - MAML2 and YAP1- NUTM1 fusion genes that can lead to tumorigenesis presumably via transactivation of the transcription factor TEAD 86 . NUT immunohistochemical staining may be used to differentiate poroid neoplasms with NUTM1 fusions from other types of adnexal tumors 86a . Clinical Features Bowel-associated dermatosis–arthritis syndrome is characterized clini- cally by constitutional flu-like symptoms, skin lesions 57 , and a variety of systemic complications (see below). It can occur from 1 to 6 years after the responsible bowel surgery. Constitutional symptoms, which are usually present and may precede the cutaneous eruption, are similar to those of serum sickness, e.g. fever, chills, malaise, arthralgias and myalgias. The characteristic skin lesions are erythematous macules which progress to papules and purpuric vesiculopustules within 48 hours and last for 2–4 weeks; they may recur at 4- to 6-week intervals. The lesions may be few or many ( Fig. 25.17 ), and they favor the proximal extremi- ties and trunk. Recurrent, tender, erythematous subcutaneous nodules are also seen in these patients and may be associated with fever. They are due to either a nodular, non-suppurative, lobular neutrophilic panniculitis (involving both the trunk and extremities and healing with depressed scars) or erythema nodosum (generally involving only the lower extrem- ities), two entities which differ clinically and histologically 58 . Question: How does kwashiorkor differ from marasmus in terms of body weight, characteristic edema finding, and skin desquamation pattern, and what is the current theory about its pathogenesis?

Unlike marasmus, kwashiorkor (severe acute malnutrition with edema) presents with peripheral edema or even anasarca due to hypoalbuminemia, resulting in a body weight that is higher than in marasmus—about 60%–80% of expected weight rather than less than 40%. Skin findings include desquamation and erosions likened to "enamel paint" and "flaky paint." While kwashiorkor was traditionally attributed to relative protein deficiency, this has been questioned because protein intake was similar in children with marasmus versus kwashiorkor, and kwashiorkor can develop within weeks of an acute illness; the current theory is that it relates to physiologic stress from acute or chronic illness, including infections. Question: According to the therapeutic approach to pseudofolliculitis barbae, what is the only reliable way to cure the disease, and what should patients with severe disease do regarding shaving?

The only reliable cure for pseudofolliculitis barbae is to stop shaving altogether. For patients with severe disease, a hiatus of several months without shaving is recommended, discontinuing shaving until all inflammatory lesions have cleared and ingrown hairs are released; during this period the beard can be trimmed to a minimum length of 5 mm using scissors or electric clippers. Question: In trichothiodystrophy (TTD), TFIIH defects impair transcription-coupled NER, yet affected individuals do not show increased carcinogenesis like patients with xeroderma pigmentosum (XP). Why is this the case, and how does the mechanism of cell damage differ in Cockayne syndrome?

In TTD, TFIIH retains residual NER function, so global genome NER (which is critical for repairing UV-induced DNA damage and preventing cancer) is not profoundly impaired, unlike in XP where TFIIH defects severely impair global genome NER and lead to carcinogenesis. In Cockayne syndrome, the abnormal transcription-coupled NER instead causes apoptosis of metabolically active cells such as neurons, rather than promoting carcinogenesis. Question: What is the inheritance pattern of epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV), which two genes are typically mutated in this disease, and which HPV types are mainly detected in EV-associated skin cancers?

Epidermodysplasia verruciformis typically follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance and is caused by truncating mutations in the TMC6 (EVER1) and TMC8 (EVER2) genes. Although about two dozen specific HPV types (all in the beta genus) have been described in EV patients, mainly HPV types 5 and 8 are detected in EV-associated skin cancers. Question: What are the two vasculitis-relevant ANCA immunofluorescent staining patterns, and what specific antigens do they target?

By immunofluorescent staining, there are two vasculitis-relevant ANCA patterns: cytoplasmic (c)-ANCAs, which are directed against proteinase 3 (PR3), and perinuclear (p)-ANCAs, which are directed against myeloperoxidase (MPO). Aquagenic pruritus presents with prickling, tingling, burning, or stinging sensations within 30 minutes of water contact, irrespective of its temperature or salinity, and lasts for up to 2 hours 1 . Typically, symptoms begin on the lower extremities and then generalize, with sparing of the head, palms, soles, and mucosae 49 ; on examination, specific skin lesions are not seen. The pathologic mechanism is unknown, although elevated dermal and epidermal levels of acetylcholine, histamine, serotonin, and prostaglandin E 2 have been described 1 . Treatment of aquagenic pruritus is difficult. Aspirin (300–500 mg daily) was of benefit in one RCT. Treatment with narrowband or broadband UVB or PUVA may also be effective. Singlet oxygen is a highly reactive form of oxygen that can induce cellular necrosis and/or apoptosis while modulating a variety of biologic processes. During the latter part of the twentieth century, PDT was synonymous with the use of systemic photosensitizers in combination with red laser light to treat cancers. Question: In current dermatologic PDT practice, what type of photosensitizing agent is applied topically, how is it converted to an active form, and what light sources may be used to activate it?

The current standard technique involves topically applying pro-photosensitizers, such as aminolevulinic acid and its derivatives, which are metabolized in situ within the skin into the photoactive compound protoporphyrin IX. This photosensitizer is then activated using non-coherent artificial light (blue or red), daylight, or other light sources to illuminate the treated skin. [Chapter: 135 Photodynamic Therapy, p.2851]

Treatment choice is influenced by tumor type and size, anatomic location, the patient's life expectancy, presence of comorbidities, and cosmetic concerns. For most solitary, benign, or relatively non-aggressive malignant neoplasms, excisional surgery with clear margins is the treatment of choice, though other modalities like cryotherapy, laser ablation, or liposuction may be preferred in certain cases. The earliest manifestations of CGD are usually staphylococcal infec- tions of the skin around the ears and nose, which may begin in the neonatal period and progress to extensive purulent dermatitis with regional lymphadenopathy during infancy. Initial presentation of CGD as ecthyma gangrenosum in the neonatal period has also been described 70 . Cutaneous abscesses occur in 40% of patients, usually due to S. aureus but also Serratia marcescens ; these infections sometimes present as large, poorly healing cutaneous ulcers 71 . Non-infectious purulent inflammatory reactions may develop at sites of minor cutaneous trauma or regional lymph node drainage and heal slowly with scarring. Sterile cutaneous granulomas, which are often nodular and necrotic, occur less frequently than infections. Additional cutaneous manifestations include acute or chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus-like skin lesions, most commonly discoid 72 ( Fig. 60.7A,B ); Sweet syndrome-like lesions; ulcers involving the oral mucosa (resembling aphthous stomatitis), the perioral area, and other cutaneous sites ( Fig. 60.7C ); and seborrheic dermatitis or folliculitis of the scalp. Female carriers of X-linked CGD occasionally present with discoid lesions, lymphocytic infiltrate of Jessner, photosensitivity, Raynaud phenomenon, severe aphthous stomatitis, and granulomatous cheilitis. The extracutaneous organs most frequently involved in CGD are the lymph nodes, lungs, liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract ( Table 60.12 ). Suppurative lymphadenitis develops in half of patients, most often affecting cervical nodes and leading to abscess and fistula formation. Granulomas of the lungs, liver, spleen, and gastrointes- tinal and genitourinary tracts occur more frequently than those of the skin. Excessive inflammatory responses may also lead to wound dehiscence, pneumonitis, and hemophagocytic lymphohistio- cytosis. Approximately 40%–80% of CGD patients develop gastroin- testinal manifestations (e.g. chronic diarrhea, fistulas) similar to those of inflammatory bowel disease; clinical presentations can also mimic sarcoidosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and IgA nephropathy 62,73,74 . UVB and PUVA in HIV-Infected Patients Treatment of psoriasis with oral PUVA has not induced progression of HIV disease nor was there an increase in side effects. PUVA for Atopic Dermatitis (See Ch. 12 ) Many patients with moderate, severe, and even erythrodermic forms of atopic eczema can benefit from PUVA therapy 53 . The treatment guide- lines are essentially the same as for psoriasis, but patients may develop a temporary flare of their dermatitis during the initial treatment phase. Although atopic dermatitis may be cleared by PUVA, recurrence rates are high and rapid, requiring frequent maintenance exposures. However, in young patients, long-term mainte- nance therapy should be avoided. A combination of PUVA with topical corticosteroids appears to be superior to PUVA alone in maintaining remissions, and in a more recent study involving patients with severe atopic dermatitis, PUVA provided better short- and long-term responses than did medium-dose UVA1. Question: Cheiralgia paresthetica and digitalgia paresthetica both result from what general mechanism, and what specific examples of causative exposures are given for each?

Both cheiralgia paresthetica and digitalgia paresthetica are sensory mononeuropathies caused by trauma or pressure to peripheral nerves. Cheiralgia paresthetica, affecting the superficial branch of the radial nerve, can result from pressure such as a tight wristwatch or handcuffs. Digitalgia paresthetica, affecting the digital nerves of the fingers and toes, can result from trauma such as carrying heavy plastic grocery bags (fingers) or long marches or hikes (toes). Question: How do humans typically acquire gnathostomiasis, and what is the classic cutaneous presentation along with its associated laboratory finding?

Humans acquire gnathostomiasis by eating raw freshwater fish (or eels, frogs, birds, or reptiles) that serve as intermediate hosts harboring third-stage Gnathostoma larvae. After ingestion, the larva penetrates the gastrointestinal mucosa and migrates to the peritoneal cavity and then subcutaneous tissues and internal organs, producing cutaneous manifestations 2–4 weeks after ingestion. The classic presentation is a migratory panniculitis characterized by a single, deep-seated, pruritic or tender inflammatory lesion, often accompanied by peripheral eosinophilia. Question: In the FANA test, what cell substrate is commonly used, how are bound autoantibodies detected, and what titer is considered a positive result?

Question: In the 2023 WHO classification (5th revision) and 2022 ICC of mature lymphoid neoplasms, what specific change was introduced compared to the 2018 WHO-EORTC classification, and what is recommended regarding skin biopsies when diagnosing suspected CTCL?

The main change in the 2023 WHO classification and 2022 ICC was reclassifying primary cutaneous acral CD8-positive T cell lymphoma as a lymphoproliferative disorder rather than a lymphoma. For diagnosis, deep punch biopsies (4–6 mm wide) or excisional/incisional biopsies from the most representative skin lesions are preferred, and in the US broad shave (tangential) biopsies are also used for suspected patch/plaque stage MF; biopsies should be taken from untreated skin since prior topical corticosteroids or phototherapy can markedly alter histology. Question: According to the excerpt, why is systemic exposure expected to be low in nursing infants for large-molecule biologic drugs such as omalizumab, etanercept, and adalimumab, even though these agents are excreted in breast milk?

These biologics are large molecules that are largely degraded in the infant's gastrointestinal tract, which limits their systemic absorption despite being present in breast milk in low amounts. For example, omalizumab is described as a large molecule likely destroyed in the infant's GI tract, and similar reasoning (large molecular weight leading to minimal absorption) is given for etanercept and adalimumab. This is why these drugs are generally considered to have low expected systemic exposure in breastfeeding infants, though caution is still advised due to limited safety data. Salmonellosis Salmonellosis refers to the spectrum of infections caused by Gram-negative aerobic bacilli in the genus Salmonella . Resultant forms of enteric fever include typhoid fever due to S. typhi and paratyphoid fever due to S. paratyphi . S. typhi is spread via direct contact with persons who have typhoid fever or are chronic carriers. In contrast, paratyphoid fever is most commonly acquired from inadequately cooked poultry or eggs as well as other contaminated food products or water, resulting in gastroenteritis. Typhoid fever is characterized by fever, headache, malaise, myalgias, cough, sore throat, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea or constipation. The characteristic cutaneous sign, “rose spots”, are pink, blanching, slightly elevated papules that measure 2–8 mm and are usually found on the anterior trunk in groups of 5–15 lesions. They occur in up to 30% of patients with typhoid fever and less often in non-typhoidal enteric fever. Rose spots often occur in crops during the second to fourth weeks of the illness, and Salmonella spp. can usually be cultured from these lesions. Other cutaneous manifestations of salmonellosis include erythema multiforme, Sweet syndrome, hemorrhagic bullae, pustular dermatitis, and a generalized erythematous eruption known as erythema typhosum. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis represents a rare complication of salmonellosis 120 . A history of travel to endemic areas (e.g. Southeast Asia, Africa), persistence of fevers, and positive cultures aid in distinguishing typhoid fever from influenza and other viral infections. Culture of Salmonella spp. from the bone marrow is the most sensitive diagnostic procedure but is rarely used in clinical practice. Blood cultures are less sensitive and PCR-based detection is limited by the low concentrations of microbial DNA in clinical samples. Since the late 1980s, S. typhi has developed resistance to the drugs that were previously used as first-line treatments (e.g. chloramphenicol, TMP-SMX, and ampicillin). Current treatment options include azithromycin, carbapenems, and (depending on resis- tance patterns) quinolones and third-generation cephalosporins 121 . Typhoid conjugate vaccines are available and are recommended for travelers to endemic areas. Though fairly common, patients rarely present with this transient, erythematous, pruritic papular or urticarial eruption at the site of inoculation. The reaction is relatively nonspecific and is more severe with S. japonicum and S. mansoni infections. Within hours of contact, macules develop and then either disappear or, more commonly, are replaced by small pruritic papules that may persist for a few days 125 . In some patients, a systemic allergic reaction ( Katayama fever ) occurs during the acute phase of a moderate or heavy infection. Affected individuals have an acute onset of fever, chills, sweats and headaches, in association with peripheral blood eosinophilia and urticaria. Katayama fever is seen most commonly with S. japonicum infections and is due to circulating immune complexes. How inflam- mation impairs healing is still not well understood, but increased protease activity (e.g. metalloproteinases [MMPs], serine proteinases) and generation of reactive oxygen species are thought to play a major role. Unraveling the underlying molecular pathophysiology of chronic wounds in humans will clearly involve studies of both regeneration and repair. IMPACT OF WOUND DEPTH ON WOUND HEALING In clinical practice, skin wounds are often categorized according to their depth ( Fig. 141.2 ). Defects that affect only the epidermis (or a portion of the epidermis) are referred to as erosions . When the wound extends into the dermis, it is termed an ulceration . In “ partial-thickness ” wounds, the epidermis and papillary dermis are missing, with the ulcer extending into the mid dermis, but the adnexal structures remain. Full-thickness wounds, on the other hand, involve the entire dermis and extend into the subcutaneous fat. As a result, adnexal structures are lost as a source of keratinocytes for re-epithelialization. The depth of a skin injury affects the capacity of the skin to repair or regenerate (see Fig. 141.2 ). When erosions heal, there is regeneration of the entire epidermis without scarring. Ulcerations, however, heal via a reparative process and are associated with scar formation. In partial- thickness wounds, the preserved adnexal structures serve as a source of epithelial cells to repopulate the epidermis. Epithelia from these structures, as well as from the wound edge, migrate across the wound surface to provide coverage. In contrast, re-epithelialization can only occur from the wound edges in full-thickness wounds because adnexal structures are lost. Healing of full-thickness wounds includes, to some extent, contraction whereas in partial-thickness wounds contraction is minimal. Contraction may be mediated by mechanical or biologic factors, e.g. the differentiation of fibroblasts into myofibroblasts. More recent studies in mice suggest that the contributions of different stem cell sources for wound fibroblasts may determine the outcome of the repair response. These include a superficial cell population that is critical for hair development and a deeper cell population that forms the lower dermis and may provide a source of locally derived wound fibroblasts that can develop into myofibroblasts 17 . Question: How does the depth of a skin wound (erosion vs. partial-thickness vs. full-thickness ulceration) determine the source of re-epithelialization and the presence of scarring or contraction during healing?

Erosions involve only the epidermis and heal by regeneration of the entire epidermis without scarring. Partial-thickness wounds extend into the mid dermis but preserve adnexal structures, so re-epithelialization occurs from both these adnexal epithelial sources and the wound edges, with minimal contraction; these wounds heal via a reparative process with scar formation. Full-thickness wounds destroy the entire dermis and adnexal structures, so re-epithelialization can only occur from the wound edges, and healing includes contraction, mediated in part by fibroblast differentiation into myofibroblasts. In adult-onset mastocytosis, the most common lesions are small (<1 cm), monomorphic, reddish-brown macules and papules, historically called urticaria pigmentosa but now termed maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis. Question: In the evaluation of a scalp lesion with a positive hair collar sign, what is the recommended imaging workup, and why might both CT and MRI be needed?

The workup begins with CT, which is the most accurate method for detecting skull defects. If CT reveals a bony defect, follow-up MRI is recommended to determine whether there is transcranial extension of soft tissue (e.g., herniation of brain or meninges/CSF) versus no transcranial connection. This distinction guides management, ranging from neurosurgical repair (if a transcranial stalk is present) to biopsy/excision or clinical/radiographic monitoring (if no transcranial connection or if consistent with membranous aplasia cutis). Inflammation A critical role of inflammation is to deliver neutrophils and other leu- kocytes to a site of injury and then activate these cells to perform their function of protecting the host against infection. Neutrophils are among the first cells to arrive at sites of inflammation. Reasons for this include their abundance in the bloodstream and their rapid response to chemo- kines. When activated, neutrophils move at speeds up to 30 microns/ min – the fastest cell in the body. The motile responses of neutrophils to microbial infection include emigration out of the vasculature and movement toward the source of the inflammatory chemoattractant. This culminates in the phagocytic ingestion of opsonized microbes. In order to arrive at the site of infec- tion, leukocytes must migrate out of the vasculature via margination, rolling, activation, and tight adhesion (see Ch. 102 ). They then move toward the site of injury or infection (see Table 25.1 ) and eventually undergo degranulation then apoptosis. The price to be paid for the defensive potency of neutrophils for destroy- ing microbes and necrotic tissues is that they can injure normal tissue. During activation and phagocytosis, neutrophils release products (e.g. lysosomal enzymes, reactive oxygen intermediates, products of arachi- donic acid metabolism [prostaglandins and leukotrienes]) not just within Neutrophilic Dermatoses the phagolysosome, but also into the extracellular space. Endothelial injury and tissue damage ensue, thus contributing to a number of acute and chronic diseases that affect the skin as well as other organs. Question: Using the ALT-70 cellulitis predictive model, what four criteria are scored, and what does a total score of ≥5 indicate?

The ALT-70 score is calculated from four criteria: Asymmetry (unilateral lower extremity involvement), Leukocytosis (WBC ≥10,000/mcl), Tachycardia (heart rate ≥90 bpm), and Age ≥70 years. A total score of ≥5 favors a diagnosis of true cellulitis, whereas 0–2 favors "pseudocellulitis" and 3–4 suggests dermatology consultation may be beneficial. Question: According to the Oslo Study of untreated syphilis (1890–1910, with 50-year follow-up), what proportion of infected men and women died as a result of the infection, and what percentage developed benign tertiary syphilis with gummas?

The Oslo Study found that 17% of men and 8% of women died as a result of untreated syphilis. Question: In UVB phototherapy for vitiligo, how should the minimal erythema dose (MED) be assessed, what percentage of the MED is used as the initial treatment dose, and what endpoint should guide subsequent dose increases?

The MED should be assessed in a normally sun-protected, vitiliginous area (e.g., buttocks, lower back, or abdomen) rather than in habitually sun-exposed skin. The initial therapeutic dose is 70% of the MED determined in lesional skin. Subsequent dose increases (no more than once weekly, by 5%–20% of the preceding dose) should be guided solely by the presence of a barely perceptible, light pink erythema in the vitiligo areas, as this faint erythema is the only useful parameter for titrating dosage. Question: In cryosurgery, what is the key difference between the semi-open (confined spray/cone) technique and the standard open (spray) technique in terms of freezing rate and effect on surrounding skin?

In the semi-open (confined spray, cone) technique, liquid nitrogen is confined to the lesion using a cone, which produces a faster freezing rate and spares the surrounding normal skin. This contrasts with the open (spray) technique, which allows for superficial or deep freezing depending on application time but does not confine the spray to the lesion. Question: How can cutaneous PNETs in adults be distinguished clinically and immunohistochemically from cutaneous metastatic neuroblastoma in children?

Clinically, PNETs in adults present as rapidly growing, often ulcerated dermal or subcutaneous nodules on the trunk or head with an almost invariably fatal outcome, whereas neuroblastoma metastases in children appear as multiple blue-purple 'blueberry muffin' papules/nodules that may blanch and develop an erythematous halo, with elevated serum/urine catecholamines and even spontaneous regression possible in stage IV-S disease. Histologically, PNETs resemble classic neuroblastoma but lack ganglionic or neuromatous differentiation. Immunohistochemically, MIC-2 (O13) is commonly expressed by PNETs but not by neuroblastomas, helping differentiate the two. Question: In erythema ab igne (EAI), what is the typical clinical evolution of skin lesions with recurrent heat exposure, and what is the most serious long-term complication, including which type of heat exposure carries the highest risk?

EAI begins as transient, blanchable macular erythema in a broad reticulated pattern resembling the shape of the heat source. With recurrent exposure, this evolves into fixed, non-blanchable dusky hyperpigmentation, sometimes with overlying epidermal atrophy, and later-stage lesions may become keratotic with bullae; lesions are usually asymptomatic aside from occasional slight burning. The major long-term risk is development of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (or less commonly Merkel cell carcinoma) after a latent period of 30 years or more, with the highest SCC risk occurring after hydrocarbon-fueled heat exposure such as peat fires, coal-fired clothing warmers, and coal-heated Kang beds. Question: How does melanoma risk differ in its relationship to nevus count between common melanocytic nevi and clinically atypical/dysplastic melanocytic nevi?

Melanoma risk increases in an almost linear, continuous fashion as the number of common melanocytic nevi increases, making common nevus counts useful as risk indicators. Question: How does Legius syndrome differ clinically from NF1 despite both presenting with multiple café-au-lait macules, and what gene is mutated in Legius syndrome?

Legius syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition with six or more café-au-lait macules in >80% of patients and intertriginous "freckling" in ~50%, but unlike NF1, patients lack neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic pathway gliomas, and the typical osseous lesions of NF1. Macrocephaly and learning disabilities are common, and a minority have lipomas, hypopigmented macules, and vascular anomalies. It is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SPRED1 gene, whose protein product normally inhibits MAPK signaling. [Chapter: 61 Neurofibromatosis and Tuberous Sclerosis Complex, p.1213-1214]

Histamine plays a primary role in the pruritus of urticaria, and H1-receptor antagonists usually decrease or eliminate this sensation as well as the wheals themselves 10 . Several other mediators are involved in the pathophysiology of urticaria, and interleukin (IL)-31 levels correlate with itch intensity 11 . Atopic dermatitis Pruritus is such an important aspect of atopic dermatitis that “the diagnosis of active atopic dermatitis cannot be made if there is no history of pruritus” 12 (see Ch. 12 ). The itch sensation typically comes in “attacks”, which may be severe and significantly impact quality of life 13 . Often, pruritus is the first indication of a disease flare. Moreover, scratching as a response to itch leads to excoriations and lichenification, which represent additional clinical features of atopic dermatitis 14 . Pruritus can be provoked by exposure to aeroallergens or ingestion of foods to which the patient is sensitized as well as non-immunologic triggers, including emotional stress, overheating, perspiration, and contact with rough fabrics or even air (atmokinesis) 15 ( Fig. 6.4 ). Although most affected children experience worsening of symptoms during the winter, others have exacerbations primarily during the summer 16 . The minimal effectiveness of antihistamines in alleviating the itch of atopic dermatitis indicates that histamine is probably not the predom- inant mediator of the pruritic sensation 17–19 . Question: Why are antihistamines minimally effective for the itch of atopic dermatitis, and what is the likely reason they provide any benefit at all in this condition?

Antihistamines show minimal effectiveness in alleviating atopic dermatitis itch, indicating that histamine is probably not the predominant mediator of the pruritic sensation in this disease. Rather, the benefit that antihistamines do provide in atopic dermatitis is most likely due to their sedative effects rather than a direct antipruritic action. Because clinical manifestations of small vessel vasculitis of the skin (e.g. palpable purpura) and histologic findings of LCV may be seen in other disease entities (e.g. IgA vasculitis), systematic evaluation and consid- eration of other types of vasculitis involving small cutaneous vessels is necessary before establishing the diagnosis of CSVV (see Table 24.1 ). Question: According to this excerpt, what clinical features may suggest a chronic course of cutaneous small vessel vasculitis (CSVV), and how should chronic or severe cutaneous disease generally be managed?

The presence of arthralgias or cryoglobulinemia along with the absence of fever may portend a chronic course of CSVV, as may an underlying cause such as an autoimmune connective tissue disease or neoplasm. Chronic (lasting more than 4 weeks) or severe cutaneous disease generally requires more aggressive systemic therapy, such as colchicine, dapsone, azathioprine, or methotrexate. Severe, ulcerating, or progressive disease needing rapid control can be treated with a short course of high-dose oral corticosteroids (up to 1 mg/kg/day prednisone) tapered over 4–6 weeks, with a steroid-sparing agent added if recurrence occurs, since corticosteroids are not appropriate for long-term management. Question: In gestational pemphigoid, what is the molecular target of the pathogenic autoantibodies, and which specific region of this protein is considered immunodominant?

The autoantibodies in gestational pemphigoid are complement-fixing IgG1 antibodies directed against BP180 (BPAG2/collagen XVII), a 180 kDa transmembrane hemidesmosomal protein, the same antigen targeted in bullous pemphigoid. As in bullous pemphigoid, the immunodominant region is the non-collagenous NC16A segment located closest to the plasma membrane of the basal keratinocyte, and circulating antibodies detected by ELISA and immunoblot in maternal or neonatal sera are almost exclusively directed against this domain. Question: In classic Dowling-Degos disease (DDD) and its variants, what specific gene mutations cause (1) classic DDD, (2) the variant with more prominent non-flexural involvement, and (3) the variant associated with hidradenitis suppurativa?

Classic DDD is typically caused by loss-of-function mutations in KRT5 (the non-helical head domain), leading to haploinsufficiency. The variant with more prominent non-flexural involvement results from heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in POFUT1 or POGLUT1, which encode enzymes regulating Notch signaling. The variant associated with hidradenitis suppurativa is caused by mutations in PSENEN, which encodes a component of the γ-secretase complex involved in Notch signaling. [Chapter: 67 Disorders of Hyperpigmentation, p.1390]

Exogenous photosensitivity Introduction and history Photosensitivity induced by exogenous agents can be divided into phototoxicity and photoallergy ( Table 87.5 ). Phototoxicity is the result of direct tissue and cellular injury following UVR-induced activation of a phototoxic agent; theoretically, phototoxicity can be induced in any individual. In contrast, photoallergy is a delayed-type hypersensitivity response consisting of a sensitization phase, an incubation period of 7 to 10 days (following the first exposure), and a clinical elicitation reaction with any subsequent challenge; only immunologically sensi- tized individuals can develop photoallergy. Phototoxic agents have been used as medications from as early as 4000 BCE, with the inhabitants of Mesopotamia (and later the Indians and Egyptians) employing plant-derived psoralens for the treatment of leukoderma. In 1913, Meyer-Betz demonstrated hematoporphyrin- induced phototoxicity on himself, while the current method of PUVA therapy was introduced in the 1970s. Photoallergy was first recognized in 1939 based on a classic study of sulfanilamide by Epstein. Epidemiology While the exact prevalences of phototoxicity and photoallergy in the general population are unknown, their frequency in photodermatology referral centers has ranged from 3% to 16% for phototoxicity and 1% to 8% for photoallergy. Question: How can phototoxicity and photoallergy be histologically distinguished, and what long-term cutaneous risks are associated with prolonged voriconazole prophylaxis?

Histologically, phototoxicity shows scattered necrotic keratinocytes ("sunburn cells") with a superficial dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes and neutrophils, whereas photoallergy shows epidermal spongiosis with a superficial dermal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, resembling other spongiotic dermatitides. Prolonged voriconazole use, often given for months to years in immunocompromised patients, can cause phototoxic reactions, actinic cheilitis, lentigines, large hypertrophic actinic keratoses, aggressive cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas, and cutaneous melanoma. Posaconazole is an alternative antifungal not associated with phototoxicity. [Chapter: 87 Photodermatologic Disorders, p.1904]

Question: What is febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha–Habermann disease (FUMHD), and what is its associated mortality rate?

FUMHD is a severe variant of pityriasis lichenoides characterized by large, confluent necrotic skin lesions along with mucosal, gastrointestinal, and pulmonary involvement, sometimes accompanied by malaise, fever, lymphadenopathy, arthritis, and/or bacteremia. This severe form has been reported to have an associated mortality rate of up to 15%. [Chapter: 9 Other Papulosquamous Disorders, p.226-227]

Treatment As with other types of vasculitis, management of IgAV is dictated by the extent and severity of systemic and cutaneous manifestations. Because IgAV is generally self-limited, resolving over the course of weeks to months, treatment may be primarily supportive. For skin-limited IgAV, dapsone or colchicine may decrease the duration of cutaneous lesions and frequency of recurrences (see Table 24.10 ) 33 . Systemic corti- costeroids are effective in treating associated arthritis and abdominal pain, as well as reducing the gastrointestinal complications and duration of skin lesions, but they do not prevent recurrences of purpura and are not suitable as a long-term therapy 34,35 . In adults, the following factors may predict relapsing disease: age > 30 years, persistent purpura > 1 month, abdominal pain, hematuria, an underlying systemic disorder, and absence of IgM on DIF 36 . In patients with renal involvement (e.g. microscopic hematuria, proteinuria), referral to a nephrologist is indicated. Corticosteroids have not been shown to be effective in preventing renal disease due to IgAV and are therefore not recommended. For example, a Cochrane review of interven- tions for preventing and treating IgAV nephritis found no difference in the risk of persistent kidney disease (up to 12 months following treatment) in children who received prednisone for 2–4 weeks at the time of presentation, as compared to placebo or supportive therapy 37 . In a randomized, double- blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 352 children with new-onset IgAV, early treatment with 14 days of prednisolone did not reduce the prevalence of proteinuria 12 months after disease onset 38 . For those who do develop evidence of IgAV nephritis, the treatment approach depends on disease severity and whether the patient is a child or adult. Individuals with limited evidence of renal involvement, mild proteinuria ( < 1 g/day), and normal serum creatinine warrant close monitoring and consideration for treatment with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEi) or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB). Those with more significant proteinuria ( ≥ 1 g/day), elevated serum creatinine, or crescentic glomerulonephritis on kidney biopsy should initially receive, in addition to an ACEi or ARB, high-dose systemic corticosteroids. In sum, the current consensus is that cortico- steroids do not prevent renal disease but should be used to treat severe nephritis 19 . Question: In treating linear IgA bullous dermatosis (LABD), which patients are more likely to require additional systemic corticosteroid therapy beyond dapsone alone, and what dapsone dosing considerations apply to adults, children, and high-dose use?

Patients with LABD who have both IgG and IgA deposits at the basement membrane zone are more likely to require additional systemic corticosteroids beyond dapsone. The average dapsone dose needed to control LABD in adults is 100 mg daily, though doses up to 300 mg daily may be required, and close monitoring is warranted if doses exceed 200 mg per day. Children typically respond to lower doses of 1–2 mg/kg daily. [Chapter: 31 Dermatitis Herpetiformis and Linear IgA Bullous Dermatosis, p.684-686]

UV light-induced effects on the immune system involve not only the cutaneous sites directly exposed to UV light, but also non-irradiated areas. An example of systemic immunosuppression is the development in non-exposed skin of antigen-specific immune tolerance to antigens that were initially applied to UV-exposed skin. This effect is known to be mediated by the release of immunosuppressive cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-10 and then ultimately by UV-induced regulatory T cells. The downside of photo-induced immunosuppression and immune tolerance is that they inhibit the recognition of tumor antigens and thereby contribute to photocarcinogenesis. The upside is the prevention of autoimmune reactions, e.g. diseases such as lupus erythematosus (LE) would likely be more prevalent without effective suppression of immune reactions against self-antigens unmasked by UV-induced cell damage. Another example of this equilibrium is polymorphic light eruption, in which less efficient UV-induced immunosuppression is balanced by a lower risk of UV-induced skin cancer 11 . Cellular photoreceptors that mediate signaling which leads to UV-induced immune responses include: DNA (via formation of DNA damage), urocanic acid in the stratum corneum (via UV-induced isomerization from the trans - to the cis -isoform) 12 , membrane lipids (via UV-induced alteration of the membrane redox potential), and activation of the NLRP1 inflammasome (see Fig. 4.2 ). The latter acts as a sensor within keratinocytes whose activation was found to be a consequence of a UVB-induced ribotoxic stress response 12a . UV exposure induces antigen-specific immune tolerance even in non-irradiated skin, mediated by immunosuppressive cytokines like IL-10 and UV-induced regulatory T cells. The stratum corneum is the key structure for barrier function. Protection against UV radiation occurs through several phenomena, including photon scattering in the stratum corneum and photon absorption by underlying melanin. Protection against dehydration and infection The most dramatic form of epidermal failure occurs in patients with toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN; Ch. 20 ). In this drug-induced disease, rapid death of keratinocytes leads to detachment of the epidermis over large areas of the body ( Fig. 1.10 ). TEN is most often associated with sulfonamides, aromatic anticonvulsants, and nonsteroidal anti-inflam- matory drugs. The mortality rate depends on the area of skin affected, and death is not uncommon. There is no specific treatment for TEN, but there is evidence that drug-induced triggering of massive keratinocyte apoptosis may underlie the disease 22 .

Herpetiform pemphigus is characterized by: (1) erythematous urticarial plaques and tense vesicles arranged in a herpetiform pattern; (2) eosinophilic spongiosis and subcorneal pustules with minimal or no acantholysis on histology; and (3) IgG autoantibodies directed against keratinocyte cell surfaces. Question: According to this excerpt, what is the mechanism of action of upadacitinib, abrocitinib, and baricitinib in reducing pruritus, and what condition shows improvement within 1–2 weeks of treatment?

Upadacitinib, abrocitinib, and baricitinib work by inhibiting JAK1 (and also JAK2 in the case of baricitinib) in immune cells and neurons. This mechanism leads to decreased pruritus within 1–2 weeks in patients with atopic dermatitis. [Chapter: 5 Cutaneous Neurophysiology, p.149-150]

Question: What immunostaining pattern helps distinguish dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) from large or highly cellular dermatofibromas, and what cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities are characteristically found in DFSP?

DFSP is characteristically CD34-positive and factor XIIIa-negative, a pattern that helps distinguish it from large/highly cellular dermatofibromas. Transmission is typically through infected saliva, although HHV-6 DNA has been isolated from the cervix and may cause perinatal infection. After primary HHV-6 infection, the virus establishes lifelong latency in CD4 + T lymphocytes, with the potential for reactivation. Immunologic Protection An intricate system of immunologic recognition, both innate and adaptive, protects the skin from infection ( Ch. 4 ) 10 . The innate immune response is the initial, rapidly deployed arm of the immune system that combats invading microbes and mediates defense against infection. It also plays a role in inflammatory conditions such as acne vulgaris and atopic dermatitis 11 . The cornerstone of adaptive immunity lies in recir- culating lymphocytes and antibodies that are specifically recruited and “tuned” to recognize “foreign” materials, primarily peptides derived from infectious agents. Initial recognition occurs when sentinel dendritic cells in the epidermis (Langerhans cells) and dermis (dermal dendritic cells) are activated. Prior to activation, dendritic cells engulf particles and metabolize complex proteins into small immunogenic fragments. Once activated, motility is induced, allowing these cells to travel out of their cutaneous residence and migrate, via draining lymphatics, to regional lymph nodes (see Fig. 4.13 ). Thus, these residents of normal skin can travel to a distant location where reactive lymphocytes are selected and then expanded. Within a lymph node, activated T helper lymphocytes assist B lymphocytes in generating antibodies, while T helper lymphocytes and cytotoxic T lymphocytes begin to recirculate preferentially to and from the skin. A population of effector memory T lymphocytes that reside within the skin has also been identified, and these cells play a critical role in immune responses 12 . Infection Cutaneous infections illustrate important aspects of skin function ( Chs. 74–85 ), ranging from a structural barrier provided by the stratum corneum to immunologic recognition and protective immunity. Examining examples of defective resistance to infection, e.g. verrucae, Hansen disease, can provide insights into these functions. Chronic and recurrent verrucae are often a vexing problem, especially when patients are immunocompromised or have epidermodysplasia verruciformis ( Chs. 60 & 79 ) 13 . Trauma to the stratum corneum disrupts a physical barrier that is normally not susceptible to viral infection.
