Question: For a patient presenting with congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma without other syndromic features, what genetic testing approach is recommended, and what would identification of biallelic ALOX12B pathogenic variants indicate?

In this scenario, a targeted panel of genes known to cause ichthyosis is the recommended testing strategy rather than sequencing a single gene or using WES/WGS. Identification of biallelic (two) pathogenic variants in ALOX12B would establish a diagnosis of autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis. If targeted panel testing is uninformative, broader approaches such as WES or WGS may then be considered. [Chapter: 54 Basic Principles of Genetics, p.1069-1070]

As with hair graft creation, hairline design should mimic, as closely as possible, what occurs in nature. Even with follicular unit transplants, this approach to hairline design often leads to cosmetic failure. The design of the frontal hairline should be such that over time it will remain balanced with the temporal and posterior hairlines. This requires recreating a frontal hairline which is higher and more receded than the one which was present before the process began. Initially, some patients will resist the idea of a higher, more receded hairline, but explaining and demonstrating with a mirror how their temporal and posterior hairlines preclude a low frontal hairline usually changes their opinion. Rather than considering the hairline to be a fixed boundary, it should be thought of as a natural transition zone of gradually increasing density from skin to terminal hair-bearing skin. Question: Why are conventional broad-spectrum sunscreens limited in their photoprotective efficacy for patients with porphyria, and which sunscreen ingredients are effective?

Conventional sunscreens have limited efficacy because the wavelengths that primarily induce porphyria reactions are in the visible light range (400–410 nm), which most sunscreens do not adequately block. Physical blockers such as titanium dioxide and zinc oxide are effective, and tinted sunscreens containing iron oxide also provide protection against visible light exposure. Question: How is granulomatous vasculitis defined histologically, and which three diseases are classically included in this pattern?

Granulomatous vasculitis is defined by the presence of histiocytes within and around blood vessel walls, in association with fibrin and/or degenerative and necrotic changes. It is a restricted pattern seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg–Strauss syndrome), and giant cell arteritis (formerly temporal arteritis). Question: According to the WHO, what three cardinal features can be used to diagnose Hansen disease, and how does the 2017 WHO classification distinguish paucibacillary from multibacillary leprosy?

The WHO diagnosis of Hansen disease requires at least one of: (1) anesthesia in a hypopigmented or erythematous skin lesion; (2) an enlarged peripheral nerve with associated sensory loss and/or weakness; or (3) acid-fast bacilli found on slit-skin smear or biopsy. The 2017 WHO classification then divides disease into paucibacillary leprosy, defined as one to five skin lesions without demonstrated bacilli on slit-skin smear or biopsy, and multibacillary leprosy, defined as more than five skin lesions, nerve involvement (pure neuritis or with any number of skin lesions), or demonstrated bacilli. Question: What specific risk should be considered in patients being treated with the C5 inhibitors eculizumab and ravulizumab, and why is plasma transfusion not recommended as a way to replace deficient complement components?

Patients treated with the C5 inhibitors eculizumab and ravulizumab are at increased risk for developing severe meningococcal infections. Additionally, plasma transfusions intended to replace deficient complement components may instead activate the complement cascade and accelerate immune complex deposition, making this approach counterproductive. Question: Between testosterone and 5α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which is the principal androgen mediating sebum production, and why? Also, what is now understood to be the true cause of sebaceous gland activity seen in infants, rather than the previously held hypothesis of persistent maternal hormonal stimulation?

DHT is the principal androgen mediating sebum production because it has 5- to 10-fold greater affinity than testosterone for the androgen receptor. Infant sebaceous gland activity is not due to persistent maternal hormonal stimulation, as previously thought, but instead results from elevated LH-driven testicular testosterone production in infant boys and increased adrenal DHEA/DHEAS from the androgen-producing fetal zone in both sexes, both of which decline substantially by about 1 year of age. Question: How can morphea be clinically distinguished from systemic sclerosis (SSc) in terms of distribution pattern and associated clinical features?

Morphea has an asymmetric patchy or linear distribution, whereas SSc presents either as symmetric tightening of the fingers and hands extending toward the forearms (limited cutaneous SSc) or as symmetrically extending sclerosis of the trunk and proximal upper extremities (diffuse cutaneous SSc). Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis includes all forms of vasculitis affecting small or medium-sized vessels (see Table 24.1 ). Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis can be differentiated from these disorders based upon the appropriate context and by the detection of circulating mixed cryoglobulins. Patients with Sjögren syndrome can also have arthralgias, arthritis, xerostomia/xerophthalmia, and the presence of rheumatoid factor and/or mixed cryoglobulins; however, they are typically SSA (Ro)/SSB (La)-positive, have distinct histopatho- logic findings in salivary gland biopsies, and less frequently are found to have hepatitis, glomerulonephritis, or hypocomplementemia 66 . Treatment The treatment of mixed cryoglobulinemia should be directed at any underlying disease. In patients with mild manifestations of vascu- litis, that may be sufficient. In general, those with moderate or severe disease should first receive immunosuppressive therapy until they have stabilized clinically, then therapy for the underlying condition can be initiated. All patients with HCV-associated mixed cryoglobu- linemia should be treated with antiviral therapy (see Table 24.10 ). Direct-acting antiviral agents are significantly more effective and better tolerated than previous interferon-containing regimens. Observational studies suggest antiviral regimens are effective in attaining a sustained virologic response, as well as improving vasculitic symptoms among those with HCV-associated cryoglobulinemic vasculitis. In a study of 148 patients, > 95% had a complete or partial clinical response, with a median follow-up of 15.3 months 72 . While rates of clinical improvement are high, correlating with sustained virologic response, clonal production of cryoglobulins persists in some patients, leading to relapses of vasculitis. Patients with mild manifestations of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (e.g. purpura, arthralgias, mild sensory neuropathy) may respond to agents such as colchicine or dapsone and/or symptomatic management with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or gabapentin. Those with moderate to severe disease should receive high-dose systemic corti- costeroids in combination with rituximab. Evidence from randomized trials and cohort studies demonstrate the efficacy and safety of this regimen compared to conventional therapy with systemic corticoste- roids, either alone or in combination with cyclophosphamide 73,74 . In addition, plasma exchange should be considered in those with acute life-threatening disease, including pulmonary hemorrhage, rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis, and hyperviscosity syndrome. As expected, prognosis depends on the severity of organ involvement and the underlying disease 75 . They consist of an external part that sits behind the ear and another part implanted below the skin. While potential for EMI exists, there are limited studies examining electrosurgery in patients with CIs. The British Cochlear Implant Group and CI manufacturer guidelines recommend against the use of monoterminal electrosurgery in the head and neck region; biterminal electrosurgery can be used safely if not within 1 to 2 cm of the CI 39 . A conservative approach may be prudent, with use of electrosurgical instruments below the clavicles and only electrocautery in the vicinity of the implant. Nerve stimulators Implantable nerve stimulators (e.g. vagal nerve, sacral nerve, phrenic nerve, spinal cord stimulators) are now available for a variety of indica- tions. There are also implantable neurostimulators (e.g., NeuroPace ® RNS ® System) for epilepsy. Some of these devices can be temporarily turned off during electrosurgery without adverse effects. Electrocautery is recommended when possible to minimize risk of EMI. Other techniques to minimize interference include use of bipolar forceps and positioning of dispersive pads away from the implanted device. When in doubt, the authors advise consultation with the prescribing physician for further recommendations. Allergies True allergic reactions to local anesthetics may be type I (immediate) or type IV (delayed-type hypersensitivity) (see Ch. 143 ). Patients with a type IV sensitivity to one major group of local anesthetics (ester or amide) are usually not allergic to members of the other group. Type I reactions are more commonly associated with the ester anesthetics and their para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) metabolite. Although the lack of cross-reactivity between ester and amide anesthetics is true for type IV sensitivity, it has not been adequately studied for anaphylaxis. If there is a possible history of a type I amide allergy, referral to an allergist for a progressive challenge protocol can be considered. It is important to consider the possibility that the allergic reaction is due to the preser- vative (e.g. methylparaben, metabisulfite). Use of preservative-free anesthetics can resolve this problem. Epinephrine (adrenaline) is a vasoconstrictive agent commonly added to local anesthetics to reduce bleeding and prolong the duration of anesthesia. Question: According to guidelines from the British Cochlear Implant Group and CI manufacturers, what type of electrosurgery should be avoided in the head and neck region in patients with cochlear implants, and under what condition can biterminal electrosurgery be used safely?

Monoterminal (monopolar) electrosurgery is not recommended in the head and neck region in patients with cochlear implants. Biterminal (bipolar) electrosurgery can be used safely as long as it is not applied within 1 to 2 cm of the cochlear implant. A conservative approach also suggests using electrosurgical instruments only below the clavicles and limiting use to electrocautery near the implant. MEDICAL THERAPY CONCLUSION Dealing with drug interactions is a challenge in clinical practice. Although no one can be expected to know all drug interactions, useful resources are available. One of the best pocket reference guides is The Top 100 Drug Interactions by Hansten and Horn ( www.hansten­ andhorn.com ) 57 . More research during the early stages of drug development is required to identify new interactions, define mechanisms of older interactions, and examine the safety of new drugs from classes that are known to cause interactions. We also need more sensitive post-marketing surveil- lance tools to identify important drug interactions that become evident over time in diseased hosts and that were not seen in pre-marketing studies of healthy volunteers. Physicians need better tools, but, in the meantime, understanding the nuances of the cytochrome P450s will help take the fear out of prescribing. Because the best evidence for clinically relevant drug interactions comes from case reports, prescribing physicians can have a major impact. Metabolism The most clinically relevant drug interactions are those caused by alter- ations in drug metabolism, and CYP isoenzymes are the key players in drug metabolism. Members of the CYP3A subfamily are the most abundant of the human hepatic cytochromes and account for up to 70% of GI cytochromes. This subfamily contains the major metabolizing isoforms for many of the drugs prescribed by dermatologists ( Tables 131.2, 131.5, 131.7 & 131.8 ; Fig. 131.4 ). CYP3A4 in particular has a pivotal role in xenobiotic metabolism and has been estimated to be involved in the metabolism of ~50% of the drugs in clinical use 33 . Although the most important isoform is 3A4, there is close structural homology to 3A5 and 3A7, and so these three isoforms are grouped together. Of note, CYP3A4 is also located in the placenta, uterus, kidney, lung, and fetus. There is significant interindividual variability in the metabolic activity of CYP3A4. The extent of variability may be as much as 20-fold and the individual level of CYP3A4 activity probably has clinical relevance. Obesity also plays a role in drug metabolism in an enzyme-specific way 19 as it decreases isoform 3A4 metabolism (see Table 131.6 ), and more than a third of Americans are obese. The successful application of information regarding CYP in order to prevent drug interactions and improve the therapeutic risk/benefit ratio can occur only if we know which enzyme is responsible for the metabolism of a particular drug. Drug interactions are also made more predictable by determining which compounds induce and inhibit which specific P450 enzymes. Question: According to the excerpt, what is a key limitation of PCSK9 inhibitors (e.g. alirocumab, evolocumab) in treating hypercholesterolemia, and what is their notable safety advantage compared to HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors?

PCSK9 inhibitors are not effective in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia because these patients lack functional LDL receptors (receptor negative), and the drugs work by decreasing LDL receptor degradation and increasing recirculation of the LDL receptor to the hepatocyte surface. Unlike HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, PCSK9 inhibitors are not associated with myopathy. [Chapter: 92 Xanthomas, p.1996-1997]

Question: How do the patterns of skin discoloration caused by hydroxychloroquine and quinacrine differ in color and distribution?

Hydroxychloroquine (and chloroquine) typically produce a gray to blue-black pigment that is most often pretibial, though the face, hard palate, sclerae, and subungual areas can also be involved. In contrast, quinacrine causes a diffuse yellow to yellow-brown discoloration rather than the gray-blue color seen with the other antimalarials. [Chapter: 67 Disorders of Hyperpigmentation, p.1375]

Question: According to Bolognia's morphological classification, how are papules and plaques distinguished from each other, and what feature can make a plaque an exception to the usual definition of 'elevated'?

Papules and plaques are both elevated, circumscribed lesions caused by increased thickness of the epidermis and/or cellular infiltrate or deposits in the dermis, and both may show secondary changes like scale or crust; they are distinguished by size, with papules being <1 cm in diameter and plaques being >1 cm in diameter. An exception is morphea, where the plaque is palpable but not actually elevated. [Chapter: 0 Basic Principles of Dermatology, p.32-33]

Barnhill Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions 112 SECTION 18 NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN Key features  Small, uniformly pigmented macules in sun-exposed sites  More common in fair-skinned individuals and more noticeable in summer than in winter  Hyperpigmentation of the basal layer of the epidermis without an increase in melanocyte density Epidemiology and Pathogenesis Ephelides are common in fair-skinned individuals, especially those with red hair, and occur more frequently in women. They first appear in early childhood and usually stabilize in number during adulthood, followed by gradual fading. Ephelides result from an increase in sun-induced melanin synthesis and transport of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes. Frequent sunburns and variants of the melanocortin-1 receptor gene ( MC1R ) play an important role in the development of ephelides (see Fig. 65.13 ) 1 . Clinical Features Ephelides are limited to sun-exposed sites – primarily the face, upper trunk, and dorsal aspects of the arms. Ephelides are well demarcated, uniformly pigmented, oval to irregular-shaped macules that are usually 1 to 3 mm in size. Depending upon the intensity of sun exposure, ephelides vary in color from light to medium brown. In the summer, they are more conspicuous and then fade during the winter. Ephelides are benign with no potential for malignant transformation. However, higher numbers of ephelides correlate with an increased risk of acquired melanocytic nevi and melanoma 2 . Pathology There is hyperpigmentation of the basal layer of the epidermis without an increase in the number of melanocytes. Compared to adjacent uninvolved epidermis, melanocytes in ephelides are larger and have more branching of dendrites and stronger DOPA positivity, indicating increased activity 3 . Differential Diagnosis Ephelides must be distinguished from simple lentigines, solar lentigines, small café-au-lait macules, and junctional nevi. In addition to being confined to sun-exposed skin, the clinical appearance of ephelides varies depending upon the amount of exposure to UVR ( Table 112.1 ). Café-au-lait macules are usually solitary and larger than ephelides. Treatment If ephelides are a cosmetic concern, sun exposure should be minimized and use of sunscreens, hats, and protective clothing recommended. Topical retinoids and hydroquinone may lighten lesions, but it is difficult to achieve an homogeneous clinical effect and potential side effects (e.g. irritation, dyspigmentation) need to be considered. Pigment- specific lasers represent an additional treatment option, but recurrences are common 4 . Chapter Contents Circumscribed Melanotic Lesions . .

Question: What treatment options are available for ephelides that are a cosmetic concern, and what are the limitations of each?

For cosmetic concerns related to ephelides, patients should minimize sun exposure and use sunscreens, hats, and protective clothing. Topical retinoids and hydroquinone may lighten the lesions, but achieving a homogeneous clinical effect is difficult and side effects such as irritation and dyspigmentation must be considered. Pigment-specific lasers are another option, but recurrences are common. [Chapter: 112 Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions, p.2382]

Question: Which macrolide antibiotics are generally considered safe during pregnancy, which one is not recommended, and which formulation is contraindicated in pregnancy and why?

Question: Why does injection of desomorphine ("krokodil") cause severe tissue damage such as limb amputation in long-term users, and what is the underlying cause of this injury?

Krokodil is synthesized by combining red phosphorus from match strikers with codeine and iodine derived from over-the-counter medications, a process that frequently leaves the drug contaminated with these and other toxic agents. Injection of this contaminated "flesh-eating drug" causes serious damage to skin, blood vessels, bone, and muscle, which can progress to limb amputation in long-term users. Notably, the tissue injury is caused by residual iodine, phosphorus, and other toxic substances left over from synthesis, not by the opioid (desomorphine) itself. Question: In nonspecific (end-stage) cicatricial alopecia, why can it be misleading to rely on histopathology alone to determine whether a patient's disease is truly 'burnt-out'?

Clinically, end-stage cicatricial alopecia shows scalp fibrosis without apparent inflammation, and the original causative disease cannot be identified from the fibrotic patches. However, the histopathologic 'end-stage' pattern does not necessarily reflect the true disease status, because this pattern can also be seen when an older, inactive area of scalp is biopsied even though there is still active disease occurring elsewhere on the scalp. For primary intention healing, wounds may be closed either by placement of a simple full-thickness suture or by layered closure. Question: According to this excerpt, how does hemostasis typically differ between a punch biopsy site and a wound created by incisional biopsy or excision in toto, and what technique is used when a large actively bleeding vessel is encountered?

For punch biopsy sites, suturing alone usually provides sufficient hemostasis, whereas wounds from incisional biopsy or excision in toto may require electrocoagulation for hemostasis before closure. If a large actively bleeding vessel is found, it should be identified, grasped with a hemostat, and tied off using an absorbable suture along with a figure-of-eight suture. Oral white plaques can also be seen in hereditary benign intraepithelial dyskeratosis, a disorder that occurs primarily in Native Americans. Although complete excision of the lesion (via scalpel, CO 2 laser, or cryosurgery) has been proposed as first-line therapy by some authors, removal of OPMDs has not been proven to prevent the onset of OSCC 25,26 . When possible, surgical removal of the entire lesion is performed to avoid sampling error and to exclude OSCC. Habit cessation (in particular tobacco use), longitu- dinal evaluation by an oral medicine specialist, and repeat biopsies as indicated are recommended for all patients. The WHO defines erythroplakia as a fiery red patch that cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other definable disease, with the diagnosis established only after excluding other red oral lesions. Question: For SSRIs used in the treatment of OCD, what is first-line, and what should be considered regarding dosing, time to response, and duration of treatment?

SSRIs are the first-line pharmacologic treatment for OCD, but they often require higher doses and a longer time to respond (e.g., 10–12 weeks) compared to their use in other conditions. Since OCD is a chronic condition with rare complete remission, most experts recommend continuing treatment once a stable, tolerable, therapeutic regimen is achieved. If discontinuation is desired, a very slow taper can be attempted with close monitoring for symptom recurrence. [Chapter: 7 Psychocutaneous Diseases, p.175-176]

The overlying skin is normal in appearance. Ultrasound can aid in the diagnosis of subtle lesions of the Achilles tendon by demonstrating hypoechoic nodules or an increase in the anteroposterior diameter of the tendon 11 . The presence of tendinous xanthomas is almost always a clue to an underlying disorder of lipid metabolism. Lipid disorders that have been associated with this type of xanthoma include familial hypercholesterolemia, dysbetalipopro- teinemia, and hyperlipidemia secondary to hypothyroidism ( Table 92.3 ). Tendinous xanthomas are most frequently seen in the setting of familial hypercholesterolemia . This disorder results from a deficiency of normal LDL receptors on cell membranes, which leads to the poor hepatic clearance of circulating LDLs and, therefore, elevated LDL cholesterol levels (Frederickson type II). This condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion with a high degree of penetrance. Homozygotes can have LDL cholesterol levels of 800 to 1000 mg/dl with widespread atherosclerosis and the appearance of xanthomas during the first decade of life. Heterozygosity for the disorder is more common and is estimated to occur in 1 in 500 individuals in the US. The types of xanthomas seen in this disorder include tendinous, tuberous, tubero- eruptive, and plane (including xanthelasma). Question: Which type of hyperlipoproteinemia is characterized by tuberoeruptive, tuberous, and plane xanthomas (especially of the palmar creases) as its most characteristic skin finding, and what is its underlying pathogenesis?

Type III hyperlipoproteinemia (familial dysbetalipoproteinemia) most characteristically produces tuberoeruptive, tuberous, and plane xanthomas, particularly involving the palmar creases, with tendinous xanthomas also occurring. It results from impaired hepatic clearance of remnant lipoproteins due to an apolipoprotein E abnormality, as most patients express only the apo E2 isoform, which interacts poorly with the apo E receptor. This leads to elevated chylomicron remnants and IDLs, causing both hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia, and increased risk of atherosclerosis. [Chapter: 92 Xanthomas, p.1991-1992]

Question: According to the excerpt, what cryosurgical technique is used for large nodular tumors, how is it performed, and what advantage does it offer?

For large nodular tumors, a technique involving passing a thick needle through the tumor is used, with one end attached to the cryogen unit (screwed on or via a Luer lock) and the other end exiting the skin to allow for liquid nitrogen release. Question: What are Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies, and what role do they play in diagnosing this stage-three (sclerotic/cicatricial) nasal disease?

Mikulicz cells are large, vacuolated, non-lipidized histiocytes containing intracellular bacteria, while Russell bodies are plasma cells with aggregates of condensed immunoglobulins. Their presence on routine histology (demonstrable with PAS, Giemsa, silver, and Gram stains, or more sensitively with immunoperoxidase studies) establishes the diagnosis, which is important since cultures are positive in only about 50% of cases. Question: How does the presence of scale versus lichenification help a dermatologist estimate the age of a skin lesion?

Scale reflects parakeratosis and, due to epidermal transit time, requires about 2 weeks to develop, indicating the lesion is not brand new. Lichenification—thickening of the skin with accentuation of normal skin markings—takes weeks to months to form, so its presence means the lesion is chronic rather than acute, regardless of what the patient reports. In the US, there is an increased incidence of sarcoidosis in African-Americans, ranging from 18 to 70 per 100 000. Middle-aged African-American women have the highest incidence (107 per 100 000), with African- American women having a lifetime risk of developing the disease of 2.7% 1 . In comparison, the incidence in White individuals in the US ranges from 10 to 14 per 100 000. Sarcoidosis in African-Americans also tends to be more chronic and severe with a higher mortality rate than in other populations 2 . Worldwide, the incidence of sarcoidosis is highest in Sweden (64 per 100 000) and the UK (20 per 100 000) and lowest in Spain and Japan (both 1.4 per 100 000). A greater number of patients with new-onset sarcoidosis are reported in the winter and spring 3 . Pathogenesis Immune mechanisms Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease characterized by hyperactivity of the cell-mediated immune system. Patients with a genetic susceptibility are exposed to a triggering antigen, leading to activation of macrophages and T cells, with subsequent granuloma formation. While classically considered a Th1-predominant immune response, the inflammatory cascade in sarcoidosis likely spans multiple pathways, including the innate immune system (via activation of pattern recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors or NOD-like receptors) and the Th17 arm of the immune system 4,5 . Specifically, CD4 + T helper cells differentiate into Th1 and Th17 effector cells that produce IFN- γ as well as Th17 cells that produce IL-17 1 . This is triggered by antigen presentation by monocytes bearing MHC class II molecules, which initiates formation of epithelioid granulomas in a variety of tissue types 6 . In the lung, an oligoclonal α / β T cell population has been described, suggesting that antigenic triggers of sarcoidosis favor a progressive accumulation and activation of specific T cell clones 7 . Increased production of Th1 cytokines, including interleukin (IL)-2, IL-12, IL-18, and interferon (IFN)- γ , as well as release of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) by macrophages and some CD8 + T cells, leads to persistent Th1 activity and persistent IFN- γ elevation. There is macrophage accumulation and hyperactivity, along with B cell stimulation and hyper- gammaglobulinemia. TNF and GM-CSF promote fusion of activated macrophages into the multinucleated cells seen within the granuloma 5 .

Although nutri- tional diseases have been better studied biochemically than structurally, there are several helpful histologic clues, including necrosis of the upper one-third of the epidermis (see Fig. 51.12G ). This distinctive reaction pattern has been reported in pellagra, acrodermatitis enteropathica, acquired zinc deficiency, and necrolytic migratory erythema. In the early stages, there is pallor and ballooning of the upper half of the epidermis. This stage is followed by the development of acanthosis, with confluent hyperkeratosis and degenerative features of the upper epidermal layers. In the late stages, the pallor of the upper epidermis is usually missing 43 . In protein–energy malnutrition, nonspecific histo- logic features are seen, such as epidermal atrophy and hyperkeratosis. Hair is a superb model of growth and differentiation. In some patients, histologic study of the hair matrix and hair shaft may provide evidence of moderate to severe degrees of protein–energy malnutrition 44 . DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS Nutritional dermatoses rarely result from the deficiency of a single nutrient, element, or vitamin as multiple deficiencies often coexist. A high index of suspicion is required in that clinical manifestations are often nonspecific and, in mild to moderate deficiencies, somewhat subtle. A few specific deficiencies do have characteristic mucocutaneous and systemic features that can be accurately recognized by the experi- enced clinician. Suspected deficiencies can usually be confirmed via laboratory analysis (see Table 51.2 ), and they readily respond to the administration of the deficient nutrient, element, and/or vitamin. TREATMENT The treatment of nutritional diseases must be individualized, taking into account the likelihood of multiple deficiencies of both macro- and micronutrients. The recommended treatment for specific nutritional diseases is reviewed in this chapter, but management frequently requires a multidisciplinary approach. Baugh Lasers and Other Energy-Based Therapies Pulsed Dye Laser The pulsed dye laser (PDL) is considered to be the laser of choice for the treatment of various cutaneous vascular lesions, especially facial telangiec­ tasias, port-wine birthmarks (PWBs), superficial hemangiomas, poikilo­ derma of Civatte, and erythematotelangiectatic rosacea 2 . Hypertrophic and keloidal scars, psoriasis, and warts are also amenable to treatment with PDL. While the initial PDL systems emitted 577 nm yellow light, slightly longer wavelength PDL devices (585 or 595 nm) were subsequently adopted to allow deeper tissue penetration of up to 1.2 mm. The choice of appropriate PDL parameters affects tissue response, in terms of both efficacy and appearance. Short pulse durations (0.45–3 millisecond [ms]) cause a purpuric reaction related to intravascular coagulation or vessel leakage ( Fig. 137.2C,D ). While very effective for telangiectasias, the bruised appearance is not cosmetically acceptable to many patients. Although slightly less effective, longer pulse durations (6–10 ms) with multiple passes or “pulse stacking”, consisting of appli­ cation of a rapid succession of pulses to a particular location with cooling to achieve “purpura-free” treatments, is quite effective and less noticeable. Epidermal protection during laser treatments, including those with PDL, is critical. Cooling helps to reduce blistering, crusting, and subse­ quent dyspigmentation, i.e. hypo- and hyperpigmentation. The most common cooling strategies are contact cooling, forced cold air, and cryogen spray. The Syneron-Candela PDL systems incorporate cryogen spray cooling (Dynamic Cooling Device™) which is deployed immedi­ ately before the light pulse, while Cynosure systems use forced cold air. In addition to protecting the epidermis from non-selective thermal damage, cooling allows for the use of higher fluences, with improved efficacy. Pathogenesis Airbag activation consists of detection, inflation, and deflation phases. The sudden deceleration caused by impact triggers sensors in the front bumper to fire a sodium azide canister inside the nylon rubber bag. The sodium azide ignites with an explosive release of hot nitrogen gas which inflates the bag in about 10 milliseconds at speeds exceeding 160 km/h. The hot nitrogen gas and other by-products are then vented out the upper sides of the bag away from the occupant, thus deflating the bag. Vented aerosol contains nitrogen, carbon mono- and dioxides, sodium hydroxide, ammonia, nitric oxide, metallic oxides and other trace gases, creating a corrosive environment. Friction and pressure from the bag, heat from the bag and gases, and contact with the corrosive aerosol may produce injury 20–22 . Clinical features The cutaneous injuries produced by airbag deployment are summarized in Table 88.6 . Chemical burns occur rarely, but appear to be a result of skin exposure to small amounts of the corrosive alkaline aerosol. The aerosolized particles need to dissolve in a water layer such as tears or sweat before creating a corrosive injury. Of note, alkali burns of the skin may continue to deepen and extend over time, unless all the corrosive chemical is washed away 20–22 . Differential diagnosis The pattern of injury and history of airbag deployment makes the diagnosis obvious. However, it is important to determine whether a burn injury is purely thermal or if it has a chemical component. Assessment of tissue pH and monitoring for continued extension of the burn help determine whether an alkali injury exists. Treatment Prevention is, of course, the most effective approach. Newer airbag designs include repositioning the exhaust vents in order to direct the escape of hot gases away from areas of potential skin contact. Seats should be positioned as far back from the airbag module as possible. Children too small to benefit from the adult three-point restraint should not be in the front passenger area. Children in any type of car seat or booster should never be put in the front seat. Question: In a patient with hypereosinophilic syndrome who is found to have a FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, what is the recommended treatment, how does it work mechanistically, and what precaution should be taken regarding cardiac monitoring during initiation of therapy?

Patients with FIP1L1-PDGFRA (or other PDGFRA/PDGFRB abnormalities) should be treated with imatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that prevents autophosphorylation of the fusion protein and phosphorylation of downstream substrates, thereby terminating the signaling cascade driving eosinophil proliferation and activation. Effective doses range widely (400 mg daily to 100 mg weekly or less) depending on individual sensitivity, and maintenance therapy is required to prevent relapse. Because endomyocardial disease may worsen during the first several days of imatinib administration, serum troponin levels should be monitored. [Chapter: 26 Eosinophil-Associated Dermatoses, p.599]

Question: For a patient with recurrent staphylococcal furuncles who is found to be a carrier, what decolonization regimen is recommended, and what key adjunctive measure should be performed for a furuncle or abscess?

For recurrent infections due to carrier state, treatment includes mupirocin 2% nasal ointment twice a day for 5 days, mupirocin 2% cream applied to major body folds (axillae, groin, inframammary) and umbilicus twice a day for 5 days, and washing the body with chlorhexidine or dilute bleach 2–3 times per week; fomites (sports equipment, keyboards, remote controls) and close contacts/pets should also be addressed as possible sources. Question: What is a key advantage of using inducible or tissue-specific gene deletion systems in transgenic mice (e.g., via tamoxifen-controlled Cre or the Tet-On/Off system) compared to deleting a gene in all mouse cells?

Inducible or tissue-specific gene deletion systems allow the gene to be deleted only in a specific cell type or tissue, and/or at a specific point in time, rather than in all cells of the mouse. This more faithfully mimics how gene deletion occurs in a specific tissue of a patient (e.g., recapitulating cancer hallmarks) and circumvents problems such as disruption of normal mouse development or embryonic death that can result from deleting the gene in all cells. Question: In athletes, what are the major rubber antioxidant allergens found in athletic shoes that can cause contact sensitivity, and what clinical features result on the feet?

The major allergens are mercaptobenzothiazole, tetramethylthiuram, and paraphenylenediamine derivatives, along with thiourea and thiuram antioxidants in the rubber compounds of athletic shoes. Contact sensitivity to these substances produces erythema, desquamation, vesiculation, fissuring, pain, and pruritus of the feet, which can be quite disabling for the athlete, especially when alternative footwear is not available. Question: How do tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) and antithrombin III (ATIII) function to down-regulate the initiation phase of clotting, and what happens to thrombin that escapes the clot site?

TFPI and ATIII bind to heparan sulfate molecules on the surface of endothelial cells, positioning them near sites of clot formation so they can capture activated clotting factors and prevent them from spreading beyond the area. ATIII neutralizes thrombin as well as factors IXa, Xa, and XIIa, and this activity is greatly enhanced when heparan sulfate or heparin binds to ATIII. Thrombin that escapes the clot site instead binds to thrombomodulin on the endothelial cell surface, which stops it from activating procoagulant factors and instead causes it to bind and activate protein C, a vitamin K-dependent anticoagulant protein. Clinical parameters that aid in the differential diagnosis are the age of the patient and the location of the tumor. Myxoid liposar- comas almost always develop in individuals older than 20 years of age, and they are located in the deep soft tissue, rather than the subcutis. Nevertheless, in a child, an immature fat tumor that contains areas of marked cellularity, loss of lobulation, and mitotic figures should raise concern for a myxoid liposarcoma. Treatment Lipoblastoma, if treated with complete excision, rarely recurs. Unusual cases of spontaneous resolution without treatment exist 51 . In a series of 14 patients with lipoblastomas/lipoblastomatosis, 22% recurred after excision 52 . Wide excision is the therapy of choice for the diffuse form of the disease. Atypical Lipomatous Tumor/Liposarcoma Synonym:  Atypical lipoma Key features  Sarcoma of deep soft tissue that is only rarely limited to the skin  Five major histologic subtypes, ranging from locally aggressive tumors without metastatic potential to malignant neoplasms with a significant risk of metastatic dissemination  Cutaneous involvement may represent superficial extension of a deeply situated tumor  Tumors confined to the skin (“primary cutaneous liposarcoma”) usually have a good prognosis Introduction Liposarcoma is the second most common soft tissue sarcoma after malignant fibrous histiocytoma. Five histopathologic subtypes are recognized by the World Health Organization (WHO), with important prognostic, cytogenetic, molecular, and epidemiologic differences. The biologic behavior of the subtypes ranges from locally aggressive tumors without metastatic potential to highly malignant neoplasms with a significant risk of systemic spread. There is considerable controversy among soft tissue pathologists regarding the nomenclature of this tumor when it is confined to the skin. Some experts prefer the term atypical lipomatous tumor for all liposarcomas in the subcutis, because these tumors recur but have virtually no metastatic potential 53,54 . Others prefer to retain the term liposarcoma because histologically and cytogenetically these tumors are the same, regardless of location, and also because these tumors carry a small risk for dedifferentiation, which confers metastatic potential 55 . Epidemiology The annual incidence of all types of soft tissue liposarcoma is estimated at 2.5 per million, based on a Swedish study. The average age at presen- tation is 50 years. Rare cases arise in children older than 10 years of age, but virtually never in children younger than 10 years of age.

Pleomorphic liposarcoma is the least common subtype; it exhibits an extreme degree of nuclear pleomorphism and resembles a malignant fibrous histiocytoma 58,59 . Question: According to the excerpt, name at least three intrinsic mechanisms that protect the skin against the photocarcinogenesis cascade following UV exposure, and give two examples of hereditary or acquired disorders that predispose to UV-induced skin cancer because these intrinsic protective mechanisms are impaired.

Intrinsic protective mechanisms listed include pigmentation, epidermal thickening/hyperkeratosis, anti-oxidative enzymes, DNA repair, high-fidelity translesional DNA synthesis, cell cycle arrest/apoptosis, and removal of mutated cells via immune surveillance. Disorders that predispose to UV-induced skin cancer due to impairment of these mechanisms include oculocutaneous albinism (loss of pigmentation), xeroderma pigmentosum and its variant (defective DNA repair), and immunosuppression such as in solid organ transplant patients (impaired immune surveillance). Question: How does the pattern of cancer genome evolution differ between lentigo maligna melanoma and acral/uveal melanomas?

Lentigo maligna melanoma, which arises in photodamaged skin of older adults, shows predominantly gradual (Darwinian/microevolutionary) genome evolution with a high mutational load, consistent with weakly oncogenic mutations being acquired gradually over a lifetime. In contrast, acral and uveal melanomas show more punctuated (macroevolutionary) genome evolution, characterized by numerous structural variants but a significantly lower mutational load. In most melanomas, both processes occur sequentially, with oncogenic hotspot mutations typically preceding copy number gains. [Chapter: 107 Principles of Cutaneous Tumor Biology, p.2264]

STSGs are composed of the full thickness of the epidermis and partial thickness of dermis. These can be sub­divided into thin, medium, and thick grafts, depending on the amount of dermis included in the graft. Composite grafts are composed of at least two different tissue types, usually skin and cartilage. Free cartilage grafts consist of cartilage with its overlying perichondrium. Question: How do the localized variants of lichen myxedematosus differ from scleromyxedema in terms of associated systemic findings, and which distinguishing features characterize discrete papular lichen myxedematosus and acral persistent papular mucinosis?

Unlike scleromyxedema, the localized variants of lichen myxedematosus are limited to the skin only and are not associated with sclerosis, paraproteinemia, systemic involvement, or thyroid disease. Discrete papular lichen myxedematosus presents with 2–5 mm symmetrical papules on the limbs and trunk, sparing the face, with non-indurated skin and slow progression without systemic involvement (though lesions rarely resolve spontaneously and progression to scleromyxedema has never been proven). Acral persistent papular mucinosis, first described in 1986, presents with ivory to skin-colored papules exclusively on the dorsal hands and extensor distal forearms, occurs with a 3:1 female-to-male ratio, and persists without systemic manifestations. Clinical Features Sebaceous tumors can present prior to (~30%), concurrently with (~10%), or after (~60%) the diagnosis of a visceral malignancy. The skin tumors sometimes appear decades before or after a visceral malig- nancy develops. In general, sebaceous tumors favor the head and neck region ( Fig. 63.6 ), and sporadic sebaceous carcinomas tend to affect the GENODERMATOSES periocular area. However, in patients with MTS, these neoplasms can occur in other locations (trunk > extremities) 42 . Sebaceous adenomas are the most common tumor type, and they present as slow-growing, yellow to pink papules or nodules, numbering from one to hundreds. Keratoacanthomas, which are keratotic skin-colored to erythematous papules or nodules that arise quickly, are seen in ~25% of patients with MTS and usually exhibit sebaceous differentiation. Fordyce granules (“free” sebaceous glands) on the vermilion lip and oral mucosa (especially the vestibule) are more common and prominent in patients with MTS than in the general population 43 . The most frequently observed malignancies in Lynch syndrome are colorectal (~50%–60% of patients with MSH2 or MLH1 mutations) and genitourinary (e.g. endometrium [15%–50% of women], ovary [10%–35% of women], urinary tract; highest risk with MSH2 mutations) carcinomas 44 . Colorectal carcinoma in Lynch syndrome most often involves the proximal colon and develops at a median age of 45 years, about one decade before it typically occurs in the general population. Question: How does prepubertal hypertrichosis typically present, and what does the presence of mildly elevated androgen levels in only a subset of affected girls suggest about its etiology?

Question: According to the hierarchical model of keratinocyte stem cell behavior in the epidermis, how do stem cells divide, what do transit amplifying (TA) cells do, and what structure results from this pattern of divisions?

In the hierarchical model, stem cells divide infrequently and asymmetrically, producing one new stem cell and one daughter transit amplifying (TA) cell. TA cells, in contrast, divide frequently and symmetrically, generating two TA cells and constituting the majority of basal keratinocytes; after a few rounds of division they exit the cell cycle, move suprabasally, and begin terminal differentiation. Each stem cell and its progeny form a vertical column of progressively differentiating cells known as an epidermal proliferation unit (EPU). [Chapter: 2 Skin Development and Maintenance, p.103]

Question: What are the three characteristic histologic zones seen on biopsy of an annular lesion suspicious for actinic granuloma (AEGCG), and what treatment approach is recommended for localized, asymptomatic granuloma annulare?

A biopsy of AEGCG that includes the border and center of the lesion shows three characteristic zones: absence of elastic fibers, granulomatous inflammation, and normal skin; longitudinal sectioning of the specimen is preferred to capture these zones. For localized, asymptomatic granuloma annulare, since it is self-limited and benign, reassurance and clinical observation may be the treatment of choice, with high-potency topical corticosteroids (with or without occlusion) and intralesional corticosteroid injections as first-line local therapies if treatment is desired. Therefore, treatment of severe rickettsial infection with macrolides or fluoroquinolones is not recommended. SCRUB TYPHUS Scrub typhus was described in association with red mites in China in CE 313. Orientia tsutsugamushi was discovered in Japan by Nagayo and Ogata in the 1920s and early 1930s. There are > 70 strains of O. tsutsugamushi , which differs from Rickettsia spp. in its cell wall proteins and ultrastructure as well as by lacking lipopolysaccharide. O. tsutsugamushi is maintained in nature via transovarial transmission by its vector, trombiculid mites (see Table 76.1 ). Eggs laid by infected mites hatch with the emergence of infected larvae (chiggers) that feed on rats. Approximately one million cases of scrub typhus occur annually, primarily affecting rural populations in Asia (from Afghanistan to Japan) and northern Australia 18 . In addition, novel Orientia spp. have been implicated in scrub typhus occurring in Dubai and Africa ( O. chuto ) as well as Chile ( Candidatus O. chiloensis) 19–21 . Immunity is strain-specific and transient, resulting in reinfections. The severity of the illness is age-dependent and varies geographically. A cutaneous eschar forms at the site of chigger feeding in 60%–90% of primary infections. This is followed by regional lymphadenopathy, fever, and headache; generalized lymphadenopathy, conjunctival hyperemia, and hearing loss may also develop 18 . A rash occurs in approximately half of patients, usually appearing as erythematous macules on the trunk 4–6 days after disease onset. Lesions then become papular, with subsequent centrifugal spread. Interstitial pneumonia occurs frequently, presenting with cough, tachypnea, and radiographic infiltrates; menin- goencephalitis is a less common manifestation 22 . In severe cases, ARDS, acute kidney injury, and hypotensive shock may develop. Tetracyclines, particularly doxycycline, are generally the first- line treatment for scrub typhus. Azithromycin has similar efficacy and represents an option for pregnant women and children, whereas chloramphenicol is less effective 15 . However, reduced responsiveness of O. tsutsugamushi infections to doxycycline and chloramphenicol treatment has been reported in northern Thailand 23,24 , and patients there have been treated successfully with azithromycin or rifampin. METABOLIC AND SYSTEMIC DISEASES These patients frequently develop recurrent infections due to their inability to mount a normal immune response. Kwashiorkor (SAM with edema) is a more acute form of childhood and adult protein–energy malnutrition (see Table 51.1 ). A characteristic finding is peripheral edema or even anasarca in association with hypoal- buminemia ( Fig. 51.5 ). One consequence of this edema is a body weight that is higher than is seen with marasmus, and it may be 60%–80% of expected weight (rather than < 40%). Some patients will have overlapping features of both disorders and this is referred to as marasmic kwashi- orkor 11 . In at-risk populations, kwashiorkor can develop after a child is weaned from breast milk and begins a diet rich in carbohydrates but deficient in protein. In addition to peripheral edema, patients with kwashiorkor also develop desquamation and erosions that have been likened to “enamel paint” and “flaky paint” ( Fig. 51.6 ). Based upon clinical observations, it was thought that kwashiorkor was due to a relative deficiency in protein intake . However, more recently, this proposed pathogenesis has been questioned based upon several findings. For example, protein intake was found to be similar in a group of children, irrespective of whether they had marasmus or kwashiorkor 12 . In addition, kwashiorkor can develop within just a few weeks of an acute, life-­ threatening illness. Both dapsone and N -hydroxy- dapsone undergo glucuronidation in the liver, which results in more water-soluble compounds that are rapidly excreted in the urine 29 . Medical Therapy Mechanism of Action Dapsone is clinically most useful in the treatment of dermatologic diseases involving neutrophilic infiltrates. Researchers have demon- strated that dapsone inhibits neutrophil myeloperoxidase, thus reducing damage from the neutrophil respiratory burst mediated by this enzyme. Furthermore, dapsone has been shown to inhibit neutrophil chemotaxis to N -formyl-methionyl-leucyl-phenylalanine (fMLP) and to interfere with the CD11b/CD18-mediated neutrophil binding that induces chemoattractant signal transduction. IgA adherence is also inhibited. It is of clinical interest that dapsone also inhibits eosinophil myeloperoxidase activity, and thus may be efficacious in diseases in which eosinophils have a central role in pathogenesis, such as eosino- philic cellulitis 30 . Dosages Dapsone is available in 25 and 100 mg tablets. The initial dose is often 50 mg/day in a single dose. Most conditions require 50–200 mg/day for adequate control of symptoms; rarely are dosages up to 300 mg/day required. In those with DH who respond to dapsone, rapid resolution of symptoms (within 48 hours) is usually noted; conversely, symptoms flare relatively rapidly after discontinuing therapy. Patients must be strictly warned against self-adjustment of the dosage, due to dose- dependent side effects. Because of potential adverse effects, any cardiopulmonary or neuro- logic symptoms should be assessed prior to therapy. Documentation of peripheral motor nerve function may occasionally be necessary before or during therapy. Table 130.3 outlines monitoring guidelines for therapy. The clinician must be aware of all signs and symptoms associated with methemoglobinemia and peripheral neuropathy to ensure proper monitoring. Major Side Effects Serious systemic side effects of dapsone may be idiosyncratic or pharmacologic. The pharmacologic and dose-dependent adverse effects include methemoglobinemia and hemolytic anemia (see Table 130.5 ). Agranulocytosis, peripheral motor neuropathy, and dapsone hypersen- sitivity are idiosyncratic reactions; however, patients on higher daily doses or long-term therapy may be more likely to develop a peripheral motor neuropathy. Although rare, dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome may be fatal. Patients present with fever, hepatitis, and a generalized cutaneous eruption. Cutaneous reactions range from an exanthem- atous eruption to toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). Liver failure has occurred in patients with the dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome 31 , and hypothyroidism may develop following resolution of the acute eruption. Thus, there

In one prospective series, non-White children and adoles- cents were more likely to present with melanomas that were clinically amelanotic, on the extremities, and nodular subtype, compared to White children and adolescents, who presented more frequently with superficial spreading melanomas 71 . Histologically, melanomas in children may resemble those of adults, but melanomas with features resembling Spitz nevus or deep penetrating nevus are reported to be more common in this age group. As noted above, the differentiation of melanoma from atypical Spitz tumor (Spitz melano- cytoma), pigmented epithelial melanocytoma, or other indeterminate melanocytic neoplasms remains a diagnostic challenge. Additional molecular tests (e.g. CGH, FISH, GEP, NGS [see below]) are often required to avoid overdiagnosis of childhood melanoma 105 . Prognosis and survival of pediatric melanoma is stage-dependent, similar to that in adults 106 . As such, treatment should follow the same rationale, regardless of age. DIAGNOSIS Early detection is a key factor for improving survival in patients with melanoma. The clinical diagnosis of cutaneous melanoma continues to be based on visual inspection and dermoscopy. A history of change in the color, shape, or size of a pigmented skin lesion over the course of months or years is the most sensitive clinical sign for melanoma, and it may be detected by the patient or by serial screening examinations plus dermoscopy. In high-risk patients, the latter may be supplemented with comparison of stored digital and dermoscopic images and/or total body photography. Public awareness campaigns have highlighted the ABCDEs of melanoma: A symmetry, B order irregularity, C olor variegation, D iameter > 5 mm, and E volution. It has been shown that patients more commonly recognize a melanoma by the development of a new pigmented lesion or by an increase in size or change in color of a pre-existing lesion, highlighting the importance of “E” 107 . Additionally, the ABCD features broadly overlap with clinically atypical melanocytic nevi, including those that are banal and have low-grade histologic dysplasia, making ABCD less specific as warning signs for melanoma in certain patients. Dermatologists often unconsciously rely on cognitive (overall pattern) and comparative (ugly duckling sign) processes rather than an algorithm of morphologic criteria (ABCD). A diagnostic clue is the so-called “ugly duckling” sign , which focuses on the morphologic differences between a single striking lesion and the surrounding benign “signature”

Question: In skin resurfacing procedures, what four clinical signs are used to assess the depth of wounding, and what findings should raise clinical suspicion of a wound infection?

Depth of wounding can be assessed by the level of frosting, the time for frosting to appear, the time for frosting to disappear, and skin turgor (as well as epidermal slide, the sliding of the epidermis off the dermis due to separation of the two tissues). Suspicion of wound infection should be raised by delayed wound healing, ulcerations, excessive necrotic material and crusting, purulent drainage, or odor, and an acneiform eruption or pustular folliculitis can also indicate infection. Such suspicion warrants immediate empiric antimicrobial therapy, culture for organism identification, and wound debridement as needed. Question: According to this excerpt, why is formaldehyde considered particularly hazardous compared to other disinfectants, and what dual role does it play in skin reactions?

Formaldehyde is more irritating than alcohols and has high chemical reactivity with proteins, allowing it to cause skin reactions even at low concentrations. It acts as both an irritant and an allergen, meaning it can provoke both irritant contact dermatitis and allergic sensitization. [Chapter: 15 Irritant Contact Dermatitis, p.360-361]

Vidimos Mohs Micrographic Surgery There are four major components: surgical excision, histopatho- logic examination, precise mapping, and wound management. The surgical component consists of removing a disc of tissue with a bev- eled surgical margin ( Fig. 150.1A ). The disc of tissue, or “layer”, ensures that the entire 360° of tumor margin is circumferentially removed and examined. The histopathologic component involves cryopreserving this disc and cutting it in a horizontal fashion, then mounting sections onto glass slides, followed by staining and micro- scopic examination for residual tumor. This processing technique differs from standard excisions in which specimens are formalin- fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) and cut in a “bread-loaf” fashion ( Fig. 150.1B ). Precise mapping entails marking any residual tumor on the map of the excision with the remaining positive area of tumor re- excised as indicated. This three-step process is repeated until there is no residual tumor identified microscopically. During this procedure, the Mohs surgeon has complete control of the excised tissue, includ- ing laboratory processing and interpretation of the tissue sections, as well as precise mapping. In the fourth step, wound management , the tumor-free defect is surgically closed or allowed to heal by second intention. INTRODUCTION Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) is a specialized method for skin cancer removal that combines surgery with pathology resulting in an excellent cure rate. The goals are to remove only the cancerous tissue while viewing the complete margin, thereby preserving the maximum amount of normal tissue (i.e. tissue-sparing). From a functional, aes- thetic and reconstructive perspective, tissue-sparing is especially impor- tant for skin cancers in the periorbital, nasal, auricular, perioral, digital, and anogenital areas. MMS is also the preferred treatment method for skin cancers that are clinically poorly defined, recurrent, and/or have a higher risk of recurrence because of histologic features or anatomic location ( Table 150.1 ). Question: During Mohs micrographic surgery, why is the scalpel held at a 30–60° angle to the skin surface when excising the first MMS layer, and what is done to the excised layer and surrounding tissue before it is fully removed to ensure correct orientation?

Question: How can donor lymphocyte infusion (DLI) affect the classic timing of acute graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD)?

Leishmaniasis and HIV Co-infection of HIV and leishmaniasis can alter the progression and presentation of leishmaniasis, especially the visceral form (see Ch. 78 ) 25 . HIV infection increases the risk of developing visceral leishmaniasis 100- to over 2000-fold, with the prevalence of visceral leishmaniasis ranging from 4% to > 15% among HIV-infected patients who live in Leishmania -endemic areas 25 . Co-infection often results in an atypical clinical presentation, reduced therapeutic response, and increased mortality. Chronic immune activation from the Leishmania infection may lead to increased HIV load and accelerated progression of AIDS, while the immunosuppressed state from the HIV infection creates an ideal environment for parasitic growth 24 . Pathology Histologically, cutaneous lesions typically show ulceration, pseudo- epitheliomatous hyperplasia, and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate composed of histiocytes, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils. Amastigotes present within dermal macrophages, especially those in the papillary dermis ( Fig. 83.12 ), are evident in ∼ 50% of skin biopsies. Over time, lesions develop an increasing number of giant cells and fewer parasites; in longstanding cutaneous leishmaniasis, tuberculoid granulomas with caseation necrosis may be observed. In the cicatricial stage, the epidermis becomes flattened and hyperpigmented in areas with dermal fibrosis. Identical changes are seen in mucosal lesions. In diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis, numerous amastigotes are present within foamy histiocytes; in contrast, the disseminated form features a primarily lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with few amastigotes. The parasite can be detected in the lymph nodes, bone marrow, and spleen in patients with visceral leishmaniasis. Question: How does integrin α6β4 differ from most other integrin heterodimers in terms of its cytoplasmic domain size and subcellular localization within epithelial cells?

Most integrin subunits have cytoplasmic domains of ≤50 amino acid residues, but integrin subunit β4 has a much larger cytoplasmic domain of >1000 amino acid residues. Unlike other integrins, integrin α6β4 is concentrated within hemidesmosomes of epithelial cells rather than being distributed more broadly. Question: In a patient taking lenalidomide, what two drug-interaction concerns should be monitored: one related to concomitant digoxin use and one related to concomitant prothrombotic agents such as estrogen, IVIg, or erythropoietin?

In general, these living skin substitutes are indicated for venous and diabetic ulcers. There are also biologic dressings that consist of just an extracellular matrix (i.e. they have no cellular component). Structural extracellular matrix components, such as collagen, fibronectin, and proteoglycans, provide a temporary scaffold that supports cellular proliferation and migration. In addition, they contain cytokines, e.g. TGF- β , bFGF, which promote wound healing. These dressings are also used for diabetic and venous ulcers. Another approach is a bio-inspired artificial hydrogel matrix that utilizes natural enzymatic reactions to become bioactive. It is able to incorporate and then deliver biomolecules (e.g. MMPs, growth factors) and at the same time be degraded and remodeled by them, ultimately being replaced by newly formed tissue. Emerging therapies include application of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal cells, mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles, and spraying of autologous fibroblasts and keratinocytes onto the wound 33,34 . Topical and oral medications Daily, short-contact application of topical tretinoin solution (0.05%; currently requires compounding) was reported to stimulate granulation tissue formation and healing of chronic leg ulcers 35 . Application of small amounts of 0.025% tretinoin cream was also observed to induce neovascularization in ischemic wound beds 15 . Daily application of 0.5% timolol maleate solution (one drop per 2 cm of wound perimeter) can also improve healing of chronic diabetic and venous leg ulcers via promotion of keratinocyte migration 36 . Topical growth factors, in particular PDGF, have been utilized to enhance wound healing (see below). Pentoxifylline, a drug that targets inflammatory cytokine release, leukocyte activation and platelet aggregation at the microcirculatory level, is occasionally a component of the treatment regimen for chronic venous insufficiency. Although evidence of a beneficial effect when the drug is used as monotherapy is largely lacking, pentoxifylline has been shown (at a dose of 1200 mg/day), in conjunction with compression therapy, to modestly improve ulcer healing as compared to compression plus placebo 37 . Question: Histopathologically, how can an irritated seborrheic keratosis (SK) be distinguished from squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and from Bowen disease, given that squamous eddies can appear in both irritated SK and SCC?

Although squamous eddies may be abundant in both irritated SK and SCC, irritated SK shows no evidence of dermal involvement, distinguishing it from invasive SCC. Bowen disease (SCC in situ) differs by showing a preponderance of atypical keratinocytes with vacuolated cytoplasm, closely crowded nuclei, abundant mitoses, and parakeratosis, with involvement of the adnexal epithelium; some cases also show a Borst–Jadassohn clonal/nested pattern with greater keratinocyte atypia. Question: What is trichorrhexis invaginata, and what characteristic appearance does it produce on trichoscopy of eyelashes and eyebrow hair in patients with Netherton syndrome?

Trichorrhexis invaginata is a hair shaft abnormality in which the distal hair shaft becomes telescoped into the proximal segment, producing a ball-and-socket appearance with a twist in the hair shaft; it is a highly characteristic light microscopic finding in clipped hairs of Netherton syndrome patients. On trichoscopy of eyelashes and eyebrow hair, this abnormality may appear as a "matchstick" or "golf tee" pattern. [Chapter: 57 Ichthyoses, Erythrokeratodermas, and Related Disorders, p.1119-1120]

Non-ablative FP uses focused, mid-IR, laser microbeams to create a pixelated pattern of microscopic columns of thermal damage, called microthermal treatment zones (MTZs). Typically, ~1 million MTZs are placed per full-face treatment. Density (percentage of skin treated) and depth of thermal damage are separately controlled. The energy delivered per MTZ accurately controls the depth of treatment which is typically up to ~2 mm, i.e. well into the reticular dermis. In general, the depth of thermal damage should correlate with the depth of skin pathology being treated, e.g. a greater depth for hypertrophic scars than for atrophic scars 33 . Desquamation of the epidermal portion of each MTZ removes some basal layer pigment and a small amount of papillary dermal debris. Question: In fractional photothermolysis (FP), what are microthermal treatment zones (MTZs), how many are typically created during a full-face non-ablative treatment, and how does the depth of thermal damage relate to the type of scar being treated?

MTZs are microscopic columns of thermal damage created by focused, mid-IR laser microbeams in a pixelated pattern; about 1 million MTZs are typically placed per full-face non-ablative treatment. The depth of thermal damage, which can extend up to about 2 mm into the reticular dermis, should correlate with the depth of the skin pathology being treated—for example, a greater treatment depth is used for hypertrophic scars than for atrophic scars. Question: According to the table on chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) prognosis, what is the prognostic significance of 13q deletion versus 17p deletion and TP53 mutation?

Question: According to the excerpt, why is salicylic acid particularly well-suited for use as a comedolytic agent in the treatment of acne, and what is its mechanism of action on the stratum corneum?

Salicylic acid is favored among hydroxy acids for acne treatment because it can penetrate into the milieu of the sebaceous unit, inducing exfoliation in the oily areas of the face. Mechanistically, it is thought to work by solubilizing the intercellular cement, thereby reducing corneocyte adhesion, and it eliminates the stratum corneum layer by layer from the outermost level downward, in contrast to α-hydroxy acids. Question: How does the site of amyloid deposition differ between localized (organ-limited) and systemic forms of amyloidosis, in relation to the site of precursor protein synthesis?

In localized (organ-limited) amyloidosis, amyloid deposition occurs at or near the site where the precursor protein is synthesized, confining disease to a single organ such as the skin. In systemic (generalized) amyloidosis, the precursor proteins are instead secreted into the circulation and amyloid deposition occurs at distant sites, leading to involvement of multiple organ systems. Question: How can urticaria and exanthematous (morbilliform) drug eruptions be distinguished based on their primary lesion type and duration of individual lesions?

Urticaria presents with edematous wheals with an erythematous flare, and each individual lesion is transient, lasting less than 24 hours (though it may become chronic overall if present beyond 6 weeks). In contrast, exanthematous drug eruptions present as pink to red-brown, blanching macules and papules (which may become purpuric on the distal lower extremities), and the eruption as a whole spontaneously resolves over 7–10 days if the inciting drug is stopped, rather than individual lesions resolving within a day. Question: Why can bacterial cultures often be negative in delayed nodules caused by biofilm formation after soft tissue filler injection, and what preventive measure is recommended prior to injection to reduce this risk?

Standard culturing techniques are not sensitive enough to detect biofilm-related bacterial infections, so cultures are often falsely negative even though infection is present. To help prevent biofilm formation, the skin should be cleansed with an antimicrobial agent such as chlorhexidine prior to injection, taking care to avoid the ear canal and eye. Question: In a woman pregnant with a fetus affected by steroid sulfatase deficiency (X-linked recessive ichthyosis), why does labor often fail to initiate or progress spontaneously, and how is this typically managed?

Steroid sulfatase deficiency in the fetal placenta prevents adequate deconjugation of DHEAS, which is necessary for estrogen synthesis, resulting in low or absent estrogen levels in maternal urine and amniotic fluid. This estrogen deficiency leads to insufficient cervical dilation, so labor often fails to start or progress spontaneously. Oxytocin administration can only partially overcome this problem, often necessitating cesarean delivery. [Chapter: 57 Ichthyoses, Erythrokeratodermas, and Related Disorders, p.1105-1106]

Question: What structural modification in ixekizumab's hinge region prevents Fab-arm exchange with endogenous human IgG4, and why is this modification important for its mechanism of action?

Ixekizumab has a proline substituted for serine in its hinge region, which prevents formation of half-antibodies (half-mers) that could otherwise undergo Fab-arm exchange with endogenous human IgG4. This ensures the antibody remains intact as a functional IgG4 monoclonal antibody capable of binding and neutralizing IL-17A homodimers and IL-17A/F heterodimers. Question: In a patient with definite or suspected HHT, what imaging test is recommended to detect hepatic AVMs, and why is liver biopsy avoided in this evaluation?

Doppler ultrasonography, multiphase contrast CT, or contrast MRI of the liver is recommended to detect hepatic AVMs, which are present in 30%-80% of HHT patients though symptomatic in less than 10%. Liver biopsy should be avoided because of the risk associated with the underlying vascular malformations, with further testing and treatment guided by imaging findings and symptoms instead. Mast cells Mast cells are a hematopoietic cell population that normally resides in skin and mucous membranes. This estab- lishes the shape of the skin and ensures that the skin retains its shape in response to mechanical stress. During tissue repair, fibroblasts next to the site of injury become activated, reconstitute new ECM, and restore proper matrix tension. In 1951, Sulzberger and colleagues 2 first reported the use of systemic cortisone and adreno- corticotropic hormone (ACTH) as therapies for inflammatory skin diseases. One year later, Sulzberger and Witten successfully treated eczematous eruptions with topical hydrocortisone. Question: Why do disorders such as hepatic or renal disease that decrease plasma binding proteins augment both the therapeutic effects and toxicities of exogenous glucocorticoids?

As exogenous glucocorticoids saturate CBG binding sites, more drug binds to low-affinity albumin, but when albumin and other binding proteins are reduced (as in hepatic or renal disease), a greater fraction of the glucocorticoid remains free (unbound). Because this free fraction is the biologically active form that enters cells and mediates glucocorticoid effects, its increase enhances both the therapeutic benefits and the toxic effects of the drug. Question: By what two mechanisms does hydroquinone reduce skin pigmentation, and why is its use recommended to be avoided during pregnancy?

Hydroquinone reduces pigmentation by competing with tyrosine as a substrate for tyrosinase, the initial enzyme in melanin biosynthesis, and by causing selective damage to melanosomes and melanocytes through production of reactive oxygen radicals. Because topical hydroquinone can be substantially absorbed systemically (about 30%–50%) and there are no adequate studies in pregnant women, its use is recommended to be avoided during pregnancy despite animal reproduction studies not consistently showing adverse fetal effects. Question: According to this excerpt, what is a cosmeceutical, and why does it not fit neatly under the US Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act's definition of a cosmetic?

A cosmeceutical is defined as a scientifically designed, useful product for external application to the body that has desirable aesthetic effects while meeting rigid chemical, physical, and medical standards, and it is intended to improve skin functioning rather than just its appearance. However, the 1938 Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act defines a cosmetic only as an article applied to the body for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering appearance, without affecting structure or function. Since cosmeceuticals are designed to influence the biologic function of the stratum corneum, they exceed this regulatory definition, and no formal regulatory category currently exists to acknowledge their scientific sophistication. Systematic Reviews A systematic review identifies completed studies that address a specific research question and then aggregates and statistically analyzes the results across studies, to arrive at a conclusion about a body of research 1 . Although traditionally applied to RCTs, systematic reviews can also draw data from observational studies. A systematic review should have a written protocol addressing the research question it seeks to answer, utilize comprehensive and unbiased methods for identifying studies, and clearly describe the statistical aspects of the review, i.e. meta-analysis. It should also include a summary estimate of effect plus CI based on the findings of all eligible studies (see Fig. 123.3 ). In addition, it should have an assessment of heterogeneity across the studies used, to indicate the degree of variability in the findings in different studies. It should address publication bias by taking into account unpublished studies, as positive studies are more likely to get published. It also usually includes subgroup analyses based on additional measures done by some or all of the studies that are supplemental to the main research question. If any of the design decisions were questionable or arbitrary, analyses should be done to assess how sensitive the findings of the meta-analysis are to decisions taken in designing particular studies or inclusion of certain studies. Here, the less sensitive the study the better. The characteristics and the findings of individual studies should be displayed clearly in tables and figures to allow the reader to visualize the data and not rely solely on the conclusions of the meta-analysis 2,23 . Question: How do glomus bodies help maintain blood supply to the distal digits in a cold environment, and where in the nail unit are they most commonly found?

In cold conditions, arteriolar constriction occurs, but arteriovenous anastomoses called Sucquet–Hoyer canals within glomus bodies help maintain adequate blood flow to the distal digits. Glomus bodies are encapsulated oval structures containing modified smooth muscle cells that dilate upon cold exposure. The two pedicle variations are: (1) a deep pedicle created immediately beneath the skin island by dissecting away surrounding superficial subcutaneous tissue to eliminate tethering, and (2) a laterally based pedicle created by tunneling beneath the island while preserving vascularized sheets of subcutaneous and muscle tissue to one or both sides. Deep pedicles work well in locations with elastic, spongy subcutaneous tissue, whereas lateral pedicles are preferred for defects in tighter skin with less spongy subcutaneous tissue, especially where a good lateral blood supply (often facial muscle) is available. Question: In clinical trials of pembrolizumab for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), what overall response rates (ORRs) were observed in patients with unresectable versus recurrent/metastatic disease, and what biomarker was associated with significantly higher response rates?

Pembrolizumab produced an ORR of 42% in patients with unresectable cSCC and 32% in those with recurrent or metastatic cSCC; it is FDA-approved for the recurrent/metastatic group. Across more than one study, patients whose tumors were PD-L1 positive had significantly higher response rates than those with PD-L1–negative tumors, supporting a role for immunohistochemical PD-L1 evaluation when considering immunotherapy. Question: How can rheumatoid vasculitis be distinguished from mixed cryoglobulinemia based on rheumatoid factor (RF) titer and complement levels, given that both conditions can present with arthritis, RF, and complement activation?

In rheumatoid vasculitis, the RF titer is significantly higher, and both C3 and C4 levels are decreased. In contrast, in mixed cryoglobulinemia, C4 levels are low but C3 levels are relatively normal. This pattern of complement consumption, along with the RF titer difference, helps differentiate the two entities despite their overlapping clinical features. Question: How does the depth of acantholysis within the epidermis help distinguish pemphigus foliaceus from pemphigus vulgaris, and what histologic feature explains this difference?

Acantholysis refers to loss of keratinocyte cohesion due to desmosome disruption, which can occur at any epidermal level, but its depth serves as a diagnostic clue.
