In 1966, the clinical features of this entity were distinguished from those of ichthyosis vulgaris 5 . The underlying steroid sulfatase deficiency was identified in the late 1970s 6 . Epidemiology The worldwide incidence is between 1 in 2000 and 1 in 9500 male births. It is an X-linked recessive disorder that is transmitted by asymp- tomatic female carriers and almost exclusively affects boys and men. Pathogenesis Diminution or complete absence of steroid sulfatase activity is caused by a deletion of the entire STS gene on chromosome Xp22.31 in ~90% of patients and inactivating mutations in others 16 . Steroid sulfatase deficiency results in impaired hydrolysis of cholesterol sulfate and dehydroepiandros- terone sulfate (DHEAS), with subsequent accumulation of cholesterol 3-sulfate in the epidermis. High levels of this metabolite can inhibit trans- glutaminase-1, explaining the partial overlap with lamellar ichthyosis. In women pregnant with an affected fetus, steroid sulfatase deficiency in the fetal placenta causes low or absent levels of estrogen in the urine and amniotic fluid because of inadequate deconjugation of DHEAS, which is necessary for estrogen synthesis. As a result, labor often fails to initiate spontaneously or progress, due to insufficient dilation of the cervix. This can only be partially overcome by oxytocin administration, often necessitating cesarean delivery. Clinical Features In ~90% of affected boys, steroid sulfatase deficiency presents during the neonatal period with mild erythroderma and generalized peeling, often with exfoliation of large, translucent scales. The typical polygonal, dark-brown, adherent scales develop later during infancy or childhood and are distributed symmetrically on the extremities, trunk, and neck ( Fig. 57.5 ). The scales are occasionally grayish or white, and they tend to be larger on the lower extremities. Involvement of the preauricular area and neck is highly characteristic, which has resulted in the descriptive term “dirty neck disease” (see Fig. 57.5D ); however, other skin folds are often not affected. The palms, soles, and remainder of the face are typically spared. Fine scaling of the scalp is frequently seen during early childhood but diminishes over time. Many human cancers are characterized by increased expression of VEGF-A by tumor cells and by increased expression of VEGF receptors by tumor-associated blood vessels. VEGF-A also promotes skin carcinogenesis, in that selective transgenic overexpression of VEGF-A in epidermal keratinocytes resulted in enhanced tumor development and metastasis 16 . Placental growth factor (PlGF) is a member of the VEGF family and two isoforms, PlGF-1 (149 amino acids) and PlGF-2 (170 amino acids), are expressed in human skin. Similar to VEGF-A, PlGF expression is upregulated in cutaneous SCCs, epidermal keratinocytes at the advancing wound edge, and hyperplastic psoriatic epidermis. In contrast to VEGF, PlGF does not activate VEGFR-2 (KDR) but selectively binds to VEGFR-1 (see Fig. 102.9 ). In addition, the heparin-binding isoform PlGF-2 binds to the neuropilin-1 receptor. Evidence from genetic mouse models indicates that PlGF and VEGF-A act in synergy to induce both angiogenesis and vascular leakage and that PlGF exerts proinflam- matory effects 17 . A number of additional pro-angiogenic molecules are upregulated in angiogenic skin conditions, including interleukin-8, PDGF, bFGF, and several angiogenic chemokines 18 . Thrombospondin (TSP)-1 and TSP-2 are major inhibitors of cutaneous angiogenesis that are expressed in normal human skin. These matri- cellular proteins mediate interactions between extracellular matrix molecules and cellular integrin receptors. TSP-1 inhibits endothelial cell proliferation in vitro and angiogenesis in vivo . In normal human skin, TSP-1 is expressed by dermal cells and by epidermal keratino- cytes. Question: Q-switched lasers are highly effective for lentigines and nevi due to their targeting of melanosomes, but why do they not perform as well as expected for melasma despite melasma also involving increased melanin in epidermal melanocytes and dermal melanophages?

Melasma histology shows an admixture of epidermal and dermal pigmentation within a single lesion rather than a clean, discrete target, and dermal melanin deposits (within melanophages) respond poorly to therapy in general. Question: What is the Auspitz sign, and what histologic changes does it reflect?

The Auspitz sign is the appearance of a wet surface with characteristic pinpoint bleeding when the superficial silvery white (micaceous) scales of a psoriatic lesion are removed. It is the clinical reflection of elongated, dilated dermal papillary vessels together with thinning of the suprapapillary epidermis. [Chapter: 8 Psoriasis, p.194]

Question: For postexposure varicella prophylaxis in nonimmune immunocompromised individuals or pregnant women, what are three options besides varicella vaccination, and what is the typical timing/dosing for each?

Options include: (1) varicella-zoster immunoglobulin, which provides passive protection lasting about 3 weeks; (2) intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) at ≥400 mg/kg, which contains high levels of varicella-specific IgG; and (3) prophylactic oral acyclovir at usual varicella dosing for 1 week, starting 7–10 days after exposure. Postexposure varicella vaccination itself is only an option for nonimmune, immunocompetent individuals ≥12 months old, not for immunocompromised or pregnant patients. The typical histo- pathologic changes of lichen sclerosus et atrophicus were published by Ferdinand Jean Darier in 1892. Unna, Westberg, von Zumbusch, and others elucidated the clinical features of LS in various case reports 69 . Question: In women and girls, what is the classic distribution and appearance of vulvar lichen sclerosus, and what architectural changes can occur with untreated or severe disease?

In women and girls, lichen sclerosus classically presents as vulvar hypopigmentation with thin, wrinkled, atrophic skin distributed in a figure-of-eight pattern encircling the vulvar and perianal region, often with focal hyperkeratosis, erosions, and fissures (especially at the perineum), plus purpura, telangiectasias, and occasionally hemorrhagic bullae. Because it is a scarring disease, architectural changes such as burying of the clitoris from midline fusion or fusion of the labia minora to the labia majora can develop, and in untreated or severe cases there may be total loss of the labia minora. Question: In a patient with suspected solar urticaria, how can phototesting with a water filter help distinguish this condition from heat urticaria, and what clinical/laboratory features help differentiate it from erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP)?

Phototesting of solar urticaria typically produces a wheal within minutes, and using a water filter in front of the light source removes heat, allowing exclusion of heat urticaria as the cause. In contrast to solar urticaria, patients with EPP report deep-seated pain after sun exposure rather than whealing, and they have elevated free RBC protoporphyrin levels. It is considered to represent a variant of Lynch syndrome, which is also known as hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) syndrome 39 . History Muir in 1967 and Torre in 1968 independently reported the syndrome that bears their names. Their two patients had malignancies in several organs plus either keratoacanthoma-like lesions or multiple tumors of sebaceous origin. Epidemiology The male : female ratio in MTS is 3 : 2, and affected individuals present with cutaneous manifestations at a mean age of 55 years. The preva- lence of Lynch syndrome in the general population is estimated to be ~1 in 350. In a study of Lynch syndrome patients, MTS was observed in 28% (14/50) of families and 9% (14/152) of individuals with a confirmed germline mismatch repair gene mutation 40 . Pathogenesis MTS is caused by heterozygous germline mutations in one of several DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, including MSH2 (90% of MTS cases), MLH1 , and rarely MSH6 or PMS2 . MMR proteins are respon- sible for detecting and repairing DNA replication errors. In patients with MTS, somatic inactivation of the other allele of the affected gene (loss of heterozygosity) results in microsatellite instability, i.e. increased variability in the lengths of repetitive “microsatellite” sequences in the genome, as well as mutations that lead to tumor formation 41 . The skin tumors sometimes appear decades before or after a visceral malig- nancy develops. Question: In Muir–Torre syndrome, what proportion of DNA mismatch repair gene mutations occur in MSH2, and what is the pathogenic mechanism by which tumors develop in affected individuals?

MSH2 mutations account for about 90% of Muir–Torre syndrome cases, with MLH1 and rarely MSH6 or PMS2 accounting for the remainder. Definite PHACE(S) can be diagnosed in two ways: (1) a hemangioma greater than 5 cm in diameter located on the head, including the scalp, plus 1 major criterion or 2 minor criteria; or (2) a hemangioma of the neck, upper trunk, or trunk and proximal upper extremity plus 2 major criteria. Question: When a cutaneous follicular lymphoma shows clear-cut Bcl-2 positivity within the neoplastic follicles, what does this suggest about the origin of the lesion, and what immunophenotypic features distinguish PCMZLD from secondary cutaneous B-CLL?

Clear-cut Bcl-2 positivity within neoplastic follicles of a cutaneous follicular lymphoma is a hint (though exceptions occur) that the lesion represents secondary cutaneous involvement by a primary extracutaneous (nodal) follicular lymphoma rather than a primary cutaneous follicular center lymphoma. To distinguish PCMZLD from secondary cutaneous B-CLL, one should note that B-CLL lacks plasma cells belonging to the neoplastic clone, whereas PCMZLD typically has monoclonal plasma cells; also, cutaneous B-CLL is usually CD5-positive, a feature practically never seen in PCMZLD. Question: PORCN encodes an O-acyltransferase required for palmitoylation and secretion of Wnt. Given Wnt's effects on fibroblast proliferation, adipogenesis, and osteogenesis, how does PORCN dysfunction explain three characteristic clinical/radiographic findings in Goltz syndrome?

Wnt signaling normally stimulates fibroblast proliferation, inhibits adipogenesis, and induces osteogenesis. Loss of PORCN function impairs Wnt secretion, leading to dermal hypoplasia (from reduced fibroblast proliferation), fat "herniations" (from disinhibited adipogenesis), and osteopathia striata, or streaks of decreased bone density (from impaired osteogenesis). Question: According to this excerpt, why do desmosomal defects often lead to both impaired keratinization (e.g., palmoplantar keratoderma) and cardiomyopathy?

Desmosomes are intercellular junctions that anchor intermediate filaments to the cell surface and provide strong cell–cell adhesion, which is critical in tissues subjected to substantial mechanical stress. Inflammation A critical role of inflammation is to deliver neutrophils and other leu- kocytes to a site of injury and then activate these cells to perform their function of protecting the host against infection. Neutrophils are among the first cells to arrive at sites of inflammation. Reasons for this include their abundance in the bloodstream and their rapid response to chemo- kines. When activated, neutrophils move at speeds up to 30 microns/ min – the fastest cell in the body. The motile responses of neutrophils to microbial infection include emigration out of the vasculature and movement toward the source of the inflammatory chemoattractant. This culminates in the phagocytic ingestion of opsonized microbes. In order to arrive at the site of infec- tion, leukocytes must migrate out of the vasculature via margination, rolling, activation, and tight adhesion (see Ch. 102 ). They then move toward the site of injury or infection (see Table 25.1 ) and eventually undergo degranulation then apoptosis. The price to be paid for the defensive potency of neutrophils for destroy- ing microbes and necrotic tissues is that they can injure normal tissue. During activation and phagocytosis, neutrophils release products (e.g. lysosomal enzymes, reactive oxygen intermediates, products of arachi- donic acid metabolism [prostaglandins and leukotrienes]) not just within Neutrophilic Dermatoses the phagolysosome, but also into the extracellular space. Endothelial injury and tissue damage ensue, thus contributing to a number of acute and chronic diseases that affect the skin as well as other organs. Evaluation of Beauty and the Aging Face ANATOMIC BASIS FOR THE AGING APPEARANCE Knowledge of facial anatomy and anatomic changes that occur with aging is essential for properly evaluating and treating the aesthetic patient. With aging, both the golden ratio (Phi) and the neoclassical canons start to shift. The upper one-third of the face elongates due to recession of the frontal hairline and brow ptosis, while proportionately the middle third remains relatively stable (but may elongate with nasal tip ptosis). However, midface volume loss can occur as a result of fat redistribution and skeletal changes. The lower third of the face becomes shortened with perioral fat redistribution and significant resorption of the bony mandible, which may also lead to shifts in dentition, further affecting aesthetics of the lower face and smile. The appearance of the aging face is multifactorial and does not appear to simply be a matter of sagging from the effect of years of gravitational forces pulling the face downwards. Rather, a complex ongoing alter- ation in proportions occurs as one ages. Notably, studies by Rohrich and Pessa 17 have shown that there is not one large confluent layer of subcutaneous fat in the face but rather multiple distinct compartments that act independently from one another (see below, Volume changes). For example, the malar fat pad in the mid cheek is composed of three separate compartments; as these compartments change in size, the ligaments separating the compartments become more evident and a smooth, rounded, youthful appearance transforms into the multi- contoured aged face. After examining numerous photographs of patients as they aged, Lambros 18 concluded that there is actually very little positional change in the midface region. Despite the common perception that the face drops inferiorly with age, he noted that the eyelid–cheek margin did not change with advancing years, nor did facial nevi of the midface descend with age. Just as individual water molecules simply move up and down rather than actually traveling with waves at sea, the wave of downward motion “seen” in an aging face may simply represent shifts in subcuta- neous tissue. With aging, the upper third of the face elongates due to frontal hairline recession and brow ptosis, while the middle third remains relatively stable in proportion (though it may elongate with nasal tip ptosis) despite midface volume loss from fat redistribution and skeletal changes. Question: According to the diagnostic microscopic changes table, what histologic finding in eccrine glands is characteristic of syringotropic mycosis fungoides, and how does the eccrine gland finding in hypothyroidism differ from it?

Syringotropic mycosis fungoides shows a dense infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes within and around the eccrine glands, often accompanied by squamous syringometaplasia. Question: Why is KHE categorized by the WHO as an 'intermediate (locally aggressive)' soft tissue tumor rather than a malignant one, and what are the two most common causes of death associated with it?

KHE is classified as intermediate (locally aggressive) because, despite rare reports of spread along or multifocal involvement of local lymphatic chains (and one case of regional lymph node spread), no true distant metastases have been reported. Question: According to the excerpt, why is methotrexate contraindicated during pregnancy for non-neoplastic diseases, and what specific effects are associated with first trimester versus second/third trimester exposure?

Methotrexate carries an embryo-fetal toxicity warning and is contraindicated in pregnancy for non-neoplastic diseases. First trimester exposure is associated with spontaneous abortions and congenital malformations, including skull anomalies, facial dysmorphisms, central nervous system abnormalities, limb abnormalities, and cardiac anomalies, along with intellectual impairment. Second and third trimester exposure is instead associated with intrauterine growth restriction and functional abnormalities. Effective contraception is recommended during treatment and for 6 months after the final dose. [Chapter: 27 Pregnancy Dermatoses, p.621-622]

Occlusive dressings are unnecessary because the epidermis is not removed intraoperatively and instead serves as a biologic dressing until peeling occurs (though areas enhanced by manual dermasanding, lacking residual epidermis, may need occlusive dressings for the first 3 days). The standard regimen involves soaking the area four times daily with warm compresses—preferably a 0.25% acetic acid solution (1 tablespoon white vinegar per pint warm water), which is physiologic for healing tissue, mildly debriding, and antibacterial—followed by application of an occlusive emollient such as petrolatum, Aquaphor, or Eucerin after each soak and as needed between soaks. This showering, soaking, and emollient routine is continued for one week postoperatively. [Chapter: 154 Chemical and Mechanical Skin Resurfacing, p.3150]

 Nail products – nail polish, nail sculptures  Cosmetics – facial foundation, blush, eyeshadow, mascara, lipstick Key features  Colored cosmetics and skin care products have an important role in the prevention of dermatologic disease and the maintenance of skin health  Hair is a non-living structure whose appearance and behavior can be improved via the use of shampoos and conditioners  Nail cosmetics primarily adorn the nails, but improper use can lead to nail disease  Cosmeceuticals are non-prescription products designed to improve the functioning of the skin, primarily by targeting the aging process  Skin, hair, and nail care products have a profound impact on these structures, and they should be part of the working knowledge of every dermatologist INTRODUCTION Cosmetics and skin care products are assuming an increasingly important role within dermatology as the sophistication of raw materials and the resulting formulations provide for the development of products that impact the functioning of the skin. It was traditionally thought that the stratum corneum was a non-living, biologically inert layer of the skin upon which skin care products and cosmetics impinge. It was also thought that the stratum corneum was a complete barrier unaffected by the application of non-prescription topical agents. An improved understanding of stratum corneum function, primarily obtained through the use of non-invasive bioengineering techniques, has demonstrated that the stratum corneum can be dramatically influ- enced by non-prescription topical agents, and that these agents can indeed penetrate the stratum corneum and influence skin function. Recognition of the biologic importance of the stratum corneum to skin health led to the development of a new category of skin care product, referred to as the cosmeceutical 1 . A cosmeceutical is a scien- tifically designed, useful product intended for external application to the human body that has desirable aesthetic effects and meets rigid chemical, physical, and medical standards 2 . Even though many cosme- ceuticals currently exist for use on the skin, hair and nails, there is no regulatory description that acknowledges the current scientific sophistication of these formulations. Rather, a cosmetic is defined by the US Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, written in 1938, as “articles intended to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled, or sprayed on, intro- duced into, or otherwise applied to the human body or any part thereof for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering the appearance”, without affecting structure or function 3 . Question: Griscelli syndrome results from mutations in myosin Va, RAB27A, or melanophilin, yet each subtype produces distinct extracutaneous phenotypes (e.g., neurologic vs. immunologic involvement). How is this variability explained, and what is the common pigmentary consequence in all forms?

The differing phenotypes among the three Griscelli syndrome subtypes are explained by the tissue-specific expression of the three genes—for example, some are expressed in neurons while others are expressed in cytotoxic T cells. However, all three genes are expressed in melanocytes, so in every form there is diffuse pigmentary dilution due to failure of melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes, with melanosomes instead congregating in the center of the melanocytes. Integrins Integrins are heterodimeric transmembrane receptors that promote cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions 21 . Ligand binding to integrin receptors modulates cell adhesion and growth, signal transduction, gene expression, and other fundamental biologic processes. All integrins are αβ -heterodimers. Numerous α - and β -subunits have been identified; several of these have alternatively spliced cytoplasmic domains (e.g. α 1 , α 3 , α 4 , α 6 , α 11b ). Although some of the α -subunits can associate with more than one β -subunit, the number of heterodimers formed is limited. Both α - and β -integrin subunits are glycoproteins with a single hydrophobic transmembrane domain and a cytoplasmic domain that is typically composed of ≤ 50 amino acid residues, although integrin subunit β 4 has a larger cytoplasmic domain of > 1000 amino acid residues. Cytologic atypia can vary markedly. Most tumors show well-circumscribed, pushing borders surrounded by compressed collagen. The lack of infiltrative growth into the surrounding stroma and abrupt tricholemmal keratinization helps to differentiate these cysts from SCC. Question: How do proliferating tricholemmal cysts and proliferating epidermoid cysts differ in terms of typical patient demographics, anatomic location, and clinical behavior/prognosis?

Proliferating tricholemmal cysts occur predominantly on the scalp (90%) and mostly in women (~85%), with a median age of 63; they generally behave benignly, though rare cases show aggressive local growth, recurrence, or metastasis, and spindle cell carcinoma may rarely arise within them. Proliferating epidermoid cysts, in contrast, are more common in men, with only 20% occurring on the scalp and the anogenital region being the most common site; in a follow-up series, 20% recurred (sometimes multiple times) and one patient died of intractable local disease, but none developed metastases. Question: When excising an epidermoid inclusion cyst, why is a liberal amount of local anesthesia injected into the surrounding tissue, and what should the fusiform excision include?

Injecting a liberal amount of local anesthesia into the surrounding tissue creates edema that establishes a plane between this edema and the cyst wall, facilitating dissection. The fusiform excision should include any poral opening or scarring attaching the cyst to the skin surface, and enough of the redundant, expanded tissue should be removed so that the resulting scar lies flat, even if this area is smaller than the region deformed by the cyst. Question: In photodynamic therapy, what is a 'type II photochemical reaction,' and by what process does the resulting reactive oxygen species eventually help terminate the light-driven reaction?

A type II photochemical (photosensitized) reaction is one mediated by oxygen, in which the excited triplet-state photosensitizer transfers its stored energy to molecular oxygen, generating singlet oxygen (and other reactive oxygen species) while the photosensitizer returns to its ground state. Because singlet oxygen and related species are highly reactive, they can chemically inactivate the photosensitizer itself—a process called photobleaching—which also destroys its fluorescence. This photobleaching is one way the light exposure during PDT automatically self-limits or shuts down the overall process. [Chapter: 135 Photodynamic Therapy, p.2851-2852]

Question: According to this excerpt, what are the characteristic cutaneous and clinical features of intravascular lymphoma, and why is it frequently diagnosed post mortem?

Intravascular lymphoma (more often B cell than T cell) presents with nonspecific skin lesions in about 40% of patients, including erythematous, sometimes painful plaques or nodules, macular or telangiectatic lesions, and occasionally retiform purpura, most commonly on the lower extremities (often with edema) followed by the trunk. Mycobacterium haemophilum Introduction M. haemophilum is a short, slightly curved rod that occurs singly or in a cord-like arrangement. It is a fastidious organism that requires ferric ions to grow, provided as hemin, hematin, hemoglobin, or ferric ammonium citrate. In initial studies, growth was only observed with the addition of hemolyzed sheep erythrocytes; as a consequence, the organism was given the name M. haemophilum 92,100 . Epidemiology and pathogenesis M. haemophilum infection occurs primarily in immunocompromised hosts, including people living with HIV, organ transplant recipients, and individuals receiving immunosuppressive medications 126 . However, this organism can also cause cervical lymphadenitis in healthy children, and cutaneous infections following tattooing (including permanent make-up) and acupuncture have been reported. The majority of affected individuals are from cities located near the ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, or the Great Lakes of North America 92,100 .The natural habitat of M. haemophilum has not yet been identified, although water reservoirs are suspected 92,100 . M. leprae and M. haemophilum are phylogeneti- cally related, which may explain why some individuals infected with M. haemophilum experience immune reconstitution events analogous to leprosy reactions (see above) 65 . Immunosuppressed adults typically present with one or more bluish- red tender pustules, papulonodules, or plaques, which evolve into abscesses and/or ulcers 92,102,126 . Lesions are usually located on the extremities, often overlying joints. M. haemophilum can also cause contiguous septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and pneumonia. In immuno- competent individuals, cutaneous inoculation can lead to papulo- nodules and pustules. Question: Why might Mycobacterium haemophilum infection be missed if a laboratory uses only routine mycobacterial culture techniques, and what special growth requirements does the organism have?

M. haemophilum is a fastidious organism that requires a source of iron (provided as hemin, hematin, hemoglobin, or ferric ammonium citrate) and a growth temperature between 30°C and 32°C, rather than standard incubation conditions. Because routine culture methods typically do not provide these specific requirements, the organism may fail to grow and thus go undetected unless the lab specifically accounts for these needs or uses PCR analysis instead. Miller 39 Diseases of the Eccrine and Apocrine Sweat Glands SWEAT GLANDS Key features  2–5 million eccrine glands are unevenly distributed over the skin surface  In healthy individuals, eccrine sweat is 99% water  Sweating is a reflex sympathetic autonomic function mediated by cholinergic neurons In humans, sweating is essential for thermoregulatory homeostasis. There are two main mechanisms for cooling the body: radiative cooling via cutaneous vasodilation and evaporative cooling via sweat. Sweat, primarily produced by the eccrine sweat glands, leads to dissipation of heat through evaporation. Few mammals except humans and horses produce sweat in sufficient quantities to affect thermoregulation. For the purposes of this discussion, the term “sweat” applies to eccrine glands and their secretory products unless otherwise specified. Although there are 2–5 million eccrine glands distributed within the skin, none are found on the clitoris, glans penis, labia minora, external auditory canal, or lips. Eccrine glands are separate from the apocrine– pilosebaceous apparatus, and by dermoscopy, eccrine ductal orifices can be seen along the dermatoglyphic ridges of the palms and soles. The average healthy adult can produce over 0.5 liters of sweat per hour, 99% of which is water. Athletes or those acclimatized to hot environ- ments can produce up to 3–4 liters per hour 1 . Compared to other indi- viduals, physically fit or acclimatized persons initiate sweating earlier and conserve sodium, chloride, and other electrolytes more efficiently. Thermoregulatory control is similar in men and women and dimin- ishes only slightly with age 2 . Sweating is a reflex function controlled primarily by the sympathetic nervous system. These nerves are anatomically sympathetic but func- tionally cholinergic, i.e. acetylcholine, rather than norepinephrine, is the principal terminal neurotransmitter. Neural impulses for sweat- ing (sudomotor impulses) travel from the anterior hypothalamus via the reticulospinal tracts to the appropriate level in the spinal cord, out through the rami communicantes to autonomic ganglia, and then within sympathetic cholinergic neurons to the secretory cells of the eccrine glands. Adrenergic innervation of eccrine glands has also been demonstrated, but is not believed to be physiologically important 3 . Question: In nonsuicidal self-injury, what are the typical methods and body sites involved, what is the purpose of the behavior, and what psychiatric conditions are most commonly associated with it?

Nonsuicidal self-injury typically involves inflicting shallow injuries via cutting, stabbing, or burning using objects such as a knife, razor, needle, cigarette, or vigorously rubbed eraser, most commonly on the dorsal forearms and anterior thighs. The behavior is done without suicidal intent, usually to reduce negative emotions or resolve an interpersonal difficulty. While classically associated with borderline personality disorder, depression and anxiety are actually more common in affected individuals. [Chapter: 7 Psychocutaneous Diseases, p.182]

Question: By what two mechanisms does HSV impair host immune cell function through induction of specific host proteins (SOCS-1 and Fas ligand)?

HSV can induce expression of suppressor of cytokine signaling-1 (SOCS-1) in keratinocytes, which abrogates the effects of IFN-γ, thereby blocking cytokine-mediated antiviral responses. Separately, HSV can induce expression of Fas ligand on the surface of monocytes/macrophages, which causes apoptosis of interacting T cells and NK cells, eliminating these immune effector cells. Question: Regarding the three-layer structure of the hair shaft, what is each layer (cuticle, cortex, medulla) composed of or responsible for?

The cuticle is the outermost layer and maintains hair fiber integrity. The cortex, which lies beneath it, contains the bulk of hair keratins and keratin-associated proteins, and hair fiber strength is largely attributable to disulfide bonding within this layer. The medulla, at the center, consists of loosely connected trichocytes with large intercellular air spaces and provides insulation in animals. [Chapter: 68 Biology of Hair and Nails, p.1406-1407]

The pathogenesis of drug-induced SLE is not well understood, but one possibility is that reactive drug metabolites, interacting with nuclear histones, could act as haptens and activate the complement cascade. For example, procainamide-induced SLE occurs more frequently in patients who are slow acetylators as compared to rapid acetylators. Question: According to classic distinctions between drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (DI-SCLE) and drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus (DI-SLE), how do their typical cutaneous findings, systemic findings, and associated autoantibodies differ?

In DI-SCLE, cutaneous findings show typical SCLE lesions, systemic findings are usually absent (sometimes arthralgias), and the associated autoantibody is anti-SSA/Ro. Question: Why is polypropylene commonly used for running subcuticular sutures, and what precaution should be taken when tying knots with it?

Polypropylene has a low coefficient of friction, allowing it to slide easily through tissue, which makes it well suited for running subcuticular closures. However, because knot strength is directly proportional to a suture's friction coefficient, slippery materials like polypropylene are more prone to knot unraveling, so several additional throws should be placed for each knot to ensure security. THE ROLE OF DERMATOPATHOLOGY IN CLINICOPATHOLOGIC CORRELATION Dermatopathology, the study of skin under the microscope, is uniquely related to the study of clinical dermatology, for few other medical specialties place so much emphasis on both the clinical and the histo- logic features of diseases within their realm 25 . However, this union exists not only because of overlapping subject matter, but because derma- tology and dermatopathology both rely heavily upon careful observation and pattern recognition. In addition, clinical dermatology represents the “gross macroscopy” of dermatopathology, as clinical examination can be regarded akin to gross examination of biopsy specimens in other organs. Experienced clinicians may anticipate associated histologic findings as they examine a cutaneous lesion or eruption (e.g. hyperkeratosis and/ or parakeratosis when scale is present clinically, or dermal hemorrhage when there is purpura clinically). As a result, a sophisticated differential diagnosis often accompanies a skin biopsy performed by a dermatol- ogist. Moreover, when the microscopic features are clearly delineated in a histopathology report, an experienced dermatologist can utilize clinicopathologic correlation to arrive at a final diagnosis. In a similar fashion, an experienced dermatopathologist can utilize clinical pictures to arrive at a final pathological diagnosis. Image-Based Tasks Solved with Neural Networks What kind of tasks can a machine learning model potentially solve? Conceptually, anything where there are enough data and the perfor- mance can be parameterized as a numeric value, e.g. accuracies of diagnoses in percentages. Classification ( Fig. 0.45A ) is the most well-known technique for a visual specialty such as dermatology. The concept is to predict a diagnosis or a list of differential diagnoses from a single image or a sequence of images. This technique can be performed on clinical 65 , dermatoscopic 66 , or histopathologic images. Utilizing modern neural networks together with large public image datasets 67 , experimental, large-scale international studies 68 have shown that the models are equal or superior to dermatologists in classification tasks. Although skin cancer recognition is the most common topic in the literature, one can also automatically grade inflammatory skin diseases or predict diagnoses in general dermatology 65,69 . Measurements for classification performance are usually chosen for the task at hand and are usually classic diagnostic values such as sensitivity or specificity, crude accuracy, Youden’s J, area under the ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve, or mean sensitivity across multiple diagnoses. Question: Why is using only one diagnostic technique (e.g., unaided clinical exam or histology alone), to the exclusion of others, potentially problematic in dermatology?

Because diagnostic techniques such as unaided clinical examination, histologic examination, dermatoscopy, confocal microscopy, and imaging are complementary, their synergistic use and clinicopathologic correlation improve diagnostic accuracy. Relying on only one technique exclusively may therefore be misleading and result in misdiagnosis. [Chapter: 0 Basic Principles of Dermatology, p.41]

Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is a group of autosomal recessive disorders characterized by defects in unscheduled DNA repair. Individuals with XP who are exposed to sunlight show a markedly increased incidence of keratinocyte carcinoma and melanoma, with cSCCs and BCCs appearing at an early age (median age 8 years); in affected individuals under 20 years old, the risk is 4800 times that of the general population. Question: How do the flushing characteristics differ among midgut, type III gastric, bronchial, and hindgut carcinoid tumors?

Midgut carcinoid tumors (small intestine, appendix, proximal colon) cause flushing only with liver metastases, lasting minutes and consisting of erythema and pallor plus a cyanotic hue. Type III gastric carcinoid tumors cause a pruritic, patchy, bright red flush admixed with white patches, likely histamine-mediated. Bronchial tumors cause a prolonged (hours to days) intensely red to purple flush, while hindgut tumors (distal colon, rectum) rarely if ever cause flushing, even with liver metastases. The average age of onset is 30–60 years, but infants, children, and the elderly may be affected; there is a female predominance of 4 to 1. Biopsy techniques By employing the appropriate biopsy technique as well as providing adequate clinical data, the quality and amount of information a clinician obtains from a skin biopsy is maximized. Question: According to the excerpt, where on the body is keloidal scarring most commonly observed following dermatologic procedures, and what technologies may help direct biopsy site selection without replacing standard biopsy techniques?

Question: In HIV/ART-associated lipodystrophy, how do lipoatrophy and lipohypertrophy differ in their typical anatomic distribution and the antiretroviral drug classes most commonly implicated?

Lipoatrophy involves loss of subcutaneous fat mainly in the face (giving a skeletal appearance from buccal/temporal fat pad loss), limbs, and buttocks, and is primarily associated with nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), especially older agents like stavudine. Lipohypertrophy involves fat accumulation in the abdominal visceral compartment, dorsocervical region ("buffalo hump"), and breasts, and has been attributed primarily to protease inhibitors (PIs) and NRTIs. Question: What discovery in 2010 shifted the understanding of LCH pathogenesis, and what did this finding, along with subsequent studies, suggest about the nature of LCH?

In 2010, 55%–60% of LCH specimens were found to harbor the BRAF V600E mutation. This strongly suggested that LCH was a clonal neoplasm, a conclusion supported by later studies demonstrating uniform clonality of CD1a+ histiocytes. In high-risk patients, the BRAF V600E mutation was also found in CD34+ bone marrow progenitor cells and circulating CD11c+/CD14+ monocytic cells, leading to LCH now being regarded as a myeloid neoplasm. Question: According to the excerpt, what mechanisms link skin barrier dysfunction to inflammation, and what is this phenomenon called?

Question: According to the J-SCAR diagnostic criteria, what distinguishes 'typical' DIHS from 'atypical' DIHS, and what are the 7 criteria used in this classification?

The J-SCAR criteria for DRESS/DIHS include: (1) maculopapular rash developing >3 weeks after starting a limited number of drugs, (2) prolonged clinical symptoms after stopping the causative drug, (3) fever >38°C, (4) liver abnormalities (ALT >100 U/L, or other organ involvement such as renal), (5) leukocyte abnormalities (leukocytosis >11×10^9/L, atypical lymphocytes >5%, or eosinophilia >1.5×10^9/L), (6) lymphadenopathy, and (7) HHV-6 reactivation. Typical DIHS requires all 7 criteria, whereas atypical DIHS requires only the first 5. [Chapter: 21 Drug Reactions, p.461-462]

Proteoglycans differ remarkably in their protein content as well as the number, type, and length of their GAG side chains ( Table 95.3 ). Heparan sulfate chains sequester growth factors (e.g. fibroblast growth factors [FGFs], vascular endothelial growth factors [VEGFs]) and present them to their receptors. Collagen XVIII, a collagen/heparan sulfate hybrid, is also present in epidermal and vascular basement membranes as well as the skin 17 . Syndecans are transmembrane heparan sulfate proteoglycans that control cell adhesion to the ECM and cytoskeletal organization. Syndecans 1, 2, and 4 are expressed in the skin and can be found in keratinocytes, dendritic cells, and fibro- blasts, where they are thought to mediate “outside-in” cell signaling 15 . Question: Which four glycosaminoglycans are known to bind proteins to form proteoglycans, and what is the functional significance of heparan sulfate chains and the proteoglycan versican in the skin?

The four GAGs that can bind proteins to form proteoglycans are chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, keratan sulfate, and heparan sulfate. Question: Why are reverse cutting needles generally preferred over conventional cutting needles for suture placement, and how do taper point needles compare in terms of tissue handling?

Reverse cutting needles have their sharp edge on the outward-facing arc, which minimizes the risk of tearing through the wound edge during suture placement, making them preferred over conventional cutting needles (whose sharp edge is on the inside arc). Question: Under the FDA's 2019 sunscreen proposal, what UVA1/UV ratio must a broad spectrum sunscreen possess to ensure sufficient UVA protection, and what additional requirement from the 2011 monograph still applies?

Chemical- and Drug-Induced Photosensitivity Key features  Phototoxicity is characterized by an exaggerated sunburn-like reaction, usually caused by medications  Photoallergy presents with eczematous lesions, most commonly related to topical photoallergens  The cutaneous porphyrias are an example of phototoxicity induced by endogenous agents  Management includes identification and avoidance of the offending agent, in addition to photoprotection. Exogenous photosensitivity Introduction and history Photosensitivity induced by exogenous agents can be divided into phototoxicity and photoallergy ( Table 87.5 ). Phototoxicity is the result of direct tissue and cellular injury following UVR-induced activation of a phototoxic agent; theoretically, phototoxicity can be induced in any individual. In contrast, photoallergy is a delayed-type hypersensitivity response consisting of a sensitization phase, an incubation period of 7 to 10 days (following the first exposure), and a clinical elicitation reaction with any subsequent challenge; only immunologically sensi- tized individuals can develop photoallergy. Phototoxic agents have been used as medications from as early as 4000 BCE, with the inhabitants of Mesopotamia (and later the Indians and Egyptians) employing plant-derived psoralens for the treatment of leukoderma. In 1913, Meyer-Betz demonstrated hematoporphyrin- induced phototoxicity on himself, while the current method of PUVA therapy was introduced in the 1970s. Photoallergy was first recognized in 1939 based on a classic study of sulfanilamide by Epstein. Epidemiology While the exact prevalences of phototoxicity and photoallergy in the general population are unknown, their frequency in photodermatology referral centers has ranged from 3% to 16% for phototoxicity and 1% to 8% for photoallergy. Both are more common in White as compared to Black individuals 3,53,54 . Pathogenesis The pathogenesis of phototoxicity involves the generation of free oxygen radicals, superoxide anions, hydroxyl radicals and singlet oxygen, which leads to a host of cytotoxic tissue effects. Other mechanisms of damage include the generation of stable photoproducts (e.g. chlorpromazine, tetracy- clines), the formation of photoadducts (e.g. psoralens), and the recruitment of inflammatory mediators (e.g. porphyrins, demeclocycline) 55 . The pathogenesis of photoallergy is identical to that of allergic contact dermatitis, with the exception of the requirement for the presence of UVR to induce photoallergen formation. Clinical features Phototoxicity Following cutaneous or systemic exposure to a phototoxic agent and appro- priate UVR, phototoxicity develops within hours. Question: How do photoallergic drug reactions differ from phototoxic reactions in terms of mechanism, clinical appearance, and distribution, and what is the risk of chronic exposure to photoallergic drugs?

Photoallergic reactions are idiosyncratic, cell-mediated hypersensitivity reactions in which UVR converts a drug (or metabolite) into an immunologically active photoallergen that induces an immune response, unlike phototoxic reactions which are direct, dose-dependent effects resembling exaggerated sunburn. Clinically, photoallergic lesions are pruritic and resemble eczema or lichen planus, primarily affecting sun-exposed sites but sometimes extending to non-sun-exposed areas, whereas phototoxic reactions (erythema and bullae) are limited strictly to sun-exposed sites. Chronic exposure to photoallergic drugs can, in occasional patients, cause extreme photosensitivity persisting for months to years after the drug is stopped, placing them within the spectrum of chronic actinic dermatitis. Question: In a patient with an apparent ichthyosis but clinically unaffected parents, what three inheritance possibilities should be considered, and what specific clue in a male patient might point to one of them?

Clinically unaffected parents could indicate: (1) a recessive ichthyosis, particularly if there is consanguinity and/or affected siblings; (2) a dominant ichthyosis arising from a new mutation; or (3) for a male patient, an X-linked recessive ichthyosis in which the mother is an asymptomatic carrier. In this last scenario, a clue would be that the mother's male relatives could also be affected. [Chapter: 57 Ichthyoses, Erythrokeratodermas, and Related Disorders, p.1099]

Question: During PDT light exposure, what are some non-pharmacologic strategies that can be used to help manage a patient's pain, and what should patients be told about the sensation of pain during treatment?

Non-pharmacologic pain management strategies during PDT light exposure include applying an ice cube or ice pack near the treatment site, spraying cold water over the area, providing a fan or directing forced cold air toward the site, and temporarily interrupting the light exposure; hypnosis and transcutaneous nerve stimulation may also be used. Patients should be reassured that the sensation of pain indicates that the appropriate PDT reactions are occurring. [Chapter: 135 Photodynamic Therapy, p.2859-2860]

The presence of Raynaud phenomenon, digital sclerosis, and involvement of the gastrointestinal tract and the lung also allows differentiation of SSc from morphea. Question: Why do antigens taken up by the DEC-205 receptor (CD205) stimulate T cells much more effectively than antigens taken up via pinocytosis or other receptors?

Question: Histologically, what feature distinguishes common warts and palmoplantar warts from flat warts in terms of surface architecture, and what characteristic vacuolated cell finding is unique to flat warts?

Common warts and deep palmoplantar warts show marked papillomatosis (with palmoplantar warts having a cup-shaped invagination from inward-bowing lateral edges), whereas flat warts show no or only minimal papillomatosis, instead featuring orthokeratosis alternating with parakeratosis and a uniformly thickened granular layer. Flat warts are distinguished by vacuolization of cells in the granular and upper spinous layers, termed "bird's eyes." [Chapter: 79 Human Papillomaviruses, p.1699]

Question: What is the human clinical phenotype associated with homozygous mutations in the gene encoding the integrin α3 subunit, and what basement membrane defect is seen in mice with targeted deletion of this subunit?

In humans, homozygous mutations in the gene encoding the integrin α3 subunit cause basement membrane disruption resulting in congenital nephrotic syndrome, interstitial lung disease, and a mild form of epidermolysis bullosa. In mice with targeted deletion of integrin α3, the kidney and skin basement membranes are disorganized and mild blistering occurs; specifically, the lamina densa appears normal beneath hemidesmosomes but is missing or sparse between them. Question: A patient who snorts cocaine presents with retiform purpura with ulceration, neutropenia, and positive ANCA (including anti-PR3) and anti-dsDNA autoantibodies. What substance adulterating the cocaine is responsible for this presentation, and what other systemic symptoms may accompany it?

Cocaine adulterated with levamisole is responsible for this presentation, which can occur with snorting or IV use, and also with smoking crack cocaine adulterated with levamisole. In addition to retiform purpura with ulceration, neutropenia/leukopenia, and autoantibodies (ANA, ANCAs including anti-PR3 and elastase, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulant), patients may develop arthralgias, pulmonary hemorrhage, seizures, and glomerulonephritis. Other Eczematous Eruptions Key features  Secondary lesions of eczema distant from the primary site of exposure or involvement  Symmetric distribution pattern  Most often associated with allergic contact dermatitis and stasis dermatitis Introduction Dermatitis caused by exogenous agents initially arises at the site of con- tact. Not infrequently, additional patches of eczema develop at distant sites. This phenomenon, termed secondary dissemination, has puzzled dermatologists for decades. It is most often observed in allergic con- tact dermatitis, particularly if associated with stasis dermatitis (see Fig. 13.8 ), but may occur with uncomplicated stasis dermatitis, other forms of eczema, and, occasionally, severe tinea pedis. Disseminated eczema appears later than the primary lesions by a few days to weeks, tends to follow a strikingly symmetric distribution pat- tern, and shows a predilection for analogous anatomic sites (e.g. exten- sor aspects of the lower and upper extremities, palms, and soles). It may even arise in the absence of and without a preceding “primary” eczema, e.g. in nummular dermatitis (see below). Disseminated eczema must be distinguished from atopic dermatitis, which arises a priori in a dis- seminated fashion. History and Pathogenesis The phenomenon of secondary dissemination of eczemas was first described by Whitfield 30 , but its pathogenesis is still not fully eluci- dated. The orderly and symmetric distribution pattern may reflect sys- temic (hematogenous) dissemination and argues against simple spread of contact irritants or allergens on the body surface. It is unclear, how- ever, as to exactly what is disseminated via the bloodstream. It could be allergens; for example, the ingestion of allergens such as nickel has been shown to elicit disseminated eczema in sensitized individuals 31,32 . Initially called a “harlequin fetus” because of the premature delivery and fatal outcome, increasing survival rates due to improved neonatal care and systemic retinoid treatment have resulted in evolution to the terms “harlequin baby” and (currently) “harlequin ichthyosis” (HI). Epidemiology This rare disorder has an estimated incidence of 1 in 300 000 births and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. HI has been reported in patients with a wide variety of ethnic backgrounds 80 . Clinical Features Individuals with HI are usually born prematurely (mean gestational age, 35 weeks) and may die within a few days or weeks because of respi- ratory insufficiency or sepsis 80 . Affected neonates are encased in a hard, armor-like, tremendously thickened stratum corneum that results in severe immobilization and restricts ventilation. Shortly after birth, the hyperkeratotic cast cracks and forms large, yellow, adherent plates separated by broad, deep, intensely red fissures ( Fig. 57.13 ). Increased transcutaneous loss of water and heat results in dehydration, electrolyte imbalances (e.g. hypernatremia), and temperature instability. The latter may impede recognition of skin infections or sepsis, which are promoted by the large fissures. The tautness of the skin results in marked eversion of the eyelids (ectropion) and lips (eclabium), rudimentary development of ear and nasal cartilage, and sometimes microcephaly, giving the face an extremely distorted appearance. The hands and feet are edematous and swollen, often covered by a mitten-like casing. Although the digits are well developed, autoamputation due to constricting skin bands occasionally occurs. Eyelashes and eyebrows are usually missing, while scalp hair may be present. Eclabium and taut facial skin prohibit effective suckling by the infant. Over the past two decades, improved postnatal care and oral retinoid therapy have led to prolonged survival in an increasing number of HI patients. More than half of affected individuals now live beyond the neonatal period, with the oldest HI patient to date being > 25 years of age 80 . All survivors develop a severe, exfoliative ichthyosiform eryth- roderma, and half have a painful PPK; dystrophic nails (e.g. small, thickened) and poor hair growth are also common. Complications in these patients include recurrent skin infections, reduced sweating with heat intolerance, ocular problems related to persistent ectropion, chronic constipation, vitamin D deficiency, anemia, arthralgias, arthritis, and joint contractures 80 . Question: How do inactivating mutations in PTCH1 versus activating mutations in SMO each lead to constitutive activation of GLI and downstream target genes in basal cell carcinoma?

Normally, Hedgehog binding to Patched (PTCH) removes repression of Smoothened (SMO), allowing signal transduction via GLI to the nucleus. Inactivating mutations in PTCH1 result in a dysfunctional Patched protein that mimics Hedgehog binding, thereby constitutively activating GLI and its downstream targets. Alternatively, an activating mutation in SMO itself causes constitutive signaling to GLI and downstream genes independent of PTCH1 status; such SMO mutations are found in sporadic BCCs where PTCH1 is intact. Question: How does the sensitivity of Gram-stained smears for diagnosing gonorrhea differ between symptomatic men and women, and why are smears not useful for detecting rectal or pharyngeal gonorrhea?

Gram-stained urethral exudate detects 95%–98% of symptomatic gonococcal infections in men, whereas Gram-stained cervical smears in women have a much lower sensitivity of about 50%. Question: How do dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (DSH) and dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria (DUH) differ in terms of distribution and underlying genetics?

DSH presents with symmetrical hyper- and hypopigmented macules confined to the distal extremities, especially the dorsal hands and feet, sparing the palms, soles, and mucous membranes; it is caused by heterozygous mutations in ADAR, which encodes an RNA-specific adenosine deaminase. DUH, in contrast, causes truncal or generalized hyper- and hypopigmented macules that can involve the palms and soles (but not mucous membranes), and is caused by mutations in ABCB6 (an ATP-binding cassette transporter) or SASH1. Both conditions usually present by age 6 and are most common in Japan. [Chapter: 67 Disorders of Hyperpigmentation, p.1391-1392]

Question: According to the excerpt, how do the natural courses of cutaneous LP and oral LP differ in terms of spontaneous remission, and how is a diagnosis of lichenoid drug eruption confirmed?

Cutaneous LP often remits spontaneously, with up to two-thirds of patients clearing within 1 year, whereas oral LP has a much longer mean duration of about 5 years, and the erosive form of oral LP rarely resolves spontaneously. A lichenoid drug eruption is confirmed by withdrawing the suspected drug and observing gradual disappearance of the lesions, followed by recurrence of lesions upon re-exposure to the drug, though rechallenge is often not performed in practice. Question: When is a combination closure technique (using multiple flaps, or a flap plus a graft) preferred over a single flap for defect repair?

Combination closures are used when a defect cannot be conveniently closed with a single flap—either because the defect is too large, or because it spans more than one cosmetic subunit. In large defects, a flap may close most of the wound while a full-thickness graft supplements it to complete coverage; grafts can be harvested from common donor sites based on tissue match. For defects crossing multiple cosmetic subunits, it is often best to repair each subunit individually with a different flap. [Chapter: 147 Flaps, p.3043-3044]

Question: In lipodermatosclerosis, how do the clinical features of the acute phase differ from those of the chronic phase?

In the acute phase, lipodermatosclerosis presents with pain, warmth, erythema, and relatively diffuse induration, typically starting on the medial lower leg above the malleolus (though other dependent sites like the lower abdominal pannus can be affected). In the chronic phase, there is marked sclerosis of the dermis and subcutis producing induration that is more sharply demarcated from surrounding normal skin, often with brown hemosiderin discoloration, giving the leg an inverted wine bottle appearance. Mast cell densities in childhood maculopapular mastocytosis and mastocytomas are 40-fold and 150-fold higher than in normal skin, respectively, and are therefore relatively easy to identify. In comparison, the density is ~30% lower in adults 28 . For nodular, papular, and macular lesions (including TMEP) of mastocytosis, mast cells have been quantified using a morphometric technique and shown to have densities of 63.2% ( ± 8.2% SEM), 16.1% ( ± 4.8% SEM), and 3.5% ( ± 1.8% SEM), respectively, compared to 0.4% ( ± 0.1% SEM) in normal skin 28 . In childhood mastocytosis, mast cells in lesional skin typically have a round or cuboidal shape, whereas they tend to appear fusiform or dendritic in adults. KIT mutations can often be detected in lesional skin and may help to confirm the diagnosis 18 . Biopsies of normal-appearing skin from patients with mastocytosis have normal concentrations of mast cells and thus are not useful for diagnosis 28 . A biopsy of the GI tract or bone marrow may be indicated in patients with mast cell mediator-related symptoms who lack skin lesions. Increased mast cell numbers in association with variable numbers of eosinophils can be observed in GI biopsies 1,33,39,50 . Question: By definition, how is linear IgA bullous dermatosis (LABD) distinguished from dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) and bullous pemphigoid (BP) using direct immunofluorescence (DIF)?

Delayed reactions are typically manifestations of the host’s immune response to proteinaceous allergens. Patients with large local reactions to insect stings, defined as a swelling measuring > 10 cm and lasting > 24 hours, often have elevated serum levels of venom-specific IgE ­ . Roughly one-quarter of reported cases of anaphylaxis are due to stings from insects in the order Hymenoptera (meaning membranous wings), which includes bees, wasps, hornets, and ants. These insects can possess specialized stingers and produce complex venoms that contain substances such as formic acid, kinins, and proteinaceous allergens. Insect sting hypersensitivity is more common in individuals with an atopic diathesis, and patients with mastocytosis may develop more severe reactions. Clinical features Characteristic insect bite reactions are grouped or disseminated, 2 to 8 mm, erythematous urticarial papules that are markedly pruritic and often excoriated ( Fig. 85.1 ); they typically resolve over 5–10 days. Occasionally, bite reactions present as evanescent wheals or longer-lasting disseminated “papular urticaria” that persists for weeks or even months, sometimes reactivating when new bites occur in different locations. Edematous plaques, targetoid lesions, purpuric papules, nodules, and vesiculobullous reactions can also occur ( Fig. 85.2 ; see Ch. 33 ). Chronic or resolving lesions are often hyperpigmented (see Figs. 67.2B & 85.6B ), and prurigo nodularis-like lesions may develop, especially on the extrem- ities. Secondary infection is common; although staphylococcal infections are seen most frequently, streptococcal infections also occur. Insect bite reactions are most frequent in children 2–10 years of age and tend to involve exposed areas of the head, neck, and extremities. Commonly, only one member of a family is affected, as most clinical manifestations relate to the individual’s immune response rather than the bite itself. Bee and wasp stings typically produce immediate burning pain, which is followed by the development of local erythema and swelling that usually subsides within a few hours to days but can be more severe and persistent in sensitized individuals. Atrial arrhythmias have been reported after bee stings in the absence of anaphylaxis. Killer bee and wasp attacks may be associated with myoglobinuria or hemoglobinuria and acute tubular necrosis. Although bee stings have been utilized as an alternative therapy for inflammatory arthritis, beekeepers may develop a chronic arthropathy related to stings. Pathology Histologic features suggestive of a bite or sting include the presence of a wedge-shaped perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils, endothelial prominence, and overlying spongiosis or focal epidermal necrosis. Marked spongiosis can result in blister formation, and Langerhans cell hyperplasia may be evident ( Fig. 85.3 ). Differential diagnosis Arthropod reactions account for many “cryptic” chronic skin eruptions. Features that should suggest an arthropod reaction include grouping of papules, patterns of eruption that correlate with exposure, and the histo- logic features noted above. When an arthropod reaction is suspected, a detailed history of outdoor exposures, pets, work environment, and hobbies may prove helpful. Treatment Camphor and menthol lotion and gel formulations may be useful in the control of pruritus. Topical anesthetic preparations can also be helpful, and those containing pramoxine are readily available and present a low risk of contact dermatitis. For more persistent bite reactions, topical corticosteroids are often required. In young children, mid-strength corticosteroid preparations may suffice, while in older children and adults, class 1 or 2 corticosteroids are preferable. These agents can be applied under occlusion to enhance efficacy, but for a predetermined time period to avoid potential side effects of cutaneous atrophy and striae. When topical agents fail, intralesional corticosteroid injection (e.g. triamcinolone 5–10 mg/ml) or excision of the pruritic nodule may be necessary. Occasionally, pseudolymphomatous nodules may require higher triamcinolone concentrations (e.g. 20–40 mg/ml). Cutaneous atrophy can occur, especially if a higher concentration of corticosteroid is injected superficially or into uninvolved surrounding skin. Side effects include first- and second-degree burns. Cupping is another method used to stimulate acupuncture points. It is accomplished by igniting alcohol-soaked cotton, placing the burning cotton in a jar, and placing the jar on the skin. A vacuum is created, and circular areas of erythema and ecchymosis may result ( Fig. 133.2 ). Nowadays, some practitioners use a vacuum device that negates the risk of fire. Complementary and Alternative Medicine Skin scraping, also known as coining or spooning, is commonly practiced in Southeast Asia to improve circulation. A tool is used to rub skin that has been treated with oil; symmetric, linear ecchymoses may result ( Fig. 133.3 ). Any patient with cutaneous lesions in patterns suggestive of external causes should be asked about traditional medicine before accusations of abuse arise. HOMEOPATHY Homeopathy is a system of healing founded in Germany at the end of the 18th century. It is composed of two theories: (1) “like cures like” – the suggestion that a disease can be cured by a substance that produces similar symptoms in people who do not have the disease; and (2) “law of minimum dose” – the concept that the lower the dose of the medication, the greater the efficacy of the medication 51 . Homeopathic remedies come from substances that are derived from plants, minerals or animals, many of which are considered toxic in their crude form. Serial dilutions and “succussion” – a process by which a solution is violently shaken a given number of times between dilutions – create the final product. Homeopathic remedies are often prepared as sugar pellets to be placed under the tongue, but they may also be formulated as ointments, gels, drops, or creams. The FDA regulates homeopathic remedies, but unlike traditional medications, it does not evaluate them for safety and effectiveness. In dermatology, homeopathy is most often used for the treatment of atopic dermatitis and psoriasis 52 . In general, there is little evidence to support the effectiveness of homeopathic therapies for skin disease 53 , and some evidence from controlled clinical studies suggest that homeopathy is actually ineffective for eczema 54 . Subsequently, chemical peeling experienced a tremendous growth in popularity and has become an important part of our armamentarium in the management of various cosmetic as well as non-cosmetic skin problems. Currently, chemical peeling is the third most commonly employed cosmetic procedure, after injectable neurotoxins and soft tissue fillers. Since Kromayer’s original report of motorized dermabrasion in 1905, there has been considerable growth not only in chemical resurfacing procedures, but also in mechanical resurfacing. Mechanical resurfacing is most often known as dermabrasion, but it refers to any procedure that involves surgical planing of the skin using an abrasive surface. The use of dermabrasion was originally limited to the treatment of scars, but its role expanded during the latter half of the twentieth century to include a multitude of indications including improvement of elevated skin grafts and rejuvenation of photodamaged skin 2 . Recent adaptations of the traditional techniques of dermabrasion have led to the development of a less invasive procedure, known as microdermabrasion 3 . Dermasanding, which is a manual technique of dermabrasion utilizing abrasive paper, has been in use for centuries, but recently has experienced a resur- gence 4,5 . Although overshadowed by ablative and non-ablative laser resurfacing (see Ch. 137 ), mechanical resurfacing procedures remain a popular option for both patients and physicians. Question: Why is it important for a clinician to ask a patient about the use of traditional practices such as moxibustion, cupping, or skin scraping (coining) before suspecting abuse when they observe skin lesions with patterns suggestive of an external cause?

These practices can produce skin findings that mimic signs of abuse: moxibustion can cause first- and second-degree burns, cupping can leave circular areas of erythema and ecchymosis, and skin scraping (coining/spooning) can cause symmetric, linear ecchymoses. Because these traditional treatments are common (e.g., coining is widely practiced in Southeast Asia) and can create externally patterned lesions, patients should be asked about such practices before accusations of abuse are made. Vidimos Mohs Micrographic Surgery There are four major components: surgical excision, histopatho- logic examination, precise mapping, and wound management. The surgical component consists of removing a disc of tissue with a bev- eled surgical margin ( Fig. 150.1A ). The disc of tissue, or “layer”, ensures that the entire 360° of tumor margin is circumferentially removed and examined. The histopathologic component involves cryopreserving this disc and cutting it in a horizontal fashion, then mounting sections onto glass slides, followed by staining and micro- scopic examination for residual tumor. This processing technique differs from standard excisions in which specimens are formalin- fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) and cut in a “bread-loaf” fashion ( Fig. 150.1B ). Precise mapping entails marking any residual tumor on the map of the excision with the remaining positive area of tumor re- excised as indicated. This three-step process is repeated until there is no residual tumor identified microscopically. During this procedure, the Mohs surgeon has complete control of the excised tissue, includ- ing laboratory processing and interpretation of the tissue sections, as well as precise mapping. In the fourth step, wound management , the tumor-free defect is surgically closed or allowed to heal by second intention. INTRODUCTION Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) is a specialized method for skin cancer removal that combines surgery with pathology resulting in an excellent cure rate. The goals are to remove only the cancerous tissue while viewing the complete margin, thereby preserving the maximum amount of normal tissue (i.e. tissue-sparing). From a functional, aes- thetic and reconstructive perspective, tissue-sparing is especially impor- tant for skin cancers in the periorbital, nasal, auricular, perioral, digital, and anogenital areas. MMS is also the preferred treatment method for skin cancers that are clinically poorly defined, recurrent, and/or have a higher risk of recurrence because of histologic features or anatomic location ( Table 150.1 ). Question: Why should a biopsy specimen for suspected erosive lichen planus include the edge of the erosion along with the surrounding lacy reticulated skin, and what is the value of histologic evaluation in this setting?

Because erosive lichen planus involves loss of the epithelium within the erosion itself, a specimen from the erosion alone would not capture diagnostic features; including the edge of the erosion plus adjacent lacy reticulated skin gives the best chance of showing characteristic changes. Even so, histology cannot always unequivocally confirm lichen planus, but it remains useful for excluding other entities in the differential diagnosis, such as autoimmune bullous disease, Zoon vulvitis, or HSIL/SCC. Question: In Naegeli–Franceschetti–Jadassohn (NFJ) syndrome, how do truncating mutations in KRT14 lead to the characteristic reticulated hyperpigmentation seen histologically?

NFJ syndrome results from truncating mutations in the non-helical head domain of KRT14, causing haploinsufficiency. This increases keratinocyte susceptibility to TNF-induced apoptosis, leading to pigment incontinence—seen histologically as melanophages in the upper dermis—which produces the clinical reticulated hyperpigmentation. Question: What overlapping clinical and histologic features between lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP) and cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma (C-ALCL) support classifying LyP as a low-grade variant of CTCL rather than a purely benign condition?

Question: How is essential fatty acid (EFA) deficiency diagnosed biochemically, and under what circumstances can an isolated EFA deficiency occur?

EFA deficiency is diagnosed by finding decreased plasma levels of linoleic and linolenic acids together with increased levels of eicosatrienoic acid, which is normally undetectable. An isolated EFA deficiency is uncommon but can occur with parenteral nutrition lacking lipid supplementation or with overly aggressive low-fat diets; more often, however, EFA deficiency occurs alongside other nutritional deficiencies. Question: According to the lipid-lowering medications table, what is the mechanism of action of ANGPTL3 inhibitors such as evinacumab, and what specific patient population is this drug class used to treat?

ANGPTL3 inhibitors like evinacumab bind to ANGPTL3, a protein expressed mainly in the liver that normally inhibits lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase; by blocking ANGPTL3, these drugs rescue the activity of these enzymes and promote VLDL processing and clearance upstream of LDL formation, lowering LDL-C (independent of LDL receptor presence), HDL-C, and triglycerides. They are used to treat homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and are administered intravenously in combination with other lipid-lowering drugs such as statins or PCSK9 inhibitors. Question: According to Happle's classification, what are the seven patterns of cutaneous mosaicism, and which one has not yet been shown to be mosaic at the molecular level in any condition?

Happle categorized cutaneous mosaicism into seven patterns: (1,2) narrow or broad bands along the lines of Blaschko; (3) checkerboard (block- or flag-like); (4) lateralization (affecting only one side of the body); (5) phylloid (leaf- or flower-like); (6) patchy without midline separation; and (7) sash. It is delivered in a monoterminal (concentrative) fashion (see Fig. 140.1 ). If the electrode is held at a slight distance from the tissue, a spark is formed between the electrode and the tissue. This technique, termed electrofulguration , achieves very superficial destruction because the surface carbonization it produces insulates the underlying tissues from thermal heat spread. Dermatologists who employ a Hyfrecator ® or similar device often utilize this type of waveform. As the surface becomes charred by sparking at the surface, it is common for blood to appear in droplets that penetrate through the surface char. This is because the electrical current does not penetrate deeply enough to seal nearby blood vessels. PIBIDS stands for Photosensitivity, Ichthyosis, Brittle hair, Intellectual impairment with low IQ, Decreased fertility, and Short stature. Question: In a woman with PCOS who is at higher risk for VTE (e.g., obesity, age ≥40 years), what type of combined OCP formulation is recommended, and why should levonorgestrel-containing cOCPs be avoided in this population?

For women at higher VTE risk, the recommended cOCP should contain the lowest effective dose of ethinyl estradiol (usually 20 mcg) combined with a low VTE-risk progestin such as norgestimate or norethindrone. Levonorgestrel, although associated with low VTE risk, is the most androgenic progestin and may have adverse metabolic effects, making it less suitable for patients with PCOS. Question: In levamisole-induced vasculopathy, what laboratory finding pattern helps distinguish this condition from a primary ANCA-associated vasculitis?

Levamisole-induced vasculopathy is associated with a high rate of ANCA positivity (~95%), but isolated cANCA positivity occurs in fewer than 5% of patients, with most having both anti-myeloperoxidase and anti-proteinase antibodies. Because of this, the finding of cANCA positivity alone is unusual for levamisole-induced vasculopathy and should raise strong suspicion for a primary ANCA-associated vasculitis instead. Question: Why is polypropylene suture (e.g., Prolene) particularly well-suited for use as a running subcuticular suture, and what are its main disadvantages?

Polypropylene has a low coefficient of friction that allows a gentle, smooth pull through tissue and permits easy withdrawal even after extended periods without disrupting the wound, making it ideal for running subcuticular closures. It also has high plasticity, stretching with tissue swelling to reduce postoperative track marks. Its main disadvantages are memory, which compromises knot security, and higher cost compared to nylon. [Chapter: 144 Wound Closure Materials and Instruments, p.2976]

Early-stage wound macrophage activation is mediated by cytokines, in particular interferon- γ (IFN- γ ), followed by Toll-like receptor (TLR)-mediated triggers such as lipopolysaccharide signaling via TLR4. Key mediators of late-stage macrophage activation are IL-4 and IL-13, acting through the common receptor chain IL-4R α . T cells During the tissue remodeling phase, when wound closure is complete and local infections have been overcome, cells of the adaptive immune response, in particular T cells, are the most frequent leukocyte subset in human skin wounds 44 . CD4 + T cells can differentiate into different subsets, e.g. Th1 and Th2 cells (see Ch. 4 ), thereby influencing the wound microenvironment by secreting distinct cytokine profiles (see are the major source of IL-4 and IL-13. These cytokines have a major effect on the state of macrophage activation. Thus, even though they are not mandatory for wound healing, CD4 + T cell cytokines influence two important components of wound healing: macrophage function and angiogenesis. However, additional investigations are needed to under- stand why wound healing appears to be unaffected in T cell-deficient mice (e.g. RAG1 knockout mice). Mast cells Mast cells are a hematopoietic cell population that normally resides in skin and mucous membranes. They are an important source of a number of mediators such as prostaglandins and biogenic amines as well as pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. TNF, IL-8) that strongly influence inflammation, tissue modulation, and vascular modeling. However, almost entirely normal wound healing was observed in mice genetically depleted of mast cells, suggesting that mast cells may only play a fine-tuning role during wound repair 46 . Fibroblasts Connective tissue, including the dermis, is usually composed of large amounts of ECM in which a small number of relatively quiescent fibroblasts are embedded. During development, fibroblasts establish a “resting” tension by actively synthesizing and cross-linking fibrillar ECM proteins such as collagen and elastin (see Ch. 95 ). This estab- lishes the shape of the skin and ensures that the skin retains its shape in response to mechanical stress. During tissue repair, fibroblasts next to the site of injury become activated, reconstitute new ECM, and restore proper matrix tension. To achieve these goals, fibroblasts acquire smooth muscle cell-like features including contractile stress fibers and de novo expression of α -smooth muscle actin ( α -SMA), thus differentiating into myofibro- blasts ( Fig. 141.7 )

For mpox, clade I infection tends to show a centrifugal distribution that often involves the palms and soles, whereas clade IIb favors the genital, perianal, and oropharyngeal sites of inoculation. Question: Why does salicylic acid remain on the stratum corneum while α-hydroxy acids penetrate more deeply, and what practical effect does this have during a salicylic acid peel?

Salicylic acid is oil-soluble, so it stays on the surface of the stratum corneum, whereas α-hydroxy acids are water-soluble and readily penetrate into the stratum corneum. Because salicylic acid is self-neutralizing, the peel ends with formation of white salicylic acid crystals on the skin; these crystals rinse off the surface but remain in the follicular ostia, providing a prolonged keratolytic effect. Question: A patient presents with a painful genital ulcer that has a purulent base and soft, undermined edges, developing 3–10 days after exposure. Painful unilateral inguinal lymphadenitis is also present. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what organism causes it?

This presentation is characteristic of chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Chancroid has an incubation period of 3–10 days and produces painful ulcers with purulent bases and soft, undermined edges, often accompanied by painful inguinal lymphadenitis (unilateral in about 40% of men), which can progress to bubo formation and rupture.
