Question: What is the underlying pathogenesis of scombroid poisoning, and which fish are typically implicated?

Scombroid poisoning occurs when fish with high levels of free histidine in their muscle tissue (originally fish of the family Scombridae such as tuna and mackerel, but also mahi mahi, bluefish, marlin, bonito, amberjack, sardines, anchovies, herring, and swordfish) are improperly refrigerated, allowing bacterial histidine decarboxylase to convert histidine into histamine. Ingestion of this histamine-laden fish delivers a large histamine dose that causes prompt effects via histamine receptor binding, though other factors such as potentiation of histamine absorption, inhibition of its catabolism, an unidentified "scombrotoxin," and histamine intolerance may also contribute. Fractional Photothermolysis Fractional photothermolysis (FP) represents a treatment strategy in which numerous small zones of thermal injury are created ( Fig. 136.6 ), stimulating turnover and remodeling of both the epidermis and dermis 32 . Non-ablative FP uses focused, mid-IR, laser microbeams to create a pixelated pattern of microscopic columns of thermal damage, called microthermal treatment zones (MTZs). Typically, ~1 million MTZs are placed per full-face treatment. Density (percentage of skin treated) and depth of thermal damage are separately controlled. The energy delivered per MTZ accurately controls the depth of treatment which is typically up to ~2 mm, i.e. well into the reticular dermis. In general, the depth of thermal damage should correlate with the depth of skin pathology being treated, e.g. a greater depth for hypertrophic scars than for atrophic scars 33 . Tissue spared around each MTZ initiates rapid repair and stimu- lates remodeling. Desquamation of the epidermal portion of each MTZ removes some basal layer pigment and a small amount of papillary dermal debris. Non-ablative FP has been reported to improve several skin conditions including scars, fine rhytides, telangiectasias, derma- toheliosis, and poikiloderma. There are a myriad of commercially available non-ablative, as well as ablative, FP devices (see Ch. 137 ). Ablative FP uses carbon dioxide or erbium (Er:YAG) lasers to vaporize many small vertical channels that can extend deeply into the skin. Because remodeling is provided by tissue between the columns of ablation, the depth of ablation can be far deeper than with traditional ablative resurfacing procedures. Care must be taken to avoid scarring, especially in areas where thin skin has limited adnexal structures such as the infraorbital and neck regions. By creating deep channels into the dermis, ablative FP is also an effective mechanism for enhancing topical drug delivery (see below) 34–37 . Clinical applications of fractional lasers include treatment of photo- aging, striae distensae, poikiloderma, and scars. Ablative FP has been shown to significantly improve the elasticity and appearance of hyper- trophic traumatic or burn scars 38–40 . The mechanisms by which micro- scale burns within the narrow, deep, FP-induced laser wounds lead to improvement of scars from thermal burns remain largely unknown. Question: In fractional photothermolysis, what are microscopic treatment zones (MTZs), and why does the surrounding unaffected skin matter for healing?

MTZs are precisely calibrated columns or cylinders of epidermal and dermal thermal (coagulative or ablative) injury delivered in controlled, defined depth, width, and density with each scan or stamp of a fractional device, rather than treating the entire spot size as with traditional lasers. Each MTZ is surrounded by normal, unaffected skin that acts as a reservoir for healing, allowing these micro-wounds to resolve quickly and with minimal discomfort; histologically they appear as microscopic epidermal necrotic debris (MENDs), which are extruded as the skin surface heals within about 7 days. In addition to thermal burns, cutaneous complications of fluoroscopy include allergic drug reactions, irritant and allergic contact derma- titis, non-target embolization to the skin, intravascular catheter- related infections, and radiation dermatitis 17 . The mechanism behind fluoroscopy-induced radiodermatitis is related to the dose of radiation that is delivered, the interval between radiation exposures (dose fraction- ation), and the size of the irradiated area 16 . Repeated procedures are notorious for increasing the risk 18 . Additional potential risk factors include smoking, diabetes mellitus, obesity with overlapping skin folds, autoimmune connective tissue diseases (e.g. systemic sclerosis), genetic DNA repair defects, and various drugs including chemothera- peutic agents 16,17 . Radiation recall, which can occur days to years after fluoroscopy, has been observed following the administration of drugs such as methotrexate 16 . Clinical features Thermal burns appear soon after MRI, and may be partial- to full- thickness (see Table 88.3 ). The shape and size of the burns are deter- mined by the conductor causing the injury (e.g. circular burns under ECG electrodes; figurate burns conforming to the shape of metallic wires or tattoo pigment deposition) 15,19 . Fluoroscopy-induced radiation dermatitis may be acute, but, as time passes and the acute injury resolves, the patient may continue to develop further changes, including epilation of hair, desquamation, telangiectasias, permanent erythema, and eventual ulceration due to dermal necrosis ( Fig. 88.5 ). The left upper back is a characteristic location for patients with cardiovascular disease who have had cardiac catheterizations with attempts at revascularization (e.g. angioplasty, stent placement) 18 . Although often referred to as cutaneous compli- cations, severe radiation injuries can extend into the subcutaneous fat and muscle 16 . Rarely, skin burns develop at the site of an indif- ferent electrode in those undergoing radiofrequency catheter ablation of cardiac arrhythmias 18a . Timing of the event plus the sensation of a burn rather than pruritus should allow a distinction. Pathogenesis Although the precise cause of MRI burns is unknown, the presence of both pulsed radiofrequency and pulsed magnetic gradient fields is thought to play a role. If an electrically conductive loop is formed between the patient and an electrode, patient and wiring, or even small areas of skin–skin contact, current can be produced by the changing magnetic flux, causing a thermal or electrical burn. Alternatively, the burn may result from formation of a resonant conducting loop with an extended wire creating a resonant antenna, heating maximally at the antenna tip 15,19 . Question: What is the characteristic anatomic location for fluoroscopy-induced radiation dermatitis in patients who have undergone cardiac catheterization procedures, and what late clinical changes may develop at this site as the injury evolves over time?

The left upper back is the characteristic location for fluoroscopy-induced radiation dermatitis in patients with cardiovascular disease who have undergone cardiac catheterizations with attempts at revascularization (e.g., angioplasty, stent placement). Although the injury may initially be acute, over time it can evolve to show epilation of hair, desquamation, telangiectasias, permanent erythema, and eventually ulceration due to dermal necrosis. Severe cases can extend beyond the skin into the subcutaneous fat and muscle. [Chapter: 88 Environmental and Sports-Related Skin Diseases, p.1920]

Local recurrences of melanoma, particularly the persistent disease- type, can occur several years (rarely decades) after excision of the primary lesion. When a lesion previously diagnosed histologically as a melanocytic nevus recurs locally more than two years after removal, re-evaluation for possible melanoma should be considered. NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN Management of Regional Metastatic Melanoma (Stage III) In ~70% of patients, metastatic spread of melanoma is locoregional, i.e. confined to the site of the primary melanoma, its draining lymph nodes, and the lymphatics between the primary tumor and regional lymph nodes. Locoregional metastasis may manifest as clinically occult lymph node micrometastasis, clinically evident (i.e. palpable) lymph node macrometastasis, or as satellite/in-transit metastasis (discussed above). The vast majority of stage III patients are identified with micro- scopic nodal disease following SLNB. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) and completion lymph node dissection SLNB was introduced in the 1990s as a method for determining whether the melanoma had microscopically spread to regional nodes and was based upon the presumed migration of melanoma cells from the primary tumor to an initial draining regional lymph node(s). SLNB thereafter replaced elective lymph node dissection (ELND), which was previously considered standard of care for intermediate thickness melanoma until four multicenter, randomized, prospective trials failed to show a survival benefit for patients treated with ELND plus wide excision compared to wide excision alone 206–209 . Approximately 15%–20% of patients with clinically node-negative cutaneous melanoma > 1 mm in depth will exhibit microscopic lymph node involvement on SLNB 210 . Increased rates of SLNB-positivity occur with greater tumor thickness and other adverse histologic features in the primary melanoma, e.g. ulceration, high mitotic index, lymphovascular invasion. SLNB is optimally performed in the same operative setting as the surgical excision. Preoperative lymphatic mapping is performed to identify the first draining lymph node(s) within the lymph node basin(s) using technetium sulfur colloid and/or blue dye injected into the skin surrounding the melanoma biopsy site. Lymphoscintigraphy demon- strates the lymphatic drainage pattern from a given melanoma site and can be combined with 3D CT imaging. Question: According to the PUVA treatment schedule, how should the UVA dose be adjusted during the clearing phase if a patient develops painful erythema with or without edema or blistering, and how does this differ from the response to minimal (asymptomatic) erythema?

If a patient develops painful erythema (with or without edema or blistering), treatment should be withheld until symptoms subside, and then the last dose should be reduced by 50%, with further increases limited to 10% increments thereafter. In contrast, if a patient develops only minimal or persistent asymptomatic erythema, treatment is resumed after symptoms resolve and the UVA dose can be increased by 30%. This reflects a more cautious approach when erythema is painful or accompanied by blistering, compared to mild asymptomatic erythema. [Chapter: 134 Ultraviolet Therapy, p.2843-2844]

disease, usually lethal in male fetuses  Cutaneous lesions are characterized by four phases: vesicular, verrucous, hyperpigmented, and hypopigmented/atrophic  Extracutaneous manifestations are most commonly dental, ophthalmologic, and neurologic Incontinentia pigmenti (IP) is an uncommon X-linked dominant multi- system disease that presents within the first 2 weeks of life in 90% of patients and is lethal in male fetuses unless they have X chromosome aneuploidy (e.g. Klinefelter syndrome) or genomic mosaicism (see Ch. 62 ). IP is caused by mutations in IKBKG (inhibitor of NF- κ B kinase regulatory subunit γ ), which is also known as NEMO (NF- κ B essential modulator). Its protein product confers protection against apoptosis induced by the tumor necrosis factor family of cytokines (see Fig. 130.4 ). Cutaneous lesions follow the lines of Blaschko and occur in four classic phases (see Fig. 62.5 ). The vesicular first phase usually lasts 1–2 weeks, with intermittent recurrences for up to a year and occasionally later in childhood in association with febrile illnesses. Streaks of vesicles most often develop on the extremities and scalp but can also appear on the trunk ( Fig. 34.13A–C ); the face is usually spared. The verrucous second phase of IP features hyperkeratotic linear plaques. The third phase, characterized by linear and whorled grayish-brown hyper- pigmentation, occurs most often on the trunk and in some patients represents the only cutaneous feature (see Fig. 67.19 ). The first three phases typically resolve during infancy or childhood. The fourth phase, consisting of subtle atrophic, hypopigmented thin streaks favoring the calves, may persist indefinitely. Clinical stages of IP can overlap, occur in utero , or occasionally be skipped entirely. Additional cutaneous findings may include patchy scarring alopecia (typically at the vertex), areas of woolly hair, nail dystrophy, and anhidrosis within atrophic linear streaks. The most common extracutaneous manifestations are: (1) dental abnormalities such as hypodontia and conical teeth; (2) CNS involvement resulting in seizures, delayed psychomotor development, or spastic paralysis; and (3) ocular disease characterized by retinal vascular abnormalities with potential for blindness. During the vesicular phase, patients often have peripheral blood leukocytosis and eosinophilia. Skin biopsy is often helpful in confirming the diagnosis. Histologically, lesions from the vesicular stage of IP demonstrate eosinophilic spongiosis with scattered or grouped necrotic keratinocytes ( Fig. 34.13D ). A dermal infiltrate composed predominantly of eosinophils is also present 5 . The cutaneous lesions generally do not require therapy.

Question: Incontinentia pigmenti (IP) is usually antenatally lethal in boys, yet occasional boys are born with clinically typical IP. According to the excerpt, what two mechanisms explain the occurrence of IP in males, and what is the underlying genetic cause of IP in general?

IP is caused by mutations in IKBKG (NEMO) located at Xq28, with about 80% of patients having a common large deletion of exons 4–10 that typically arises during paternal meiosis. Clinically typical IP in boys can occur due to Klinefelter syndrome (in about 10% of male patients, providing an extra X chromosome) or due to genomic mosaicism from a half-chromatid or postzygotic NEMO mutation, in which case skin lesion distribution may be relatively limited. Both types of atypical target lesions are round, EM-like lesions with only two zones and/or a poorly defined border. Question: Why might delaying full-thickness skin graft (FTSG) placement for 7–14 days be beneficial when reconstructing deep nasal tip or alar defects with exposed cartilage, particularly in smokers or patients with prior radiotherapy?

Delaying graft placement allows granulation tissue to fill in the defect, which can achieve a better contour, and the early granulating wound provides an excellent vascular bed. This is especially useful in patients with reduced wound bed vascularity, such as smokers or those with prior radiotherapy, as it increases the likelihood of graft survival. Question: Why is direct immunofluorescence (DIF) considered the most reliable diagnostic test for pemphigus, and what should be suspected if the DIF result is negative?

DIF directly demonstrates in vivo bound IgG deposition on keratinocyte cell surfaces in perilesional skin or mucous membrane, and IgG deposition is found in up to 100% of patients with active pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus, making it the most reliable and sensitive diagnostic test for all forms of pemphigus. If the DIF is negative, the diagnosis of pemphigus should be seriously questioned. [Chapter: 29 Pemphigus, p.647]

Other systemic adverse effects Ophthalmologic effects The most common ocular retinoid effects are dryness and irritation. Xerophthalmia due to decreased Meibomian gland secretions may prohibit the use of contact lenses and can lead to blepharoconjunc- tivitis, keratitis, or corneal opacities (especially with isotretinoin). Question: In systemic mastocytosis (SM), how is the diagnosis of indolent SM, smoldering SM, aggressive SM, and mast cell leukemia (MCL) distinguished based on the presence of B and C findings and bone marrow mast cell percentage?

Indolent SM is diagnosed when there are fewer than 2 B findings and no C findings. Smoldering SM is diagnosed when there are 2 or more B findings but no C findings. When at least 1 C finding is present (with or without B findings), the diagnosis is either aggressive SM, if bone marrow smears show less than 20% mast cells, or MC leukemia, if bone marrow smears show 20% or more mast cells. Question: According to the excerpt, why does lipoatrophy from insulin injections tend to be prevented by rotating injection sites, and why is it now fairly rare with certain modern insulin therapies?

Repeated use of the same injection site increases the risk of lipoatrophy, so regularly rotating injection sites largely prevents it. Lipoatrophy is also fairly rare with the use of human insulin (as opposed to non-human insulin) and with insulin pump therapy, likely reflecting reduced immunogenicity and less repetitive trauma to a single site. Question: According to the key features for phlebology and treatment of leg veins, what general principles should guide the order and technique of treating the superficial venous system with sclerosing agents?

All affected portions of the superficial venous system should ideally be treated in one session, beginning with the most proximal veins, and larger veins should be treated before smaller ones, proceeding from proximal to distal. In this 2018 update, the terminology and defini- tions of the different types of CTCL are identical to those in the 2016 revision of the WHO classification 3 . In the 2023 WHO classification (5th revision) as well as in the 2022 International Consensus Classification (ICC) of mature lymphoid neoplasms, only minor changes have been introduced, namely, primary cutaneous acral CD8-positive T cell lymphoma has been listed as a lymphoproliferative disorder rather than a lymphoma 3a,3b . PRACTICAL GUIDELINES FOR DIAGNOSIS, CLASSIFICATION AND STAGING OF CTCL Diagnosis The first step in the evaluation of a patient suspected of having CTCL is to decide if it represents a lymphoma or a benign condition. Skin biopsies – preferably deep punch biopsies 4–6 mm wide or an excisional or incisional biopsy from the most representative skin lesions – should be performed. In the US, broad shave (tangential) biopsies are also done for suspected patch/plaque stage MF. Since prior treatment with topical corticosteroids or phototherapy (narrowband UVB, PUVA) may change the original histology profoundly, biopsies from untreated skin lesions are preferred. Even if an adequate biopsy specimen is obtained, a definite diagnosis is not always possible. First, several types of CTCL, such as MF, are often preceded for years by skin lesions that are neither clinically nor histologically diagnostic. The gradual progression from this prediagnostic phase to overt lymphoma explains why it has always been so difficult to reach a consensus on the minimal histologic criteria needed for an unequivocal diagnosis of MF 4 . In most cases, repeated biopsies, when appropriate, will ultimately result in the correct diagnosis. Secondly, atypical T cell infiltrates are found not only in CTCL but also in reactive conditions, e.g. lymphomatoid drug eruptions (T cell pseudolymphomas). NF1 is an autosomal dominant disorder occurring in about 1 in 2000–3000 births, with up to 50% of cases arising from new spontaneous mutations rather than inheritance. Characteristic clinical features include café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, axillary/groin freckling, Lisch nodules, bony defects, and nevus anemicus. Although in vitro systems have been developed to test the effects of certain drugs on the metabolism of other drugs, these systems may not accurately predict the effect in patients receiving drugs with complex metabolism. In addition, problems with the detection of adverse events after a drug has been released arise mainly because such events are rare. It takes a surveillance system with a high degree of sensitivity to detect such problems 20 . Furthermore, most in vivo and in vitro studies of drug interac- tions evaluate two-drug regimens, and the results may not apply to the multidrug regimens used clinically. This is especially true for a regimen consisting of three or more drugs with opposing effects on CYP3A4 metabolism. The lack of studies of multiple drug interac- tions provides little assistance to the prescribing physician, who is left to rely on adverse events or treatment failure to demonstrate whether an interaction has occurred. In addition, the design of in vivo studies is sometimes poor (choice of prototype substrate, doses, schedule of administration, number of volunteers), with the risk of minimizing the real potential for interaction. To link in vitro and in vivo studies, several authors have suggested using extrapolation techniques, based on the comparison of in vitro inhibition data with the active in vivo concentra- tions of the inhibitor. However, the lack of knowledge with regard to one or several important parameters, such as the role of metabolites and intrahepatocyte accumulation, often limits the ability to make safe and accurate predictions. The uncertainty and inaccuracy of predicting the extent and duration of in vivo drug interactions currently stems from a lack of definitive models by which to assess likely substrate and inhibitor concentrations at the active site of metabolism. Additional issues contributing to the uncertainty of predicting drug interactions include assumptions of the contribution of presystemic drug extraction and the effect of inhibitors on the processes involved. Therefore, these methods are useful for complementing in vivo studies and helping to design clinically relevant in vivo studies, but in the near future they will not totally replace in vivo investigations. Question: How does the age distribution of precursor B lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia differ from other cutaneous B cell lymphomas, and how should even apparently skin-limited cases be managed?

Unlike other cutaneous B cell lymphomas, precursor B lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia shows a clear predilection for children and young adults. Patients typically present with solitary large erythematous tumors on the head and neck, and elevated serum LDH reflects its aggressive, often systemic nature. Because of this aggressiveness, all patients—even those without documented systemic involvement at presentation—should be assumed to have, and treated for, systemic disease. Question: How is an open use test performed, and what is the purpose of a repeat open application test?

In an open use test (the "poor man's patch test"), the patient applies the suspected product twice daily for 1–2 weeks to a predetermined, non-dermatitic site such as the antecubital fossa or flexor forearm; if dermatitis develops, the patient is considered to be reacting to that product, though this method cannot identify the specific causative ingredient. Repeat open application tests serve a related but distinct purpose: they help establish the clinical relevance of a positive patch test result, for example confirming whether a low concentration of an allergen (like fragrance) that did not react on initial patch testing is still clinically significant when used in an actual product. Question: In immunocompetent individuals with latent HSV-1 infection, recurrent herpes labialis most commonly appears at which site, and what other, less common sites can be affected?

Question: What causes carpet beetle dermatitis, what is the typical clinical presentation, and how is it managed?

Carpet beetle dermatitis is a hypersensitivity reaction to the hastae (larval hairs) or hemolymph of Dermestidae beetles (Attagenus, Dermestes, Anthrenus, Trogaderma spp.), whose larvae feed on household organic materials like wool and hide in rugs and furniture. Contact typically produces a pruritic papulovesicular eruption, though superficial bullae, erosions, urticarial papules, vasculitis, lymphadenopathy, and eye/upper respiratory inflammation can occur. Question: How does chimerism differ fundamentally from mosaicism, and what pigmentary pattern is typically seen in the skin of chimeric individuals?

Chimerism differs from mosaicism in that its different cell clones originate from two distinct organisms (e.g., from fusion of two dizygotic zygotes or fertilization of one egg by two sperm), rather than arising from genetic changes within a single organism. Pigmentary variation in chimerism typically presents as a checkerboard pattern, though streaks along Blaschko's lines and irregular mixtures of light and dark skin not corresponding to recognized mosaic patterns have also been described. Question: When paring a keratotic lesion on the foot to distinguish it from a wart, what findings would indicate a corn versus a callus, and how does this differ from what is seen in a wart?

Paring a corn reveals a central translucent whitish-yellow core, whereas paring a callus reveals layers of yellowish keratin without a central core. In contrast, paring a wart (verruca vulgaris or mosaic plantar wart) reveals intracorneal hemorrhages and multiple punctate bleeding points, which are absent in corns and calluses. LIPOSUCTION Indications and Contraindications Tumescent liposuction is indicated for improving localized adiposities. Certain areas of subcutaneous fat are often not fully responsive to diet and exercise alone, and there are no exercises capable of spot reduction of adiposity. Most liposuction patients complain that the troublesome areas of fat excess “run in the family”. Furthermore, areas of excess subcuta- neous fat can be resistant to caloric restriction or exercise. Tumescent liposuction is able to specifically target these localized areas of excess subcutaneous fat as a complement to, not a replacement for, diet and exercise. INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND Liposuction is an effective method for surgically improving localized areas of excess subcutaneous fat. Liposuction has undergone many changes since initial reports in the late 1970s 1–3 . Modern liposuction is performed using dilute local anesthesia, via the tumescent technique, together with small cannulas connected to a vacuum aspirator. When performed correctly using the tumescent techniques, liposuction can be safely performed in an office setting with very few complications. Substantial amounts of fat can be aspirated with minimal blood loss and excellent aesthetic results. Patient selection remains paramount in achieving good results. Liposuction is currently among the most common invasive cosmetic procedures performed in the US. However, recent survey data have shown a decrease in the number of liposuctions being performed. This is likely due to the increased availability of non-invasive technologies that are currently approved by the FDA for the treatment of localized adiposity. These technologies generally have fewer side effects than tumescent liposuction but deliver more modest results. When choosing between liposuction and non-invasive treatments, it is important that patients have realistic expectations.

OBSERVATIONAL STUDIES Participants in observational studies are observed and certain outcomes are measured, without external manipulation or an attempt to affect the outcome. Descriptive Studies Many of the studies currently being done in dermatology are descriptive. These include case reports and case series. A case report is a detailed description of an individual patient’s demographics, clinical presen- tation, diagnosis, treatment, and disease course. A case series reports on some aspect(s) of a disease, diagnostic procedure, or treatment in a group of patients with common characteristics 20 . Case reports and series are useful for determining the manifestations of rare condi- tions, reporting the preliminary outcomes of experimental therapies, and generating hypotheses for larger studies. A major limitation of case series is the lack of a control group ( Table 123.4 ) 20,21 , although previous data (e.g. on the prevalence of risk factors in the general population) can sometimes be utilized for comparison. Question: According to the excerpt, what is a case report, what is a case series, what are they useful for, and what is a major limitation of case series?

A case report is a detailed description of an individual patient's demographics, clinical presentation, diagnosis, treatment, and disease course, while a case series reports on some aspect(s) of a disease, diagnostic procedure, or treatment in a group of patients with common characteristics. Both are useful for determining the manifestations of rare conditions, reporting preliminary outcomes of experimental therapies, and generating hypotheses for larger studies. A major limitation of case series is the lack of a control group, though prior data such as population risk-factor prevalence can sometimes be used for comparison. Conclusions In drawing conclusions about the results, the factors that support causality for the association in question should be determined (see whether the association makes biological and clinical sense. If it does not make sense, a type I error may have occurred, where a statisti- cally significant association is found when one does not truly exist (false positive). The more statistical tests that are performed for a study, the more likely a statistically significant association will be found based on chance alone. In studies utilizing large databases where many compar- isons are made, the false discovery rate increases and statistical methods (e.g. the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure) should be used to adjust P values in order to mitigate the risk of type I errors 35 . Alternatively, if an association is not found when one would be expected, a type II error may have occurred, where no statistical significance is found when one truly exists (false negative). This can be caused by a study not having enough power. The conclusions that can be drawn given the type of study design must be recognized, taking into account the strengths and limitations, including potential biases. In extrapolating the results, the generaliz- ability of the study must also be considered. This pertains to how appli- cable the results are to the greater population and groups that did not participate in the study. It should also be noted if a trial was industry- sponsored. Lastly, it is important to consider the implications of the study on current clinical practices and the direction of future research. Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) and the Consolidated Standards for Reporting Trials (CONSORT) There is a need to ensure appropriate reporting of findings from dermatologic studies. Question: How is the ankle–brachial index (ABI) calculated, and what does an ABI value greater than 1.40 suggest, including which patient populations are prone to this finding?

The ABI is calculated by dividing the highest systolic pressure obtained from the dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial artery by the higher of the two brachial artery systolic pressures, measured with the patient supine. A value greater than 1.40 suggests incompressible tibial arteries due to medial calcification, which is seen in patients with diabetes mellitus, chronic renal insufficiency, or older age. In these patients, the toe–brachial index should be measured instead. [Chapter: 105 Ulcers, p.2235-2236]

Question: In Mal de Meleda, what clinical complications can arise from hyperkeratosis of the fingers, and what histologic feature is characteristic of this condition?

Hyperkeratosis of the fingers in Mal de Meleda can progress to sclerodactyly and digital constrictions known as pseudoainhum. Histologically, in addition to orthohyperkeratosis, hyper- or normogranulosis, acanthosis, and a moderate perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, papillomatosis is a characteristic finding in Mal de Meleda. Question: How do CD28 and CTLA-4 differ in their effects on T cell activation despite both binding B7-1 (CD80) and B7-2 (CD86), and how does this relate to the mechanism of immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy?

CD28 binding to B7 molecules delivers an activating signal, inducing antiapoptotic genes and cytokine production such as IL-2. In contrast, CTLA-4 binds the same B7 molecules with even higher avidity but delivers a negative regulatory signal, downregulating IL-2 production and cell cycle progression; blocking CTLA-4 signaling therefore prolongs T cell activation. Tumor cells can exploit CTLA-4 (along with PD-L1/PD-L2) to escape immune responses, and antibodies like ipilimumab that neutralize CTLA-4 act as immune checkpoint inhibitors, an approach also used effectively in malignancies like metastatic melanoma, though it can cause autoimmune side effects such as colitis, hepatitis, and hypophysitis. A critical diagnostic feature of the cutaneous eruption of dermato- myositis is poikiloderma. This feature may occur both in patients with dermatomyositis, where it is frequently characterized by a pink–violet color, and in patients with lupus erythematosus, where the poikiloderma is typically more red in color. However, in patients with skin phototypes I and II, the hue of the poikiloderma of dermatomyositis may be pink– red rather than truly violet ( Fig. 42.6A ). Photodistributed poikiloderma is very characteristic of dermatomyositis, often involving the upper chest ( V-neck sign ) and the upper back ( shawl sign ). Poikiloderma can also affect photoprotected areas, such as the lateral thigh, referred to as the holster sign ( Fig. 42.6B,C ). If the clinician misses the poikiloderma, the eruption of dermatomyositis may occasionally be misdiagnosed as psoriasis, especially when there are well-defined plaques on the elbows and knees with fine silvery scale. The cutaneous lesions of dermatomyositis are often intensely pruritic ( Fig. 42.7 ), and this can significantly affect patients’ quality of life 44 . IL-31 may play a role as it does in other pruritic disorders. Of note, pruritus is a feature that can occasionally help to distinguish dermato- myositis from LE. An additional clinical clue to the diagnosis of dermatomyositis is nail-fold changes. Cuticular dystrophy (i.e. “ragged” cuticles and cuticular hypertrophy) is quite characteristic, as are nail-fold telangiectasias in which dilated capillary loops alternate with capillary dropout ( Fig. 42.8 ). If the photodistribution and nail-fold changes are missed, the eruption may be misdiagnosed as other conditions characterized by poikiloderma, such as cutaneous T cell lymphoma. Often, the dermatologist correctly notices the photodistribution but considers the diagnosis of photodrug eruption or lupus erythematosus rather than dermatomyositis. Question: What type of skin discoloration and histologic feature is characteristic of minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation type III, and how does this differ from types I and II?

Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation type III presents as diffuse 'muddy brown' pigmentation most prominent in sun-exposed areas, with histology showing increased melanin within the basal epidermis and/or dermal melanophages. This differs from types I and II, which show blue-black discoloration (also potentially involving nails, sclerae, oral mucosa, bones, thyroid, and teeth) with iron-containing pigment granules in the dermis representing hemosiderin and/or a minocycline derivative plus chelated iron, and only type II additionally contains melanin-containing granules. Q-switched pigment-directed lasers may help decrease discoloration in types I and II, but this is not mentioned for type III. [Chapter: 67 Disorders of Hyperpigmentation, p.1376-1377]

Question: In a patient with NF1 who has an established plexiform neurofibroma, what clinical changes should raise concern for malignant transformation into a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST)?

Concerning changes in an established plexiform neurofibroma include the onset of rapid growth, increased firmness, or persistent pain, as well as the development of a new neurologic deficit. These findings may herald malignant degeneration into an MPNST, which occurs in 8%–15% of NF1 patients, peaks in young adulthood, and can be very aggressive and often fatal. THE CELL PERSPECTIVE Functional Capabilities Acquired by Cancer Cells Oncogenic driver mutations alter the physiologic behavior of cells The comprehensive analysis of large numbers of cancer genomes has increased the number of oncogenic driver mutations within protein coding sequences to several hundreds. Mechanistic studies in cell culture systems and in model organisms have helped to understand how these alterations contribute to the malignant phenotype of cancer cells. Such endeavors have provided fundamental insights into the biology of cell behavior analogous to how the study of pathogens has elucidated the mechanisms of immune defense. Many oncogenic driver mutations were found to alter the function of proteins that regulate cell division, faithful genome replication, and cell survival, confirming the concept that oncogenic driver mutations confer a selective growth advantage during cancer evolution. A limited number of oncogenic signaling pathways have emerged that control these essential cellular processes and serve as a map to functionally classify oncogenic driver genes. Prominent examples include the RTK– RAS–MAPK (receptor tyrosine kinase–RAS–mitogen-activated protein kinase) and the PI3K–AKT–mTOR growth factor signaling pathways (see Figs. 55.3, 55.4 & 113.1 ), in addition to p53–Rb cell cycle control ( Fig. 107.4 ) and DNA damage response pathways 15 . To better illustrate the complex molecular mechanisms that contribute to malignant transformation, a set of hallmark capabilities has been defined that reflect the biologic consequences of oncogenic driver mutations, particularly aberrant proliferation and survival of cancer cells. Predominantly intrinsic cellular capabilities are sustained proliferative signaling, deregulated metabolism, evasion of growth suppressors, and resistance to cell death, as well as acquisition of replicative immortality and genome instability (see Fig. 107.1 ) 3 . This section reviews the fundamental principles of how oncogenic driver mutations compromise the physiologic regulation of cell division and genome replication, with a focus on the development of skin cancer. Functional analyses characterized Ras proteins as simple, binary, on-off switches that connect the activity of growth factors bound to their cell surface receptors to growth responses. Question: Which specific extracutaneous condition is associated with EBS caused by mutations in plectin (PLEC), and why is this association biologically expected?

Autosomal recessive EBS due to PLEC mutations is associated with muscular dystrophy. This is expected because plectin is expressed not only in the hemidesmosomes of basilar keratinocytes but also in skeletal muscle, so its loss affects both tissues. [Chapter: 32 Epidermolysis Bullosa, p.688]

Question: According to the comparison table, how do lichenoid drug eruptions typically differ from idiopathic lichen planus with respect to mean age, distribution, morphology, and mucous membrane involvement?

Lichenoid drug eruptions tend to occur in older patients (mean age ~65 years) compared to idiopathic LP (~50 years). They are more generalized and symmetric, often sparing LP's classic sites (wrists, flexor forearms, dorsal hands, presacral area, lower legs, genitalia), and their morphology is more eczematous, psoriasiform, or pityriasis rosea-like rather than the shiny, flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules of LP. Mucous membranes are usually spared in drug-induced lichenoid eruptions, whereas they are often involved in idiopathic LP. [Chapter: 11 Lichen Planus and Lichenoid Dermatoses, p.267]

In immunocompetent hosts, it is a benign, self-limited illness charac- terized by tender regional lymphadenitis that lasts for weeks to months. Over 90% of patients report a recent scratch and/or bite from a cat. Epidemiology and pathogenesis CSD occurs worldwide, and ~12 500 cases are diagnosed annually in the US 106 . Exposure to cats is the primary factor for CSD. Although flea- vectored transmission to humans has not been documented, it could explain some cases in which there is no history of exposure to cats. Lymphadenopathy usually presents 2–4 weeks after a scratch and can last 2–6 months, or even longer if fibrosis occurs. A skin lesion (e.g. a red or crusted pustule) develops at the inoculation site in most patients. Other skin findings can include a morbilliform eruption, erythema multiforme, granuloma annulare, and erythema nodosum 107 . Although most patients are otherwise well, the lymphadenopathy can be accompanied by fevers, malaise, fatigue, weakness, and headaches. Additional manifestations such as encephalopathy, hepatic granu- lomas, osteomyelitis, and pulmonary involvement develop in up to 15% of patients. The oculoglandular syndrome of Parinaud – unilateral conjunctivitis and ipsilateral preauricular lymphadenopathy – occurs in ~5% of individuals with CSD. Immunosuppressed patients (e.g. those with HIV infection) are prone to a more severe and complicated disease course. Question: Based on the classification criteria in Table 20.1, how do EM minor, EM major, SJS, SJS/TEN overlap, and TEN differ in terms of body surface area (BSA) of epidermal detachment, and what are their most common precipitating factors?

EM minor and EM major do not involve significant epidermal detachment and are most commonly precipitated by herpes simplex virus (and other infectious agents, with EM major occasionally due to drugs). Question: Why does filariasis preferentially affect the lower extremities and genitalia, and how does the clinical presentation differ in travelers who acquire the infection versus those in endemic areas?

Filariasis favors the lower extremities and genitalia because the female mosquito flies close to the ground and thus more often bites the lower limbs (with retrograde spread to the inguinal region), and because gravitational forces predispose the legs to venous hypertension and valvular incompetency, increasing susceptibility to chronic lymphedema. Question: What are the histologic hallmarks seen in a molluscum contagiosum lesion, and what happens to them as they move toward the skin surface?

Histologic evaluation of a molluscum contagiosum lesion shows large, intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies known as molluscum bodies (or Henderson–Patterson bodies) within epidermal keratinocytes. These inclusion bodies increase in size as they move toward the skin surface. A variably dense dermal infiltrate may also be present and can occasionally have pseudolymphomatous features. Question: On histopathology, what staining findings confirm that the pale-appearing keratinocytes in clear cell acanthoma contain glycogen, and what other clear cell neoplasm must be distinguished by its differing cytoplasmic content and staining pattern?

In clear cell acanthoma, PAS stains the pale keratinocyte cytoplasm red, and this material is diastase-sensitive, confirming it is glycogen; electron microscopy likewise shows abundant cytoplasmic glycogen. This must be distinguished from sebaceous neoplasms, whose sebocytes have multiloculated cytoplasm containing lipid rather than glycogen and stain positively for epithelial membrane antigen or adipophilin. The adult worms reside in the definitive host’s intestines (including humans) and are often associated with minimal clinical manifestations (see Fig. 83.26 ). In intermediate hosts, the larval stage can lead to clinical disease, e.g. cysticercosis or echino- coccosis in humans 136 . Epidemiology The four most common human cestodes (tapeworms) are Taenia solium (pork tapeworm), Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm), Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm), and Hymenolepis nana . In humans, they cause primarily gastrointestinal symptoms, but the larval stage of T. solium also causes cysticercosis. Larvae of T. solium and T. saginata , respec- tively, can cause cysticercosis in pigs and cattle. Cysticercosis has a worldwide distribution, affecting more than 50 million people, and it is more common in rural areas. Echinococcosis occurs in tropical and subtropical countries worldwide, primarily in sheep- and cattle-raising areas. Endemic regions include the southern province of Brazil, the Middle East, parts of Asia, and Northern and East Africa. It is particularly common in Lebanon and Greece 136,137 . Question: In humans, why do larval-stage infections with Taenia solium and Echinococcus species (e.g., cysticercosis and echinococcosis) cause more significant clinical disease than adult tapeworm infections, and what organs are typically involved?

Humans act as intermediate hosts for the larval stages of these cestodes, and it is this larval stage—not the adult worm residing in the intestine—that leads to clinical disease such as cysticercosis or echinococcosis. In echinococcosis, the larval stage forms hydatid cysts primarily in the liver and lungs, whereas adult tapeworms living in the intestine typically cause only minimal clinical manifestations. PREOPERATIVE HISTORY AND CONSIDERATIONS The preoperative assessment of patients undergoing electrosurgery should concentrate on potential hazards to either the patient or the treatment team. A patient history of previous allergic reactions to skin cleansers, anesthetics, or postoperative topicals and dressings should be sought. Electrosurgery should be used with care in patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices. Smoke evacuation equipment should always be available to safely remove the smoke plume when extensive electrosurgery, particularly electrosection, is performed. In such procedures, the operator and assis- tants should wear masks and use eye protection to prevent exposure to smoke-borne microbes and noxious particles. Gloves should always be worn when electrosurgical procedures are performed. Preparatory to electrosurgery, the lesion and surrounding skin should be cleansed with a non-alcoholic skin cleanser such as chlorhexidine or povidone iodine. This prevents the development of a depressed scar subsequent to the procedure. In erythrodermic MF/Sézary syndrome, biopsy specimens are non-diagnostic in about one-third of cases because epidermotropism of neoplastic lymphocytes is less commonly seen than in conventional MF, whereas psoriatic erythroderma more frequently shows diagnostic histologic findings. Question: In infants, why is pyoderma gangrenosum most often located on the perineum, and what is the basis for its diagnosis?

In infants, pyoderma gangrenosum most often involves the perineum, possibly due to pathergy. The clinical features, such as an undermined violaceous border, resemble those in older children and adults, and biopsies show a sterile neutrophilic infiltrate. However, the diagnosis is usually one of exclusion, made after ruling out other causes of ulceration such as infection, immunodeficiency, thrombosis, and vasculitis. Question: Why does acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) represent a disproportionately high percentage of melanomas diagnosed in Black, Asian, and Hispanic patients compared to non-Hispanic White patients, even though its incidence is similar across all racial and ethnic groups?

ALM's incidence itself does not vary by race or ethnicity, but individuals with darker skin phototypes develop far fewer UV-related melanomas overall. Since ALM is not UV-related, it makes up a much larger share of the total melanomas diagnosed in these populations (up to 36% in Black, 22% in Asian, and 9% in Hispanic patients) compared to only 2% in non-Hispanic White patients, who have a much higher baseline rate of UV-induced melanomas. Question: How do dermal ("superficial") leiomyosarcomas differ from subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas in terms of typical treatment and metastatic risk?

Dermal leiomyosarcomas, limited to the dermis, are typically cured by simple excision and only rarely metastasize, though they can recur; this favorable behavior has led to the suggested alternate term "atypical intradermal smooth muscle neoplasm." In contrast, subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas require wide excision and carry a much higher metastatic risk of approximately 25%–40%. Question: In patients treated with PUVA, how does the risk of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) compare to basal cell carcinoma (BCC), and what confounding factors complicate attributing this risk solely to PUVA?

In PUVA-treated patients, the risk of SCC is significantly increased compared to matched controls in a dose-dependent manner, whereas BCC risk is not significantly increased. However, attributing this risk solely to PUVA is complicated because many affected patients had prior exposure to excessive sunlight and other carcinogenic treatments, including arsenic, UVB, and antimetabolite therapy, with high UVB exposure in particular appearing to increase keratinocyte carcinoma risk in PUVA-treated patients. Notably, non-White individuals receiving long-term oral PUVA did not show increased skin cancer risk, and low exposure (<150 treatments) had at most modest effects on SCC risk. For example, there are some dermatoses that have a cephalocaudal progression over time, such as measles and pityriasis rubra pilaris. If lichenification is present, the lesion has not appeared acutely, despite what the patient may believe. In otherwise healthy individuals, there are several diseases whose cutaneous manifestations are often acute in nature, in particular urticaria, morbilliform drug eruption, viral exanthem, acute allergic or irritant contact dermatitis, and pityriasis rosea. However, since 1953, dapsone (the parent compound of sulfoxone) has been the mainstay of treatment for DH. Dapsone is 80% orally bioavailable, peaks in the serum between 2 and 6 hours post-administration and has a half-life of 24–30 hours. Being highly lipophilic, it has excellent cell penetration. Dapsone and its major metabolite monoacetyldapsone are strongly protein-bound and undergo enterohepatic recirculation. Thus, dapsone may be found in the bloodstream up to 1 month following a single dose 29 . Dapsone is metabolized by N -acetylation and N -hydroxylation in the liver 29,30 . Acetylation yields monoacetyldapsone, which is then de-acetylated to dapsone, yielding an equilibrium between dapsone and monoacetyldapsone. Hydroxylation via CYP enzymes produces N -hydroxy-dapsone, the metabolite which is believed to be responsible for the majority of dapsone side effects. Both dapsone and N -hydroxy- dapsone undergo glucuronidation in the liver, which results in more water-soluble compounds that are rapidly excreted in the urine 29 . Medical Therapy Mechanism of Action Dapsone is clinically most useful in the treatment of dermatologic diseases involving neutrophilic infiltrates. Researchers have demon- strated that dapsone inhibits neutrophil myeloperoxidase, thus reducing damage from the neutrophil respiratory burst mediated by this enzyme.

Question: Which drugs can increase dapsone levels/side effects, and what are the mechanisms by which they do so?

Probenecid increases dapsone levels by decreasing its renal clearance, while trimethoprim and other folate antagonists such as methotrexate can also raise dapsone levels. Additionally, cimetidine increases absolute dapsone levels but actually reduces toxicity because it lowers formation of the more toxic hydroxylamine metabolite, resulting in less methemoglobinemia. Sulfonamides and hydroxychloroquine do not raise dapsone levels per se but worsen hemolysis by increasing oxidative stress on red blood cells. [Chapter: 130 Other Systemic Drugs, p.2788-2789]

Question: According to this excerpt, why do skin grafts generally not take well when used to treat chronic non-healing radiation-induced ulcers, and what alternative approach is preferred?

Chronic radiation-induced ulcers occur in poorly vascularized tissue, and grafts do not take well on irradiated tissue because of this poor vascular bed. Instead, healing requires importing well-vascularized tissue, typically via local skin flaps or, sometimes, staged skin–muscle or axial pedicle flaps taken from non-irradiated tissue. Pathology The key histologic feature of formalin-fixed gouty tophi is the presence of deposits of amorphous material within the dermis and subcutis, corresponding to sites of crystal deposition. These deposits contain needle-like clefts (which represent dissolved urate crystals) surrounded by a granulomatous infiltrate with multinucleated giant cells ( Fig. 48.3 ). Secondary calcification or even ossification can occasionally be seen in older lesions. In order to preserve the crystals, the biopsy specimen needs to be placed in an ethanol-based fixative, such as Carnoy’s fluid. Then, under regular or polarized light, brightly refractile brown sheaths of fine needle-like crystals can be seen. Upon staining with 20% silver nitrate solution, the crystals appear black and the surrounding tissue yellow, whereas with the De Galantha stain, the crystals appear brown to black 7 . Differential Diagnosis The differential diagnosis of acute gouty arthritis includes pseudo­gout (see below), osteoarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis (previ- ously referred to as Reiter disease), and septic arthritis. Given its destructive nature, septic arthritis needs to be considered even in patients in whom the diagnosis of gout has been previously established. The presence of needle-shaped crystals with negative birefringence in an aspirate of joint fluid is diagnostic of gout, while Gram stain and culture exclude septic arthritis. Occasionally, patients are misdiagnosed as having cellulitis. The differential diagnosis of cutaneous gouty tophi includes xanthomas, rheumatoid nodules, and calcinosis cutis. Examination of expressed fluid or chalky material by polarized light can provide a “bedside” diagnosis. By ultrasonography, central clear spaces are seen within tophi whereas rheumatoid nodules contain central echodense areas 6 . Question: For gout, what histologic appearance do dermal deposits have in formalin-fixed specimens, what do polarizing light and the De Galantha and silver nitrate stains show, and which fixative is best for preserving the urate crystals?

In formalin-fixed specimens, gout shows dermal deposits of amorphous material with needle-like clefts surrounded by a granulomatous infiltrate with giant cells. Under polarizing light (fresh preparation), fine needle-like crystals with negative birefringence are seen; a 20% silver nitrate solution stains urate crystals black with surrounding tissue yellow, while the De Galantha stain colors crystals brown–black. The best fixative to preserve the crystals is an ethanol-based fixative such as Carnoy's fluid. [Chapter: 48 Deposition Diseases, p.962-963]

Question: In the RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK (MAPK) signaling pathway relevant to melanocytic neoplasia, what proportion of cutaneous melanomas and melanocytic nevi harbor a mutation in either NRAS or BRAF, and what is the functional consequence of PTEN inactivation on the related PI3K–AKT pathway?

Either NRAS or BRAF is mutated in up to 80% of all cutaneous melanomas and melanocytic nevi, underscoring the central role of the MAPK pathway in melanocytic neoplasia. PTEN normally acts as a key inhibitor of the PI3K–AKT pathway, and its inactivation—through mutations, deletions, or promoter methylation—leads to increased activity of the PI3K–AKT signaling pathway, which regulates cell survival, growth, and apoptosis. Cutaneous findings are classified into the following groups: acute papular onchodermatitis, chronic papular onchodermatitis, lichenified onchodermatitis, onchocercal atrophy, and depigmentation ( Fig. 83.31 ) 103 . Patients first present with subcutaneous nodules that are usually located over bony prominences; they favor the upper part of the body in patients living in South America and the lower part of the body in those from Africa. The subcutaneous nodules represent fibrous tissue surrounding adult worms. An intermittent, intensely pruritic acute papular onchodermatitis follows, in which small papules form around the microfilariae (called “craw-craw” in Africa). In chronic onchocerciasis, the skin becomes thickened and wrinkled; this is accompanied by lichenification and hyperpigmentation and is sometimes referred to as “lizard” or “elephant” skin or “sowda”. The back, thighs, and lower trunk are frequently affected, and hyper- pigmentation may develop on one lower extremity in association with inguinal lymphadenopathy (see Fig. 83.31 ). Atrophy and a loss of pigment with sparing of perifollicular skin are also seen in late stage onchocerciasis. The latter changes, sometimes referred to as “leopard” skin, are most often evident on the shins (see Fig. 83.31 and Ch. 66 ) 104 . Chronic lymphatic obstruction and involvement of the inguinal lymph nodes can lead to hanging groin or elephantiasis of the genitalia (see Fig. 83.31 ). In Central America, young patients who are heavily infested may develop erythema on the face or upper trunk (erisipela de la costa). Older patients may have violaceous papules or plaques (mal morado), which can lead to leonine facies. In addition to skin lesions, microfilariae can also be found in the conjunctivae; from there they can move through the cornea into the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye, leading to conjunctivitis, sclerosing keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinal lesions, optic atrophy, and glaucoma 97 . Blindness occurs in the most severe cases. Dead microfi- lariae in the cornea can induce a tissue reaction that produces charac- teristic “snowflake” opacities. Pathogenesis Onchocerciasis is transmitted by the bite of an infected black fly ( Simulium spp.). Because these flies often assume a “hump-backed” stance, they are sometimes referred to as “buffalo gnats”. Black flies feed by “rasping” (abrading) the surface of the skin until a pool of blood forms, which they lap up. Microfilariae previously residing in the dermis are present in this blood, and they penetrate the gut wall of the insect and migrate to its thoracic muscles, where they develop into larvae. The larvae then migrate to the proboscis, from which they will be transmitted to another human host during a blood meal (see Fig. 83.23 ) 99 . Wolbachia bacterial endosymbionts are required for normal development of O. volvulus larvae and embryos, are thought to support the survival of adult worms, and drive immune responses that contribute to disease pathogenesis 101 . Once in their human host, larvae take almost a year to reach maturity. The adult worms are large, measuring up to 50 cm in length. They are encapsulated within fibrous tissue and reside in nodules close to the surface of the skin or near joints. These nodules are known as onchocercomas ( Fig. 83.30 ). Each female worm produces hundreds of microfilariae, which live for 1–2 years and migrate into the skin, connective tissue, eyes, and lymph nodes. It is the microfilariae that cause most of the serious clinical features of onchocerciasis 102 . There is little inflammation until the microfilariae degenerate, which triggers a hypersensitivity reaction. In the skin, this results in intense pruritus and dermatitis. Question: When suspecting medium-sized vessel vasculitis versus evaluating an ulcer, how should biopsy technique and site selection differ, and why should incidental vasculitis found under an ulcer not be considered diagnostic?

For suspected medium-sized vessel vasculitis, a deep punch, double-trephine ("telescoping") punch, or incisional biopsy including sufficient subcutaneous tissue should be performed, ideally sampling a nodule rather than an ulcer edge or livedo racemosa, since nodule biopsies have higher diagnostic yield. Ulcers should instead be biopsied at their edge, including the peripheral rim of inflammation if present, because vasculitis found incidentally underlying an ulcer is common but not diagnostic of true vasculitic disease. Anetoderma is an elastolytic disorder charac- terized by localized areas of flaccid skin, which may be depressed, macular or papular; the latter can reflect herniation of the subcutaneous tissue. Anetoderma may be idiopathic or associated with an inflam- matory disorder of the skin. History The first case of primary inflammatory anetoderma was reported by Jadassohn in 1892 11 . A year previously, Schweninger and Buzzi described a 29-year-old woman with multiple, non-inflammatory, sac-like tumors on the trunk and upper extremities 12 . Epidemiology Several hundred cases of anetoderma have been reported in the world literature. Primary anetoderma favors young adults between 15 and 25 years of age and occurs more frequently in women than men. The epidemiology of secondary anetoderma reflects that of the underlying etiologies (see Table 99.3 ). Pathogenesis The pathogenesis of anetoderma is not known. These lesions could be considered unusual scars, since scars also have decreased elastic tissue. The loss of dermal elastin may reflect an impaired turnover of elastin, caused by either increased destruction or decreased synthesis of elastic fibers. There are a number of proposed explanations for the focal elastin destruction, e.g. the release of elastase from inflammatory cells, the release of cytokines such as interleukin-6, an increased production of progelatinases A and B 13 , and the phagocytosis of elastic fibers by macrophages. More recently, a decrease in fibulin protein expression was observed, suggesting defective elastic fiber reassembly 6 . Immunologic mechanisms may also play a role, providing an expla- nation for associated findings such as antiphospholipid antibodies (see below). Based upon a few isolated patients, a link may exist between anetoderma and mutations in genes that encode enzymes in the citric acid cycle 14 . In primary anetoderma, there is no underlying associated disorder and lesions arise within clinically normal skin. It has classically been subdivided into two major forms: those with preceding inflammatory lesions (the Jadassohn–Pellizzari type) and those without preceding inflammatory lesions (the Schweninger–Buzzi type) ( Table 99.2 ). This clinical classification is primarily of historical interest, since the two types of lesions can coexist in the same patient and their histopathology is often the same; the presence or absence of clinical inflammation at the onset of the disease is not related to prognosis 15 . Question: Which class of shampoo surfactants provides deep cleansing but may leave hair harsh, and which class is non-irritating to the eyes with mild cleansing?

Anionic surfactants (e.g., lauryl sulfates, laureth sulfates, sarcosines, sulfosuccinates) provide deep cleansing but may leave hair harsh. Amphoteric surfactants (e.g., betaines, sultaines, imidazolinium derivatives) are non-irritating to the eyes, provide mild cleansing, and impart manageability. History Aspergillosis was among the first mycoses recognized, with the initial report of a human case by Sluyter in 1847. In 1855, Kurchenmeister isolated Mucor from the lung and described zygomycosis. Benham distinguished cryptococcosis from blastomycosis in the 1930s. Epidemiology With the exception of several dimorphic fungi, opportunistic fungal infec- tions occur worldwide and have no geographic predilection. Question: According to this excerpt, what environmental reservoirs are associated with Aspergillus/Fusarium/Mucormycetes, Cryptococcus neoformans, and Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei, and how has voriconazole prophylaxis affected the epidemiology of opportunistic mycoses in high-risk oncology patients?

Aspergillus spp., Fusarium spp., and Mucormycetes are soil saprophytes found in decaying vegetation, Cryptococcus neoformans is isolated from avian (especially pigeon) droppings, and T. marneffei is endemic to Southeast Asia and China with a reservoir thought to be bamboo rats. The use of prophylactic voriconazole in high-risk oncology patients (e.g., neutropenic patients with hematologic malignancies or hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients) has decreased the incidence of disseminated candidiasis and aspergillosis, though voriconazole lacks activity against Mucormycetes, which require newer antifungals like posaconazole or isavuconazole. Question: What happens when benzoyl peroxide is applied together with tretinoin, and what visible side effect can occur when topical dapsone is used concomitantly with benzoyl peroxide?

When benzoyl peroxide is applied together with tretinoin, it can decrease the activity of tretinoin. Separately, concomitant use of topical dapsone and benzoyl peroxide can occasionally cause a temporary yellow–orange staining of the skin and hair. [Chapter: 127 Antimicrobial Drugs, p.2709]

Adapted Biology of the Extracellular Matrix Glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans GAGs are polysaccharides composed of sulfated and acetylated sugars with negative charges that bind large amounts of ions and water. The most prominent and ubiquitous protein-free GAG is hyaluronic acid, a giant polysaccharide composed of thousands of N-acetylglucosamine/ glucuronic acid disaccharides. However, other GAGs bind to proteins via a serine hydroxyl group, forming proteoglycans ( Fig. 95.7 ) 15 . There are four classes of proteoglycans based upon their tissue localization: intracellular, cell-surface, pericellular, and extracellular 15 . Proteoglycans differ remarkably in their protein content as well as the number, type, and length of their GAG side chains ( Table 95.3 ). Four known GAGs can bind proteins to form proteoglycans; they are chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, keratan sulfate, and heparan sulfate 15 . The correct balance of chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate is necessary for skin function and integrity 16 . Versican, which contains these two GAGs, is an important dermal proteoglycan that can be synthesized by fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, and epithelial cells. It is associated with the elastic fiber system and forms large complexes with hyaluronic acid, which provide the skin with its tautness (see Fig. 95.7 ). Heparan sulfate chains sequester growth factors (e.g. fibroblast growth factors [FGFs], vascular endothelial growth factors [VEGFs]) and present them to their receptors. Perlecan is a major heparan sulfate- containing proteoglycan found in all basement membranes, including the epidermal basement membrane. Syndecans are transmembrane heparan sulfate proteoglycans that control cell adhesion to the ECM and cytoskeletal organization. Syndecans 1, 2, and 4 are expressed in the skin and can be found in keratinocytes, dendritic cells, and fibro- blasts, where they are thought to mediate “outside-in” cell signaling 15 . Glypicans are membrane-anchored heparan sulfate proteoglycans that interact with growth factors and other extracellular proteins in the skin to regulate developmental and regenerative events 18 . Within the areas of involvement, the lesions are often coalescent centrally. Associated fine scale may be obvious or only apparent upon scratching or stretching the skin. The distribution is usually symmetric and favors the upper trunk and shoulders; lesions sometimes develop on the lower trunk, body folds, neck, and face (see Ch. 77 ). Of note, facial tinea versicolor may occur in association with protective mask use 128a . While the contrast between the hypomelanotic infected skin and the surrounding normal skin is striking in darkly pigmented patients, or following a tan in lightly pigmented patients, Wood’s lamp examination may be required to locate all the lesions. In the hypopigmented skin, there is a decreased density of melano- somes within keratinocytes, but no change in the melanocyte density. Abnormal melanosome production, decreased melanin synthesis, and a partial block in melanosome transfer to keratinocytes have all been suggested as underlying defects. Question: In tinea versicolor, what is the underlying change in melanosome density and melanocyte density within the hypopigmented skin, and what compound has been implicated in causing decreased melanin synthesis?

In hypopigmented tinea versicolor skin, there is a decreased density of melanosomes within keratinocytes, but melanocyte density itself is unchanged. Abnormal melanosome production, decreased melanin synthesis, and a partial block in melanosome transfer to keratinocytes have been proposed as underlying defects. Azelaic acid, a competitive inhibitor of tyrosinase produced by Malassezia furfur, may contribute to the decreased melanin synthesis. Question: In neutral lipid storage disease with ichthyosis (NLSDI), what characteristic finding on a fresh peripheral blood smear helps distinguish it from Refsum disease, and why might automated blood-counting methods fail to detect it?

NLSDI is characterized by the Jordan anomaly—numerous lipid-containing vacuoles within circulating granulocytes and monocytes—which is detectable only on a fresh peripheral blood smear, not by automated blood-counting methods. While vacuolated cells can be seen in both NLSDI and Refsum disease, lipid droplets on a peripheral blood smear are specific to NLSDI and are not seen in Refsum disease. Question: Why is infliximab specifically contraindicated in patients with an allergy to murine proteins, and what other conditions should generally be avoided when considering treatment with any TNF inhibitor?

Infliximab is a chimeric anti-TNF antibody that contains mouse (murine) protein components, so patients allergic to murine proteins are specifically contraindicated from receiving it. Beyond drug-specific hypersensitivity, all TNF inhibitors should be avoided in patients with significant active infection, malignancy, congestive heart failure (especially if unstable), multiple sclerosis, or other demyelinating diseases. Question: In contact hypersensitivity (CHS), which subset of T cells predominates as effector cells (in contrast to other delayed-type hypersensitivity responses), what determines the balance between effector T cells and Tregs, and what type of cells can present hapten antigen during the elicitation phase in the skin?

Unlike most delayed-type hypersensitivity responses, which are mediated by CD4+ T cells, CHS is mediated predominantly by CD8+ effector T cells, with Treg populations also induced to inhibit the response. The balance between effector T cells and Tregs depends on the dose of antigen applied, since extremely low doses induce tolerance rather than sensitization. During elicitation in the skin, antigen presentation can be performed not only by classical APCs but also by keratinocytes, dermal mast cells, and macrophages, at least in an MHC class I-restricted fashion. Question: In the RAS–MAPK signaling pathway, what are the distinct roles of SOS1 and neurofibromin in regulating RAS activity, and which genodermatosis results from loss of neurofibromin function?

SOS1 is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor that is recruited to the activated receptor complex and increases levels of active RAS-GTP, thereby promoting signaling. In contrast, neurofibromin is a GTPase activating protein that promotes hydrolysis of RAS-GTP to RAS-GDP, which terminates signaling; loss of neurofibromin function (as occurs in neurofibromatosis type 1) leads to unchecked RAS activation. Although eruptions are usually observed in 0.1% to 1% of patients enrolled in pre-marketing trials of most systemic drugs, up to 5% of patients treated with antibiotics or aromatic anticonvulsants may develop a cutaneous eruption. In the mid 1990s, it was estimated that 1 of every 1000 hospitalized patients had a serious cutaneous drug reaction 1 . The former is more common than the latter. Phototoxicity Phototoxic drug reactions are usually predictable. They occur immedi- ately after exposure to ultraviolet radiation (UVR) and are often dependent on the dose of the drug and/or UVR. There is a direct inter- action of UVR with the drug (or its metabolite) within the skin such that an unstable singlet or triplet state is created, leading to the generation of reactive oxygen species. Surgical Complications and Optimizing Outcomes Prophylactic antibiotics Antibiotic prophylaxis is administered to prevent surgical site infection, bacterial endocarditis, or infection in implanted prosthetic devices. The risk and consequences of infection must be weighed against the risk and cost of the antibiotic. Wounds are placed into four general categories ( Table 151.1 ). The majority of dermatologic surgical procedures are clean or clean-contam- inated and do not need prophylaxis. However, prophylactic antibiotics may be helpful in certain clean-contaminated wounds. For example, antibiotics can be considered for procedures involving the oronasal mucosa, axilla, or anogenital region, although there are no controlled studies. Procedures that approach the ear canal may be at higher risk for infection with Gram-negative organisms. Long procedures are also more likely to develop wound infections: the infection rate almost doubles with each hour of operation. Prophylactic antibiotics are recommended for procedures at increased risk for surgical site infection, including surgery on the lower extremities or in the groin, wedge excisions of the lip or ear, flaps on the nose, all skin grafts, and in patients with extensive inflammatory skin disease 34 . When possible, prophylactic antibiotics should be prescribed in anticipation of these types of repairs. Unless the patient is in a special group (see below), some surgeons limit prophylactic antibiotics to just excisions on the lower extremities and ears, especially if the cartilage is exposed. Antibiotics are therapeutic, not prophylactic, for contaminated and infected wounds. Two special patient groups should be considered for antibiotic prophylaxis: (1) those at risk for infective endocarditis; and (2) those at risk for bloodborne infection of total joint replacements ( Table 151.2 ) 34 . In patients with total joint replacements or specific cardiac diseases, no prophylaxis is indicated if the surgical procedure is in a non-infected cutaneous site. In general, prophylactic antibiotics are no longer recommended by the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons and American Dental Association for patients with prosthetic joint replace- ments undergoing dental procedures; possible exceptions, including mucosal incision in a patient with a history of joint surgery complica- tions, are outlined in Table 151.2 35,36 . However, to date, recommen- dations specific to dermatologic procedures are lacking. Table 151.3 summarizes suggestions for antibiotic prophylaxis regimens. If any question arises, consider consultation with the patient’s cardiologist, internist, or orthopedic surgeon. Implantable electronic medical devices Cardiac defibrillators

Question: In Hansen disease, how are the lepromatous and tuberculoid forms distinguished in terms of the immune response involved and the number of organisms found in the dermis?

Hansen disease is divided into two major clinicopathologic forms based on the type of immune response: lepromatous disease is characterized by a predominantly Th2 response, while tuberculoid disease is characterized by a predominantly Th1 response. Correspondingly, the lepromatous form shows multiple organisms present in the dermis, whereas the tuberculoid form has only a few organisms. [Chapter: 75 Mycobacterial Infections, p.1587-1588]

Question: How do generalized essential telangiectasia (GET) and cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy (CCV) differ in terms of patient demographics, distribution pattern, and distinguishing histopathologic features?

GET typically shows a female predominance and begins on the distal lower extremities with a characteristic proximal "upward march" over time, whereas CCV lacks a clear female predominance, may involve just the trunk and/or proximal extremities, and does not show this progressive upward spread. Histopathologically, CCV is distinguished by ectatic superficial blood vessels with hyalinized, laminated concentric concretions around the vessel basement membrane that are PAS-positive, diastase-resistant, and react with antibodies against collagen type IV, with ultrastructural deposits showing abnormal collagen banding (Luse bodies) — features not seen in GET. Both conditions are benign and lack association with systemic illness. [Chapter: 106 Other Vascular Disorders, p.2254-2255]

Question: Compare primary and secondary cutaneous aspergillosis in terms of portal of entry and pathogenesis, and identify the major risk factor for developing invasive or disseminated disease.

Primary cutaneous aspergillosis results from direct inoculation of the skin at sites such as burns, trauma, surgical wounds, IV catheters, or macerated skin under occlusive dressings. Secondary cutaneous aspergillosis, the more common form, occurs when inhaled conidia cause a primary lung infection that later disseminates to the skin. Immunosuppression—particularly neutropenia combined with chronic corticosteroid use, and sometimes late-stage AIDS—is the major risk factor for invasive or disseminated aspergillosis. MUIR–TORRE SYNDROME (VARIANT OF LYNCH SYNDROME) Synonym:  Cutaneous sebaceous neoplasms and keratoacanthomas, with gastrointestinal and other carcinomas Key features  An autosomal dominant disorder associated most commonly with adenocarcinoma of the colon, followed by genitourinary carcinomas  The cutaneous manifestations are sebaceous neoplasms and keratoacanthomas  Caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes ( MSH2 >> MLH1 > MSH6, PMS2 ) Introduction Muir–Torre syndrome (MTS) is an uncommon autosomal dominant genodermatosis that is characterized by sebaceous neoplasms (adenoma, sebaceoma, or carcinoma; see Ch. 111 ), and internal malignancies. It is considered to represent a variant of Lynch syndrome, which is also known as hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) syndrome 39 . History Muir in 1967 and Torre in 1968 independently reported the syndrome that bears their names. Their two patients had malignancies in several organs plus either keratoacanthoma-like lesions or multiple tumors of sebaceous origin. Epidemiology The male : female ratio in MTS is 3 : 2, and affected individuals present with cutaneous manifestations at a mean age of 55 years. The preva- lence of Lynch syndrome in the general population is estimated to be ~1 in 350. In a study of Lynch syndrome patients, MTS was observed in 28% (14/50) of families and 9% (14/152) of individuals with a confirmed germline mismatch repair gene mutation 40 . Question: What is cutaneous extramedullary hematopoiesis (CEMH), what are its most common associations in neonates versus adults, and what histologic finding characterizes the dermal infiltrate?

CEMH reflects bone marrow dysfunction and presents as widely disseminated erythematous to violaceous papules and nodules (the neonatal form is called "blueberry muffin baby"). In neonates, it is most commonly associated with TORCH infections, while in adults it is most often associated with myelofibrosis (as well as other myeloproliferative neoplasms like polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia). Histologically, it shows a diffuse dermal infiltrate of immature erythrocytes, leukocytes, and megakaryocytes. [Chapter: 121 Other Lymphoproliferative and Myeloproliferative Diseases, p.2633]
