The orderly, symmetric distribution pattern of disseminated eczema argues against simple surface spread of contact irritants or allergens, suggesting instead a systemic (hematogenous) process. Question: In photodynamic therapy (PDT), what is the formula used to calculate exposure time from fluence and irradiance, and what does the principle of drug–light dose reciprocity mean in terms of photosensitizer amount and light fluence?

Drug–light dose reciprocity refers to an inverse relationship between photosensitizer level and light fluence: a high photosensitizer concentration combined with a low fluence can theoretically produce an equivalent amount of singlet oxygen as a low photosensitizer concentration activated by a high fluence, since net singlet oxygen production depends on both factors. Question: What clinical and demographic features characterize inverted follicular keratosis (IFK), and what histologic findings help distinguish it from tricholemmoma and squamous cell carcinoma?

IFK typically presents as an asymptomatic, firm, white-tan to pink papule usually under 1 cm, occurring most often on the face (about 85% of cases, especially cheek and upper lip) of middle-aged to older White individuals, with men affected twice as often as women. Histologically it shows an endophytic, bulbous proliferation of eosinophilic keratinocytes with basaloid/squamous differentiation surrounding follicular canals, often with inflammation and squamous eddies. Unlike tricholemmoma, which shows a predominance of clear cells with basal cell palisading and a thickened basement membrane, IFK lacks these clear cell features; and while rare mitoses may be seen in IFK, the overt cellular atypia characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma is absent. Question: Why do patients with HPS10 (AP3D1 mutations) develop neurologic manifestations while patients with HPS2 (AP3B1 mutations) do not, despite both affecting subunits of the AP-3 complex?

HPS2 and HPS10 result from mutations in AP3B1 and AP3D1, which encode the β1 and δ1 subunits of the AP-3 complex, respectively. A neuron-specific AP-3 heterotetramer requires the δ1 subunit but not the β1 subunit. Therefore, only HPS10, caused by loss of δ1, leads to neurologic manifestations, whereas HPS2, caused by loss of β1, does not. [Chapter: 66 Vitiligo and Other Disorders of Hypopigmentation, p.1347]

Question: How do the clinical presentation and dermoscopic features of membranous aplasia cutis congenita differ from the stellate/angulated type, and what is the proposed etiology of each?

Membranous aplasia cutis congenita presents at birth as a sharply marginated, oval or round, 'punched-out' defect covered by a thin, translucent, glistening membrane that may appear bullous from serous fluid before flattening into an atrophic scar; dermoscopy shows no follicular openings, telangiectatic vessels, and radially oriented 'starburst-like' hair follicles at the periphery. In contrast, the stellate or angulated type presents as ulcers of variable depth with a raw, hemorrhagic, or granulating base, and is thought to result from vascular abnormalities and/or intrauterine ischemic events, as seen in Adams–Oliver syndrome or with fetus papyraceus and placental infarction. The patient should be queried as to duration and relative change in intensity and/or distribution over time. For example, there are some dermatoses that have a cephalocaudal progression over time, such as measles and pityriasis rubra pilaris. Of course, the time course is more prolonged in the latter as compared to the former. The dermatologist is at an advantage because the skin is so acces- sible. Information provided by the patient can be readily compared to the physical examination. With experience, a dermatologist can usually determine by observation if cutaneous lesions are acute, subacute, or chronic. As an example, scale (not to be confused with crust) reflects parakeratosis, and due to epidermal transit time, it requires 2 weeks to develop. Intact tense bullae are rarely more than a week old. Lichenification, i.e. thickening of the skin with accentuation of normal skin markings, takes weeks to months to develop. If lichenification is present, the lesion has not appeared acutely, despite what the patient may believe. In otherwise healthy individuals, there are several diseases whose cutaneous manifestations are often acute in nature, in particular urticaria, morbilliform drug eruption, viral exanthem, acute allergic or irritant contact dermatitis, and pityriasis rosea. This does not mean these skin diseases require emergent management, but rather that the rashes appear abruptly and are distinguished, particularly from neoplasms or chronic dermatoses, by temporal acuity. Question: Why are individuals with the P1k or p blood group phenotypes naturally resistant to parvovirus B19 infection, and what sequence of immune events following infection correlates with the appearance of the rash and arthralgia?

Parvovirus B19 binds to the erythrocyte P antigen (globoside) as its cellular receptor, so individuals who lack this antigen (P1k or p phenotypes) are naturally resistant to infection. After initial respiratory tract infection, viremia occurs, and anti-B19 IgM antibody appears about 8–10 days post-inoculation, accompanied by reticulocytopenia lasting 7–10 days. One week after IgM appears, anti-B19 IgG appears, and this coincides with the onset of the rash and arthralgia, suggesting an immune-mediated mechanism given the temporal disconnect between viremia and symptom onset. Upon further irradiation with UV wavelengths between 280 and 360 nm, the normal isomers of 6,4-photoproducts can be converted to their Dewar valence isomers, which are less mutagenic than the normal isomers but may still contribute to solar mutagenesis 28 . Although eightfold fewer in number than CPDs, 6,4-photoproducts can activate the ATR-CHK1 DNA damage response pathway and may be the major trigger for UV-induced DNA damage responses 29 . A few other rare DNA photoproducts have been described, such as complex purine lesions and pyrimidine hydrates, but their physiologic significance in cutaneous photobiology is unknown. The absorption maximum of DNA is at 260 nm. This makes UVC the most effective wavelength for the induction of DNA photoproducts in naked DNA. However, in vivo , due to the absorption of shorter wavelengths in upper layers of the epidermis, 300 nm (UVB) is the most effective wavelength for inducing DNA photoproducts in the basal layer of the epidermis ( Fig. 86.10 ) 30 . It is now well recognized that when solar-available doses are compared, UVA can also generate pyrimidine dimers, albeit at a lower frequency than UVB 31 . While formation of UVB-induced pyrimidine dimers results from the direct absorption of photons by bases of DNA, UV irradiation can also damage DNA indirectly. After absorption of photons by chromophores other than DNA, energy can be transferred either to DNA (type I photo- sensitized reaction) or to molecular oxygen, with reactive oxygen species in turn being able to damage DNA (type II photosensitized reaction). Many of the biologic properties of UVA, including its toxicity to cells, are dependent upon the presence of molecular oxygen, which points to a prominent role for reactive oxygen species. Question: What are 'dark CPDs' and how does their formation differ mechanistically and temporally from typical UV-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers?

'Dark CPDs' are cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers formed through photoexcitation of melanin and generation of peroxynitrite, a mechanism that occurs only in melanin-containing cells. Because the reactive molecules involved have a long half-life, this pathway continues to add to CPD formation for hours after the UV irradiation has ended, unlike the direct photon absorption mechanism that produces typical CPDs immediately upon UV exposure. Question: Explain the historical confusion regarding the eponyms 'Unna–Thost' and 'Vörner' types of palmoplantar keratoderma, and how this confusion was ultimately resolved.

Although the term 'Unna–Thost type' was traditionally used for non-epidermolytic PPK (NEPPK) and 'Vörner type' for epidermolytic PPK (EPPK), a 1992 review by Küster et al. of Thost's original family found histologic evidence of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, the hallmark of the Vörner type. This was later confirmed when keratin mutations identified in EPPK were also found in descendants of Thost's original family, showing that Thost had actually described EPPK, not NEPPK. This underscores the need for careful histologic examination, sometimes requiring multiple biopsies, to correctly identify epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. Question: In Giroux–Barbeau syndrome (erythrokeratodermia with spinocerebellar ataxia, a variant of spinocerebellar ataxia-34), what gene is implicated, what are the characteristic infantile skin findings, and what neurologic features develop later in life?

Giroux–Barbeau syndrome is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in ELOVL4 (an elongase involved in very long-chain fatty acid/ceramide synthesis). In infancy, patients develop migratory erythematous patches and/or erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaques with fine, white, adherent scale over the knees, ankles, elbows, and wrists, which tend to diminish or disappear in adulthood. During the 4th–5th decades of life, progressive neurologic symptoms emerge, including nystagmus, ataxia, dysarthria, and hyporeflexia. Previously, polymy- ositis was thought to represent the same disease process but limited to the muscles; however, there is robust evidence that the pathogenetic mechanisms of polymyositis and dermatomyositis differ significantly. In polymyositis, clonally expanded, autoreactive CD8 + T cells invade myocytes expressing MHC class I antigens and cause necrosis via the perforin pathway. In contrast, there are data to support the theory that autoantigens activate a humoral immune process in dermatomyo- sitis, in which complement is deposited in capillaries causing capillary necrosis and ischemia 1 . Because an appreciation of these pathogenetic differences occurred relatively recently, previous studies often pooled cases of dermatomyositis and polymyositis, making interpretation of their data challenging. Dermatomyositis is characterized by a bimodal age distribution, with both adult and juvenile forms, and up to one-quarter of patients in the adult group having an associated malignancy. Patients with juvenile dermatomyositis do not have an increased risk of malignancy, but do have an increased incidence of calcinosis cutis and associated small vessel vasculitis. There is a subset of patients in whom the cutaneous manifestations of dermatomyositis exist without objective evidence of muscle inflammation, referred to as amyopathic dermatomyositis, and formerly known as dermatomyositis sine myositis. For dermatologists, establishing the diagnosis of dermatomyositis is important because it is a serious, treatable, multisystem disease that has a different prognosis - nancy association in adults provides the dermatologist with an oppor- tunity to assist medical colleagues in detecting the tumor at an early stage because the skin disease often precedes the onset of symptoms related to the malignancy. Question: Compare type 1 (reversal reaction) and type 2 (erythema nodosum leprosum) leprosy reactional states in terms of immune mechanism, leprosy category affected, and first-line treatment.

Type 1 reversal reaction is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction with a Th1 cytokine pattern, occurring in borderline (BT, BB, BL) leprosy or tuberculoid disease undergoing immunologic upgrading, and is treated with prednisone (40 mg/day, tapered over 12-36 weeks). Type 2 erythema nodosum leprosum results from excessive humoral immunity with a Th2 pattern and immune complex formation (sometimes with increased cell-mediated immunity and neutrophils), occurring in lepromatous and BL>BB leprosy, especially with high bacterial index; severe disease is treated with thalidomide (400 mg/day, tapered to lowest effective dose). Question: In postinfectious purpura fulminans occurring after group A streptococcal infection or varicella-zoster, approximately how many days after the initial infection does the condition develop, what antibody-mediated mechanism drives thrombosis, and what are the therapeutic options given the lack of a commercial protein S concentrate?

Postinfectious purpura fulminans develops about 7–10 days after the onset of the initial infection, coinciding with production of infection-triggered antibodies that inhibit protein S function. Because protein S is a key cofactor for tissue factor pathway inhibitor (which normally suppresses tissue factor:factor VIIa-triggered coagulation), reduced protein S activity enhances thrombosis. Since no commercial protein S concentrate exists and antibody-mediated inhibition is hard to overcome, treatment options include plasma exchange, plasmapheresis, or plasma replacement combined with corticosteroids, low-molecular-weight heparin, and sometimes IVIg. In women pregnant with an affected fetus, steroid sulfatase deficiency in the fetal placenta causes low or absent levels of estrogen in the urine and amniotic fluid because of inadequate deconjugation of DHEAS, which is necessary for estrogen synthesis. However, one rare exception is the offspring of an affected male and a female carrier. The inheritance risk for the offspring depends on the parent trans- mitting the disease allele. An affected father will transmit his mutated X chromosome (but not the complete disease) to all his daughters, but to none of his sons. Thus, his daughters become obligate carriers and will transmit the mutated allele to 50% of their children. As a result, the sons and daughters of a carrier mother will have a 50% chance of being affected or carriers, respectively. Examples of recessive X-linked diseases in dermatology include hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia and X-linked recessive ichthyosis (steroid sulfatase [STS] deficiency; see Ch. 57 ). Because the STS gene is located on a region of the X chromosome that partially escapes inacti- vation, female carriers do not show any features of the disorder. Unless male-lethal, these disorders occur in both males and females. However, because females are heterozygous rather than hemizygous, they generally have a milder and/or mosaic phenotype (see below). There is no male-to-male transmission, and the trait appears in successive generations ( Fig. 54.1D ). The risk of the offspring inher- iting the disease depends on the transmitting parent. Question: Why are patients with crusted scabies highly contagious, and what factors contribute to this compared to typical scabies infestations?

In crusted scabies, patients may harbor thousands of mites on their skin, compared to fewer than 100 (often only 10–15) in typical scabies infestations. Additionally, mites shed from crusted scabies patients can survive up to 7 days off the host by feeding on sloughed skin (versus 3 days or fewer for typical scabies mites), and live mites can be recovered from bedding, floors, curtains, and chairs in the patient's environment. This high mite burden and prolonged environmental survival make crusted scabies patients highly contagious. [Chapter: 84 Infestations, p.1837]

Question: Who developed tumescent local anesthesia for liposuction, and what maximum lidocaine dosage did he demonstrate could be safely used with this technique?

Tumescent local anesthesia for liposuction was developed by dermatologist Dr. Jeffrey Klein, who published his technique in 1987 using a dilute solution of lidocaine with epinephrine infiltrated into fat. He demonstrated that because dilute lidocaine-epinephrine solutions are not absorbed into the circulation to the same degree as higher 1%–2% concentrations, lidocaine dosages of up to 35 mg/kg body weight could be used safely. Question: How can patch-stage Kaposi sarcoma be histologically distinguished from the acquired pericytic vascular lesions described in this excerpt?

Kaposi sarcoma is distinguished by the presence of delicate, lymphatic-like vessels rather than the more robust, less angulated vessels seen in the pericytic lesions (which often contain red blood cells and an obvious pericytic component on H&E). Kaposi sarcoma also shows plasma cells, eosinophilic globules, and interstitial fascicles of spindle cells, and it stains positive for HHV-8. A specific example given of irritant contact dermatitis mimicking an immersion burn is laxative-induced irritant contact dermatitis, with chemical burns also resulting from topical application of garlic or apple cider vinegar. acquired, subepidermal bullous disease associated with autoimmunity to type VII collagen, the major component of the anchoring fibrils of the dermal– epidermal BMZ  Patients may present either with a mechanobullous disorder, mimicking dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, or with clinical features that resemble BP or infrequently MMP, the Brunsting–Perry variant of MMP, or LABD  Diagnosis relies on immunopathologic examinations, especially immunofluorescence microscopy, immunoserologic studies, and occasionally immunoelectron microscopy  The disease is usually chronic and more refractory to treatment than BP Introduction Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is a rare, acquired, subepidermal bullous disease associated with autoimmunity to type VII collagen, the major component of the anchoring fibrils of the dermal–epidermal BMZ 74–77 . Patients may present with either a non-inflammatory vari- ant, the features of which strikingly resemble those observed in patients with dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (EB), or with an inflammatory variant that mimics BP. Infrequently, the clinical phenotype resembles MMP, the Brunsting–Perry variant of MMP, or LABD. History The first cases of an acquired bullous disease with clinical features mimicking hereditary dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa were described by Elliot in 1895. In the early 1970s, before the advent of cutaneous immunopathology, Roenigk and colleagues proposed the initial clinical criteria for EBA. A few years later, IF microscopy studies demonstrated that EBA patients have anti-BMZ antibodies, similar to BP patients. In the early 1980s, immunoelectron microscopy studies separated EBA from BP by demonstrating that IgG deposits in EBA were located in the sublamina densa region of the BMZ. In the 1990s it was shown that EBA autoantibodies bind to type VII collagen, the major component of anchoring fibrils 75 . Epidemiology EBA has been reported in both children and adults and may occur at any age. It is one of the rarest subepidermal autoimmune bullous diseases in Western Europe, with an estimated annual incidence of ~0.25 per million people 49,77 . It may be more common in specific Asian popula- tions (e.g. Koreans) as well as in African-Americans. Pathogenesis The pathogenic role of autoantibodies to type VII collagen is sup- ported by several lines of evidence 76 . Patients with EBA have tissue- bound and circulating IgG autoantibodies against type VII collagen, the major component of anchoring fibrils (see Fig. 28.3A ). Question: In epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA), how does the level of dermal-epidermal cleavage seen on electron microscopy, and the light microscopic inflammatory infiltrate, differ between the inflammatory (BP-like/MMP-like) and non-inflammatory mechanobullous variants, and why is cleavage level not always reliable for diagnosis?

By light microscopy, BP-like or MMP-like EBA shows a variable dermal inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils, eosinophils, and lymphocytes, whereas mechanobullous non-inflammatory lesions show minimal-to-absent cellular infiltrate. Electron microscopy typically shows cleavage within the sublamina densa zone with reduced anchoring fibrils, but in some cases separation occurs within the lamina lucida due to blister formation at a locus minoris resistentiae. Because of this variability, the level of cleavage is not always a reliable criterion for distinguishing EBA from other subepidermal bullous disorders. [Chapter: 30 Pemphigoid Group, p.668]

Pathogenesis Immunohistochemical and ultrastructural studies have firmly estab- lished the endothelial nature of KS, but it remains controversial whether this endothelial phenotype is vascular, lymphatic, or perhaps a composite of both. Moreover, many, if not most cells forming the substance of a plaque or nodule of KS are spindled cells distinctly unlike normal endothelial cells in morphology, although expressing pan-endothelial markers like CD31. These spindled cells also coexpress markers of blood vascular differentiation (CD34) and lymphatic differ- entiation (VEGFR-3 102,115 , podoplanin 116 , LYVE-1 117 ). A seminal discovery was that, in vitro , Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (taxonomical name HHV-8) can infect both lymphatic and blood vascular endothelial cells and induce transcriptional reprogramming, leading to expression of lymphangiogenic molecules in infected blood vascular endothelial cells 118 and a more blood vascular profile in infected lymphatic endothelial cells 119 . Question: How does infection of endothelial cells by HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus) help explain the mixed lymphatic/blood vascular immunophenotype observed in Kaposi sarcoma spindle cells?

In vitro studies show that HHV-8 can infect both lymphatic and blood vascular endothelial cells and induce transcriptional reprogramming: infected blood vascular endothelial cells begin expressing lymphangiogenic molecules, while infected lymphatic endothelial cells acquire a more blood vascular profile. Question: In dermatomyositis, why is the triceps muscle often preferred over the deltoid as a biopsy site, and how does the initial severity of CK/aldolase elevation influence the corticosteroid treatment approach?

The triceps is a higher-yield biopsy site because the deltoid muscle is often relatively spared until late in the disease. If CK and aldolase are only minimally elevated and corticosteroids are started early, the disease typically comes under control within 2-4 weeks, allowing a taper to half the starting dose by 6 months. If the disease is advanced with high enzyme levels (e.g., CK >1000 U/L), it is harder to control and often requires intravenous pulse corticosteroids plus early addition of a steroid-sparing agent such as low-dose weekly methotrexate, with a slower taper toward 0.5 mg/kg/day by 6-8 months. Renewed eradication efforts against yaws began in 2012, and in 2016 India was the first country to be declared free of yaws by the WHO. However, the emergence of azithromycin-resistant yaws in Papua New Guinea threatens eradication efforts 133 . Pinta Pinta affects the skin exclusively and is caused by an infection with T. carateum . The disease is found only in the western hemisphere (Central and South America) in semiarid, warm climates. All ages are equally affected. The primary lesions occur 7 days to 2 months after inoculation, most often on the lower extremities. They begin as tiny macules or papules surrounded by an erythematous halo. Over a period of months, they develop into poorly defined, erythematous, infiltrated plaques that measure 10–12 cm in diameter. Secondary lesions (“pintids”) start as small, scaly papules, subsequently enlarging and coalescing into psoriasiform plaques. They are initially red but later become slate-blue, brown, gray, and black. The primary and secondary lesions are highly infectious. Tertiary pinta is characterized by symmetric depigmented, vitiligo-like lesions, which may be atrophic or hyperkeratotic and are not considered to be infectious. Biopsy specimens of primary and secondary lesions reveal moderate acanthosis, slight spongiosis, and a superficial dermal inflammatory infiltrate consisting of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils around dilated blood vessels. Some lesions show lichenoid changes, with hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, and vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer. The depigmented lesions of late pinta have epidermal atrophy and a complete absence of melanin. Except for longstanding, late depigmented lesions, treponemes can be visualized in biopsy specimens with silver stains. Question: Why can growing fungal specimens only on cycloheximide-containing media be problematic, and which types of dermatophyte infections typically require systemic rather than topical antifungal therapy?

Cycloheximide-containing media can miss clinically relevant non-dermatophyte fungi that are inhibited by cycloheximide, such as Scopulariopsis brevicaulis, Aspergillus spp., Cryptococcus neoformans, Candida tropicalis, Pseudallescheria boydii/Scedosporium apiospermum, and Trichosporon spp., particularly in nail specimens. Question: Since laminin 332 lacks the γ-domain required for nidogen binding, how is it stably anchored within the basement membrane?

Laminin 332 is stably bound to the basement membrane through a covalent association with the branch points of the short arms of laminin 311, rather than through nidogen binding. This allows it to be incorporated into the lamina densa network despite lacking the nidogen-binding γ-domain present in other laminin isoforms. Question: Regarding idiopathic atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini, describe its typical epidemiologic profile (sex ratio, age of onset) and the characteristic distribution and appearance of its skin lesions.

Idiopathic atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini is more common in women than men (6:1 ratio in adults) and usually begins insidiously in young individuals during the second or third decade of life, though cases in children under 13 and rare congenital cases have been reported. Lesions typically occur on the trunk—especially the back and lumbosacral region, followed by the chest, arms, and abdomen—while the face, hands, and feet are usually spared; distribution is often symmetric and bilateral (though a linear Blaschko-line pattern can occur). The lesions are single or multiple, round or ovoid, asymptomatic, non-inflammatory, and usually brown in color, sometimes coalescing into large irregular patches. Question: For a patient with primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma (PCMZLD) presenting as a solitary well-circumscribed lesion, what is considered the treatment of choice, and how do relapse rates compare to more time-intensive modalities like local radiotherapy?

For solitary well-circumscribed PCMZLD lesions, surgical excision with narrow margins (about 3–5 cm depending on lesion size) is considered the treatment of choice. In a series of 62 patients, their ages ranged from 6 to 72 years (median, 32 years) 18 . Lymphedema results from inadequate drainage of lymph due to hypoplasia, aplasia, or disruption of lymphatic channels. Lymphedema is divided into primary forms due to abnormal lymphatic development and secondary forms due to acquired disruption of lymphatic drainage (see Ch. 105 ). In contrast, LMs are due to hyper- plasia of the lymphatic network. This hyperplasia most commonly results in cysts, including smaller microcystic and/or larger macrocystic lesions; these cysts can develop within the skin, mucous membranes, muscles, bone, or occasionally viscera 1 . Somatic activating mutations in PIK3CA underlie most common LMs 38 . CCLAs affecting structures such as the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct result in lymphatic leakage that leads to pleural or pericardial effusions and ascites. Affected individuals are at risk for bacterial infec- tions and septicemia. Question: Why was 'hobnail hemangioma' reclassified as targetoid hemosiderotic lymphatic malformation (THLM), and what pathogenic mechanism has been proposed to explain the erythrocytes and hemosiderin seen within lesional lymphatic vessels?

The lesion was reclassified because its endothelial cells stain positively for lymphatic differentiation markers, are generally negative for WT-1, and show a low Ki-67 proliferation index, indicating it is not intrinsically proliferative; per ISSVA guidelines, the suffix 'angioma' is reserved for proliferative vascular tumors, so it was designated a malformation instead. Trauma is thought to stimulate lesion appearance by creating microshunts between small lesional blood vessels and adjacent lymphatic vessels, allowing erythrocytes to enter lymphatic channels and accounting for the hemosiderin deposits.
